docs.title: Gripora
docs.text:
Gripora is open-source stability-control firmware for RC cars -- a gyro controller that keeps the car pointed where you steer it -- along with the Gripora Configurator used to set it up.

What it does today:

  • Steering stabilization. A turn-rate (yaw-rate) gyro loop on the steering servo holds the car on the line you steer and catches slides. It corrects the right way in reverse and fades out near a standstill (Drive State), and can be switched off from the transmitter (GYRO OFF). For drifting, the DRIFT mode gives you the wheel angle directly and keeps the gyro only to catch over-rotation.
  • Drive aids. Timed ABS, traction control and launch control shape the brake and throttle you give, per PID profile (Drive Aids).
  • A car setup out of the box. Steering on S1, a reversible ESC on M1, optional rear steering and a second ESC, and the car radio channel order (Car Mixer and Channels).

Launch control and sensor-based aids are planned.

Gripora builds on the work of WingFlight, a fixed-wing flight controller, which is itself a fork of Rotorflight, which in turn derives from Betaflight. It keeps their MSP protocol, CLI, and configuration philosophy; the aircraft features have been removed.

Early-stage project

Gripora is under active development. Firmware is currently distributed as numbered snapshots (0.0.x) rather than stable releases, and both the firmware and this documentation are evolving quickly. Some screenshots and a few labels in the apps still show the fixed-wing software Gripora was forked from. If something here is wrong or missing, please open an issue or a PR.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
• New to Gripora? Start with Getting Started and Set Up Your Car.
  • Looking for a Configurator tab? See the Configurator section, organized tab by tab.
  • Want to understand what the controller does on the car (reverse, low speed, ABS, traction control, GYRO OFF)? See Driving Modes & Features.
  • Setting up from the radio? See the Ethos Lua Suite or the EdgeTX Lua Scripts.
  • Looking for CLI settings or MSP details? See Reference.
  • Want to build the firmware or configurator yourself, or contribute? See Contributing.

docs.title: Getting help
docs.text: Open an issue on GitHub for setup help, tuning advice, and project discussion.

docs.title: Configurator
docs.text:
This section documents the Gripora Configurator tab by tab, in the order they appear in the menu once connected to the controller.

The tab list adapts to the connection and the firmware: some tabs only appear when the feature behind them is set up. GPS needs a GPS port or protocol, LED Strip the LED strip feature, XACT Servo Programming a port set to FBUS output, and FBUS/S.Port Sensors and CRSF Sensors a port with that function.

New to Gripora? Start with the Setup Wizard, described in Set Up Your Car. Everything it sets can be changed later on the tabs below.

Group Tab Purpose Setup Status Live state of the controller: arming, battery, attitude, receiver Wizard Step-by-step car setup, see Set Up Your Car Configuration Board alignment, sensors, serial ports, features Power Battery voltage and current, battery profiles, SmartFuel Receiver Receiver protocol, channel order, telemetry Failsafe What happens when the radio link is lost Outputs Mixer Model type, car setup, mixer rules, gyro direction Servos Servo center, limits, direction, trim, bus servos Motors ESC protocol, throttle range, ESC telemetry, RPM, the Drive panel Curves Mixer, gain and servo balance curves Tuning Profiles PID profiles: Driving Feel, PID gains, gain attenuation, drive aids Rates Steering rate and expo Gyro Gyro filtering Modes & Logic Modes Modes on transmitter switches Adjustments Change settings live from the transmitter Conditions Logic conditions that gate mixer rules Peripherals GPS GPS module setup and status LED Strip Addressable LED strip Beepers Buzzer events Sensors Raw gyro, accelerometer and other sensor graphs ESC Programming Configure the ESC through the controller Remap FC Change what each pin of the board does XACT Servo Programming Program FrSky XACT bus servos FBUS/S.Port Sensors Sensors on an FBUS or S.Port master line CRSF Sensors A CRSF sensor accessory on its own port Diagnostics Blackbox Data logging Maintenance Calibration, save, reset and reboot CLI Command-line access

docs.title: Adjustments
docs.text:
The Adjustments tab lets a transmitter switch or knob change a setting live, without reconnecting the Configurator: a gain knob, steering trim buttons, or a profile switch, so you can try values while driving.

The functions on offer are the ones that matter on a car (the roll and pitch versions are hidden):

Group Functions Profile Selection Battery Profile, LED Profile, Profile Selection (PID profile), Rate Profile Selection Rates, RC Rates, RC Expo Steering Rate, Steering RC Rate, Steering RC Expo PID Gains Steering P, I, D, F and B gain Filters Steering Gyro Cutoff, Steering D-term Cutoff Steering Dynamics Steering Dynamic Ceiling Gain, Dynamic Deadband Gain, Dynamic Deadband Filter Driving Feel Master Gain Steering, I-Term Decay Steering, I-Term Relax Steering (see Profiles) Servo Trims Servo Trim Steering (see Servos) Setpoint Boost Steering Setpoint Boost Gain

A function under live adjustment shows its value on the tab that owns it while the switch or knob is in control.

PID and rate profile switching is a special case: each is its own function, mapped to a channel like any other, but a profile switch applies, and is confirmed with its own beep count, at once. The drive aids belong to the PID profile, so switching PID profile switches them too.

Adjustments aren't saved by themselves: they are for trying values while driving. If a value you found is worth keeping, set it on its tab (for example Profiles) and save it there. Stepped servo trims are the exception; see below.

The Setup Wizard's Trim and gain step sets up a steering trim and a gain knob for you (Master Gain Steering on a knob, 0% fully down, 75% at center, 150% fully up). See Set Up Your Car.

docs.title: Channel names
docs.text: Every channel picker in the Configurator (here, on Mixer, Conditions and Modes) uses one naming scheme: CH #N, where N is the receiver channel number, with its role where it has one. In the car channel order AUX 1-4 are CH #3-6.

docs.title: Enable Channel and Value Channel
docs.text:
Each adjustment slot has two channels:

  • Enable Channel gates whether the slot is active at all -- it only takes effect while this channel's value falls within the range you set (or set it to ALWAYS to skip gating entirely and let Value Channel control it unconditionally).
  • Value Channel is read once the slot is enabled, and drives the function according to whichever mode you pick below. Its AUTO option reuses the Enable Channel itself as the value source, for the common case of one switch/knob doing both jobs.

docs.title: Mapped vs. Stepped
docs.text:
• Mapped continuously maps the Value Channel's position across its range straight onto the function's Min/Max -- a knob or 3-position switch gives you a proportional live value, the same idea as a transmitter-side gain knob but applied on the controller side.
  • Stepped instead treats the Value Channel like a momentary increase/decrease button: entering one sub-range nudges the value up by Step each time, the other sub-range nudges it down -- useful for a 2-position switch you flick repeatedly to walk a value up or down without needing a channel that can hold a precise proportional position.

Mapped ignores small movements of the Value Channel -- anything within about 3 µs of the position it last acted on -- so a pot that isn't perfectly still (receiver or ADC noise, or resting right on a value boundary) doesn't flip the value up and down by one step every loop, which would otherwise cause a config write, a beep and a blackbox event each time and make PID values wander. Deliberate, slow movement still gets through, because the reference only moves once that small window is exceeded. Stepped is not affected.

For Servo Trims the two modes differ in more than how you drive them: Stepped changes the servo's saved trim, one step per press, while Mapped sets a live trim that is never saved. Neither changes the servo's Mid, and both together are limited to 20% of the servo's Scale.

docs.title: Modes
docs.text:
The Modes tab puts modes on transmitter switches: which switch position arms the car, turns the gyro off, turns the drive aids off, and so on.

Each mode card shows the live channel position (a marker on the slider), so you can check a switch lands inside the range you set without driving to find out. Add mode opens a searchable list of the modes, in groups.

docs.title: The modes
docs.text:
Group Mode What it does Arming & Safety ARM Arms the motor and servos. Required. The car only arms with the throttle at neutral, and arming can be blocked by other conditions; see Status. PREARM A safety switch that must be on before you can arm. FAILSAFE Triggers failsafe from a switch, for bench tests or as a panic switch; see Failsafe. Gyro GYRO OFF Turns the gyro off: the steering wheel goes straight to the steering servo, with no gyro correction. See GYRO OFF. DRIVE AIDS OFF Turns ABS, traction control and launch control off: the throttle and brake go to the ESC as you give them. The gyro still steers. See Drive Aids. LAUNCH Stages a launch for launch control: turn it on at the line, and the first forward throttle launches. See Launch control. DRIFT For drifting: the steering wheel goes straight to the steering servo, and the gyro only counter-steers turn rate beyond the allowed rate. Set it up on the Profiles tab. GYRO OFF and failsafe win over it. See DRIFT. GPS GPS BEEP SATELLITE COUNT Beeps the number of GPS satellites in view. Only with a GPS running. Beeper & Lights BEEPER Sounds the buzzer, to find the car. BEEPER MUTE Silences the beeper. LEDLOW Turns the LED strip off. Only with the LED strip feature on. Logging & Telemetry BLACKBOX Starts and stops Blackbox logging when logging is switch-controlled. BLACKBOX ERASE Erases the onboard Blackbox flash while held on. Only on boards with flash. TELEMETRY Turns telemetry on for a port shared with another function. Only with the telemetry feature on. Camera CAMERA CONTROL 1-3 RunCam camera control. Only on builds with it. User Outputs USER1-4 Switch a PINIO output (a pin set up for it). Only shown when a PINIO output is linked to it.

BEEPER, BEEPER MUTE, BLACKBOX, BLACKBOX ERASE, FAILSAFE, GPS BEEP SATELLITE COUNT and PREARM only show in Expert Mode.

Modes that Gripora removed (ANGLE, TRAINER, ATT HOLD, GPS RTH and LOITER, MANUAL, AUTO TRIM, THRUST VECTOR, TRADITIONAL, GOVERNOR and others) no longer appear. Their mode ids are kept free, so the ids of the remaining modes didn't change and existing switch assignments still work.

docs.title: Ranges and Links
docs.text:
A mode turns on from one of two kinds of assignment, and one mode can have several of either:

  • A Range watches one receiver channel: the mode is on whenever that channel's value is between the Min and Max you set. A 3-position switch can carry two modes this way.
  • A Link turns a mode on whenever a different mode is on, to bundle modes together without a spare switch. ARM can't be linked to or from, and a mode that is itself defined by a link can't be linked to (no chains).

When a mode has more than one Range or Link, each one past the first gets an AND/OR setting: the mode is on when all of its AND conditions are true, or when at least one OR condition is true.

A switch does nothing until a mix on the radio puts it on a channel. The Setup Wizard's Mode switches step puts ARM, GYRO OFF, DRIVE AIDS OFF, LAUNCH and DRIFT on switches with you and shows how to set up the radio; see Set Up Your Car.

Changes here take effect when you Save.

docs.title: Beepers
docs.text:
The Beepers tab configures which events (arming, low battery, failsafe, receiver loss and so on) sound the controller's buzzer, as a warning while driving and to find a car that stopped out of sight. The BEEPER mode sounds it from a switch.

The buzzer hardware, wiring and the beeper sequences are described in Buzzer.

docs.title: Blackbox
docs.text: The Blackbox tab configures data logging: which fields are recorded, the logging rate, and (if fitted) the onboard flash or SD card. Blackbox logs are the main tool for diagnosing tuning problems after a run, and the first thing to attach when asking for tuning help.

docs.title: When it logs
docs.text: Device picks where logs go: onboard flash, an SD card, or an external serial logger (each only appears if fitted or supported). Mode then decides when logging is active: Armed (simplest: logs every run), Normal (logs only when armed and a BLACKBOX switch is on, to keep only the runs you choose), or Switch (logs whenever that switch is on, armed or not). Grace Period keeps logging briefly after disarming, specifically to catch the moments right after a crash rather than cutting off exactly at disarm.

docs.title: Rate and fields
docs.text:
Rate of Logging is a divisor of the PID loop rate -- higher rates capture more detail (useful for chasing a specific fast oscillation) at the cost of filling storage faster; lower rates log longer runs in the same space. The field checkboxes choose which data categories are recorded at all -- turn off what you don't need to save space, but when in doubt for a tuning question, leave gyro, PID and setpoint data on, since that's what most tuning advice is read from. The throttle (rcCommand[4]) is signed: positive forward, negative brake and reverse.

Debug Mode adds a further 8 extra values on top of the normal fields, for a specific diagnostic (its exact meaning depends on which mode is selected) -- leave it on NONE unless you're chasing something specific that calls for it. Two are specific to Gripora's car features: DRIVE (the drive state: throttle, ESC state, direction, speed and gyro correction scale) and DRIVE_AIDS (the drive aids: throttle in and out, ABS and traction control). GAIN_ATTEN shows the throttle and speed gain attenuation. Modes that no longer record anything are named UNUSED_<n> and are left out of the list; see the CLI Command Reference.

docs.title: Flash storage
docs.text: Initial Erase guarantees a minimum amount of free space before recording starts, erasing old logs if needed -- note that erasing can take a while on some flash chips, so recording doesn't begin until it finishes. Rolling Erase instead overwrites the oldest logs once storage is full, trading guaranteed history for never running out of space -- logs can gain gaps if the chip is slow to erase mid-run.

docs.title: Reading mode changes in logs
docs.text:
Each log frame records which modes are active in two words, flightModeFlags and flightModeFlags2, together covering every mode. A tool that only reads flightModeFlags misses the modes past the 32nd. The separate mode change event carries only the first word.

The log header records the drive aids settings of the profile in use (drive_abs, drive_tc, drive_lc) and its DRIFT settings (drift: gain, allowed turn rate, limit).

docs.title: Log files over USB
docs.text: When the controller is plugged in as a USB drive (mass storage), log files are named after the car name (Configuration tab), followed by a sequence number and timestamp. With no car name set, the prefix is grpa (it was wflt in WingFlight and rtfl in Rotorflight), for example grpa_002_20251012_141213.bbl.

docs.title: Reviewing logs
docs.text:
Open a .bbl file in the Gripora Blackbox viewer to play the run back. The Car button shows a 3D car that follows the logged attitude (heading, pitch and roll); its position and size on the screen are set under Car Settings. Each graph stacks related fields, such as the steering setpoint against the turn rate from the gyro, then the servo and motor outputs, with the legend showing every field's value at the cursor. The strip along the bottom shows the whole log so you can jump to any part of the run. Graph setup chooses which fields each graph shows.

The Overlay buttons add analysis views on top of the graphs. The spectrum analyser plots the frequency content of a field over the visible window, with the gyro filter cutoffs marked, to find the frequency of a vibration before changing filter settings. The step response graph shows how quickly and cleanly the gyro follows a change in setpoint; a trace that overshoots well past 1.0 or keeps ringing points to gains that are too high.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
The CLI tab gives direct, text-based access to the controller's command-line interface -- the same interface documented in the CLI Command Reference.

The CLI works independently of the normal MSP-based configuration protocol, which makes it the fallback the Configurator switches to automatically when it can't fully validate a connected firmware version (see First Connection). It's also the most reliable way to take a full backup (dump all) or a compact changed-settings backup (diff all).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The Configuration tab covers system-level setup that doesn't belong to a more specific tab: board and sensor alignment, loop rates, sensors, the ready-to-arm wiggle, features and the serial ports.

Get the board alignment right early. If the controller isn't mounted flat and facing forward in the car, the alignment here corrects for it, so the gyro's yaw axis is the car's vertical axis and the steering correction works on the right axis.

docs.title: Board Alignment
docs.text: Board Alignment is the coarse correction for how the controller is physically mounted, typically in 90° steps (sideways, upside down, rotated). Rather than working out the rotation by hand, Auto-Align FC detects it for you: place the car flat and disarmed, press Start, then briefly lift the rear by at least 20° within 15 seconds. The wizard reads the accelerometer movement and reports the detected roll, pitch and yaw. It needs a calibrated accelerometer and only runs while disarmed.

docs.title: Mounting Trim
docs.text:
Mounting Trim is a separate, fine correction (in degrees) for a mounting surface that isn't perfectly level, applied after Board Alignment rather than by changing it. Keep the two apart: Board Alignment's roll, pitch and yaw are applied in a fixed order, so once a 90° correction is on one axis, a small correction entered as more board alignment can end up on the wrong axis. Mounting Trim always corrects the intended physical axis, whatever the board alignment.

Roll and pitch mounting trim can be detected automatically: place the car level and disarmed, press Auto-Detect Trim and don't touch it. Yaw can't be measured from a resting accelerometer and stays manual. If the remaining tilt is over 30°, Board Alignment itself is usually wrong; run Auto-Align FC first, then try again.

Mounting Trim rotates the gyro as well as the accelerometer, so use it to square the board up with the car, not to make the attitude display read level on a sloping bench.

docs.title: System configuration
docs.text:
• Gyro update frequency and PID loop frequency set how fast the gyro is read and the steering loop runs. The real-time load should stay under 70% at the loop rate you choose.
  • Accelerometer, Barometer and Magnetometer turn those sensors on or off. The accelerometer is used for the board orientation and level. Altitude and compass heading are not used by the control loops; they are only reported, for example in telemetry.
  • Ready-to-arm steering wiggle moves the steering briefly when the car becomes ready to arm, as a visual confirmation. See Ready-to-Arm Wiggle.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: Car name names the car. It shows in the Configurator, in telemetry, and as the prefix of Blackbox log files.

docs.title: Features
docs.text: Optional features of the firmware. If a feature is off again after Save and Reboot, this controller or build doesn't support it.

docs.title: Serial Ports
docs.text:
Each serial port (UART) gets a function and a speed, for example Receiver: Primary, Receiver: Backup 1 / Backup 2, ESC: Telemetry, ESC: SRXL2, GPS, Bus: S.BUS Output, Bus: F.BUS Master, Bus: S.PORT Master, Bus: CRSF Sensors, a telemetry protocol, Blackbox Logging or MSP. Changes need Save and Reboot.

The CLI command serialdebug helps when a device on a port isn't working; see the CLI Command Reference.

docs.title: CRSF Sensors
docs.text: CRSF Sensors is a dedicated listener for a CRSF-protocol sensor accessory (GPS, battery, barometer, per-cell voltage, or RPM module) wired to its own spare UART -- separate from the receiver link itself. It's for accessories that speak CRSF telemetry frames independently, not for reading data off your main RX link, and it's unrelated to Backup RX Input's own CRSF option, which is about failing over the control link, not reading a sensor.

docs.title: Setting it up
docs.text:
1. Wire the sensor's data line to a spare UART, then assign that port the Bus: CRSF Sensors function from the port function dropdown on the Configuration tab's serial ports list. The port runs at CRSF's fixed baud rate -- there's nothing to pick.
  2. If the sensor doesn't show data once wired, try flipping set crsf_sensors_pinswap = OFF (it defaults on, since real-world CRSF sensor accessories commonly wire up the opposite way round from this port's natural, un-swapped pin) -- then save and reboot.
  3. Open the CRSF Sensors tab (Diagnostics group) to confirm it's actually receiving before wiring anything downstream to it -- see The diagnostic page below.

docs.title: What it feeds, and how to enable it
docs.text:
Nothing downstream is enabled automatically just by wiring the sensor up -- each consumer needs its own source set explicitly:

  • GPS -- set GPS Protocol to CRSF on the GPS tab. With a CRSF Sensors port that is all GPS needs. Position, ground speed, heading, and satellite count come from the sensor's GPS frames.
  • Battery voltage/current -- set Voltage Meter Type and/or Current Meter Type to CRSF Sensor on the Power tab. See Battery source below for which frame type actually feeds the voltage reading when a sensor sends more than one kind.
  • Barometer altitude -- set crsf_sensors_use_baro = ON (CLI-only, not yet on this tab). This replaces an already-detected physical barometer's altitude reading with the sensor's each cycle -- it doesn't create a virtual barometer if no physical baro chip is fitted on the board at all.
  • RPM -- set crsf_sensors_use_rpm = ON (CLI-only). See RPM below -- this one comes with a real caveat, read it before wiring anything to it.

docs.title: RPM
docs.text:
crsf_sensors_use_rpm = ON is a direct override, the same shape as crsf_sensors_use_baro: each motor's normal RPM value (whatever it would otherwise be -- DShot telemetry, a frequency sensor, none) is replaced with the sensor's decoded reading for that index, feeding straight into motor1Speed/motor2Speed (Blackbox, this firmware's own outbound CRSF telemetry), the RPM filter and the car's speed from RPM (the drive state and speed attenuation) alike. The override replaces the values only: on its own it doesn't count as an RPM source for the drive state. There's no separate protocol selection involved, and no ESC Telemetry setting on the Motors tab to touch.

Warning

This is telemetry-rate, not motor-rate. It is not a substitute for bidirectional DShot or a dedicated RPM/frequency-pin sensor, and use at your own risk applies if you turn this on with the RPM filter active -- see the Gyro tab's note on the same limitation. Where the motor also has another RPM source, the drive state then takes this RPM as the car's speed, so a slow or stale reading makes the gyro fade in and out late. It's fine for Blackbox or telemetry display, where the update rate doesn't matter.

Only voltage/current has a source-selection setting (crsf_sensors_battery_source, below) -- RPM has nothing else to choose between, since only one CRSF frame type carries it.

docs.title: Battery source
docs.text:
A sensor can report battery data as an aggregate frame (voltage, current, capacity used, and remaining % all together) or as a set of individual cell voltages with no current data -- some sensors only ever send one or the other, and a few devices marketed as separate "current sensor" and "cell voltage sensor" products exist specifically because of that split. crsf_sensors_battery_source (CLI-only) picks which one feeds Voltage Meter Type = CRSF Sensor on the Power tab:

Value Behavior AUTO (default) Prefer the aggregate frame; fall back to summed cell voltages only if the aggregate one isn't present. CURRENT Always use the aggregate frame, no fallback -- named for the field only it has, since the cell-voltage frame carries no current data at all. VOLTAGE Always use summed cell voltages, even if an aggregate frame is also present on the bus.

Current always comes from the aggregate frame regardless of this setting -- there's nowhere else for it to come from.

Note

If an individual cell reads back an implausible value (tens of volts on a single tap -- almost always a bad connector/balance-lead connection on the sensor itself, not a wiring or firmware issue), that one channel is excluded from the pack total rather than corrupting it. The resulting total will read low by roughly that cell's worth until the connection is fixed, rather than showing a dangerously wrong high reading.

docs.title: The diagnostic page
docs.text:
The tab only appears once a port is assigned the CRSF Sensors function, and polls twice a second:

  • Link -- whether the port opened, plus raw byte/sync/CRC counters. Bytes-received-but-zero-sync-frames points at a baud/protocol mismatch on the wire; sync-frames-but-zero-CRC-OK points at signal integrity issues; both at zero with a powered, wired sensor points at the physical connection itself (wrong pin, no shared ground, or genuinely not a CRSF device).
  • GPS / Battery / Barometer / Cell Voltages / RPM -- each shows a Receiving or No data badge and the latest decoded values for whichever frame types the sensor actually sends. A card reading "No data" just means that particular frame type has never arrived -- most sensor accessories only send one or two of the five types this feature understands.

Only five CRSF frame types are decoded: GPS (0x02), RPM (0x0C), the aggregate Battery Sensor (0x08), Altitude/vario (0x09), and per-cell Voltages (0x0E, per the TBS CRSF spec). Anything else on the wire is safely ignored.

docs.title: CLI settings
docs.text:
Setting Default Meaning crsf_sensors_timeout_ms 2000 How long without a fresh frame before that sensor's data is dropped as stale. Range 500-10000. CLI-only. crsf_sensors_use_baro OFF Replace a physical barometer's altitude reading with the sensor's, see above. CLI-only. crsf_sensors_pinswap ON Swap which physical pin this UART uses for RX, see Setting it up. CLI-only. crsf_sensors_battery_source AUTO Which frame type feeds Voltage Meter Type = CRSF Sensor, see Battery source. CLI-only. crsf_sensors_use_rpm OFF Override each motor's RPM with the sensor's reading -- see RPM for the important caveat before using this for filtering or the drive state. CLI-only.

None of these are on the Configurator UI yet -- set them from the CLI, then save.

docs.title: Curves
docs.text: The Curves tab has three categories -- Mixer, Gain and Servo -- selected from the tabs along the top. Mixer and Gain each hold a pool of up to 8 reusable curves. You edit a curve here, then assign it by number wherever it's used -- a Mixer rule, or a Profiles gain -- rather than defining the shape inline there. That reuse is the point: editing curve 3 here updates every rule or axis currently assigned to curve 3, so one curve can shape several things identically at once. Servo balance curves work differently: there is one per physical servo, not a shared pool (see Servo Balance Curves).

docs.title: Mixer Curves
docs.text: X: the mixer rule's input value. Y: the value substituted in its place once weighted onto the output. Both share the rule's own -1000..1000 scale. The default is a straight diagonal -- input passes straight through unchanged -- so there's nothing to assign until you deliberately bend it: more resolution near center, a dead zone, an asymmetric steering throw, a non-linear throttle-to-ESC curve, and so on. A curve on the ESC rule shapes both sides of neutral, forward and brake/reverse. Assign one to a rule from the Mixer tab.

docs.title: Gain Curves
docs.text:
X: steering deflection, 0% (centered) to 100% (full lock); the same curve applies in both directions. Y: a gain multiplier, 0-500%, where 100% means no change. The gain actually used is Master Gain (set in Driving Feel on the Profiles tab, with the curve assigned in the Gain Curves panel) multiplied by this curve's value at the current stick position, so a flat line at 100% has no effect at all. Drag a point below 100 to taper the gain out towards full lock, or above 100 to sharpen it there.

Assigned to the Throttle row, the X axis is throttle (0-100%, forward and brake/reverse alike) instead of steering deflection. Assigned to the Speed row, it is the car's speed, from 0 to the speed curve range set in the Gain Curves panel; see Speed.

docs.title: Servo Balance Curves
docs.text:
When two servos drive the same steering (dual steering servos), small differences in the servos or linkages mean they never track each other perfectly, and they fight each other or bind at full lock. A balance curve trims one servo's travel to match its partner across the whole throw, the same idea as the "Balance channels" tool on FrSky ETHOS.

There is one curve per servo, labeled Servo 1, Servo 2 and so on to match the Servos tab; if none are configured yet, the tab asks you to set up servos first.

X: the servo's own output, -100% to +100%. Y: a small correction added on top of it at that point, -10% to +10%. It is a corrective delta, not a reshape, so the default flat line at 0 adds nothing. The correction is applied after mixing, and after geometry correction if the servo has it enabled.

To balance a pair, pick one servo to leave flat and nudge the other servo's curve up or down at the points where the two disagree -- usually near full deflection. A servo with an active curve shows a curve icon on the Servos tab that jumps straight to its curve.

docs.title: Editing a curve
docs.text:
• Drag a point to move it, click empty plot space to add one, or right-click a point to remove it -- or use the point table alongside the plot for exact numeric values. Mixer and Servo curves allow up to 9 points; Gain curves up to 6.
  • The first and last point are pinned to the curve's domain extremes (-1000/1000 for Mixer, -100%/100% for Servo, 0%/100% for Gain) and can't be deleted or dragged in X, only Y -- they define where the curve starts and ends, so at least two points always exist and always span the full range.
  • Reset Curve returns the currently selected slot to a neutral straight line (no reshaping, no gain change).
  • Compare with overlays a second curve of the same category on the plot without letting you edit it, so you can line one up against another -- typically a paired servo's balance curve while you trim this one. Editing picks the curve you're actually changing.

docs.title: ESC Programming
docs.text:
The ESC Programming tab reads and writes the settings of a supported ESC through the controller: AM32, BLHeli_S and Bluejay, and ESCs from Hobbywing (V5), Scorpion, YGE, OMP, ZTW, XDFly and FlyRotor, over the controller's USB connection, without a separate ESC programming card.

The flow is: pick your ESC's manufacturer/firmware, select which ESC to target if more than one is connected, wait for detection, then edit its parameters directly -- Change ESC at any point restarts this from the beginning if you picked wrong or want to program a different ESC.

Programming an ESC can make the motor turn unexpectedly, so the tab asks you to confirm the wheels are off the ground before it starts. The car must be disarmed throughout; programming is blocked while armed. An ESC with no remote link needs a power cycle after saving for the changes to take effect.

On an AM32 ESC, the reverse setting decides which ESC behaviour the controller needs on the Motors tab: with RC car reverse turned on, set Brake, then reverse.

docs.title: Failsafe
docs.text:
The Failsafe tab sets how the controller detects a lost radio link, what value each channel takes once it has, and what the car does if the link stays down.

Set up and bench-test failsafe before driving: with the wheels off the ground, turn the transmitter off and check that the controller enters failsafe and does what you expect.

Note

If a Backup RX Input is configured, losing the main link doesn't reach any of the stages below on its own: control switches to the backup receiver instead. The staged failsafe on this page only takes over if the main link and every backup link are down.

docs.title: Pulse Width Limit
docs.text: Minimum Pulse Width and Maximum Pulse Width (default 885-2115 µs) set the valid channel range. A channel outside it counts as failed, which feeds the Channel Fallback below and the link-loss detection.

docs.title: Channel Fallback
docs.text:
What each channel does once it is judged failed:

  • Auto sets a safe value: center for the steering, and neutral for the throttle. Auto is only offered for the steering and throttle channels (and the unused roll and pitch slots).
  • Hold keeps the channel at its last good value. This is the default for every channel after the control channels, so an arm or mode switch that was on stays on.
  • Set sets the channel to a value you choose, in µs.

The Configurator's help text says Auto sets the throttle "low". On a car the firmware sets it to neutral (the Channel Center from the Receiver tab), so the ESC neither drives nor brakes.

docs.title: What happens when the link is lost
docs.text:
1. Detects the loss. No valid frame for about 100 ms, a receiver failsafe flag, or a control channel outside the Pulse Width Limit counts as a bad signal. Arming is blocked from here on until the link is back.
  2. Holds for 300 ms. Each channel keeps its last good value.
  3. Applies Channel Fallback (stage 1). After 300 ms each channel takes its fallback value: with the defaults, steering to center and throttle to neutral, aux channels held. The controller keeps steering with the gyro at this point.
  4. Runs the Stage 2 procedure if the link is still down after the guard time.

If the car was armed but the throttle had been at neutral for at least Failsafe Throttle Low Delay when the link was lost, it skips the procedure and disarms at once instead. This catches a car that was left armed on the bench, or a transmitter switched off after the car stopped.

docs.title: Stage 2 - Failsafe Procedure
docs.text:
Once the guard time (Guard time for stage 2 activation, failsafe_delay, 0.1 s units, default 1.5 s) has passed with the link still down:

  • Drop (the default, DROP in the CLI) disarms the car at once, which stops the motor.
  • Stop (AUTO-LAND in the CLI) sends the Failsafe throttle (failsafe_throttle, default 1500 µs = neutral) to the ESC for Delay for turning off the Motors (failsafe_off_delay, 0.1 s units, default 1 s), then disarms.

While a failsafe is active:

  • The throttle is the Failsafe throttle, not the throttle channel's fallback value, and the drive aids don't shape it. Leave it at 1500 (neutral) unless you have a reason not to; a value below neutral brakes (and on some ESCs reverses).
  • GYRO OFF and DRIFT are ignored, so the normal gyro loop steers even if one of those switches was on when the link went.
  • Once the link returns, the controller needs Failsafe Recovery Delay (failsafe_recovery_delay) of good signal before you can arm again.

Older configurations may still hold failsafe_procedure 2 (GPS Rescue), which the Configurator then shows as GPS Rescue. GPS Rescue no longer exists; choose Drop or Stop.

docs.title: Setting up a safe failsafe
docs.text:
The receiver's own failsafe is still your first line of defence. It acts faster (no 100 ms detection) and doesn't depend on the controller:

  1. On your receiver or transmitter, set failsafe to steering centered and throttle at neutral, or to "no pulses" so the controller detects the loss.
  2. Aux channels default to Hold on the controller side. To make a mode switch fall back to a known position, set that channel to Set with the value you want, or in the CLI:
rxfail 4 s 1900

rxfail <channel> <a|h|s> [value], with the channel counted from 0. a is Auto (control channels only), h is Hold and s is Set. 3. Pick the Stage 2 procedure and check the Failsafe throttle is neutral. 4. Test it: wheels off the ground, turn the transmitter off, and check the wheels and the steering for the procedure you use. A receiver that keeps sending normal-looking frames after the link is lost can't be detected by the controller.

docs.title: Failsafe Test Switch
docs.text:
The FAILSAFE mode on the Modes tab triggers failsafe from a switch, to bench-test your settings or as a panic switch. Failsafe Switch Action picks what it does:

  • Stage 1 treats the control channels as invalid, as on a real signal loss: after the 300 ms hold and the guard time it runs the Stage 2 procedure.
  • Stage 2 skips stage 1 and runs the procedure at once.
  • Kill disarms at once.

docs.title: FBUS/S.Port Sensors
docs.text: The FBUS/S.Port Sensors tab is a diagnostic and forwarding-control page for boards acting as an FBUS or S.Port master -- reading telemetry directly from third-party FrSky-ecosystem sensors (GPS, current sensors, RPM sensors, smart servos, and more) wired to a spare UART, rather than talking to a receiver on it. The tab only appears once a serial port is assigned the FBUS_OUT or SPORT_MASTER function on the Configuration tab.

docs.title: Reading sensors: direct use vs. forwarding
docs.text:
Sensors observed on the bus can be put to work two different (non-exclusive) ways:

  • Direct use -- the firmware reads certain sensor types itself and feeds them straight into existing systems. A FrSky current/voltage sensor can become a battery voltage/current source -- set Battery Voltage/Current Source to FrSky Sensor on the Power tab. A FrSky ESC sensor can become an ESC telemetry source (voltage, current, RPM, temperature, consumption) -- set ESC Telemetry Protocol to FrSky F.BUS on the Motors tab (or set esc_sensor_protocol = FBUS from the CLI). Nothing needs enabling on this page for direct use -- it happens automatically as soon as the sensor is observed. !!! warning The RPM this feeds is telemetry-rate, not motor-rate -- use at your own risk for the RPM Filter, which needs bidirectional DShot or a dedicated RPM/frequency-pin sensor to track real motor speed. Nothing in firmware stops you selecting it there anyway. It's fine for Blackbox logging or telemetry display, where the update rate doesn't matter.
  • Forwarding -- relays a sensor's raw telemetry frames back out over the receiver link, so your transmitter/radio displays them directly. This matters most for sensor types the firmware doesn't consume itself (a temperature or vario sensor, for example) -- forwarding is the only way to see those values on the radio. The Forwarded toggle on this page controls it.

docs.title: The sensor table
docs.text:
Each row is a sensor physical ID actually observed talking on the bus, refreshed roughly once a second:

Column Meaning Physical ID The sensor's hardware-defined identity (e.g. GPS, FLVSS, ESC) -- see the Sensor ID Reference for the full list Source Which physical bus it was seen on -- FBUS or S.Port Sensor Name Resolved sensor name, or ID_<n> if the physical ID isn't recognized App IDs The specific data types seen from this sensor (e.g. altitude, speed) -- see the reference page for what the numbers mean Packets Running packet count since the last connect or Clear Forwarded Whether this sensor is currently relayed back to the receiver -- see Forwarding below

Clear resets the observed-sensor table and packet counts -- useful after rewiring, to confirm what's actually present now rather than what was seen earlier in the session. It doesn't affect Forwarding configuration.

docs.title: Forwarding
docs.text:
Toggling Forwarded takes effect immediately -- no reboot needed -- and persists across power cycles. Up to 8 sensors can be forwarded at once; toggling a 9th while all 8 slots are in use is refused, so turn one off first.

The Forwarded toggle is only enabled when the receiver protocol itself is FrSky-family -- F.Port, F.Port2, or FBUS, set on the Receiver tab; otherwise it shows dimmed, and hovering it explains why. It works by relaying frames over that protocol's own telemetry return channel, which other protocols (CRSF and the rest) don't have. Reading sensors as a bus master, and using them directly, both work regardless of receiver protocol -- only forwarding to the radio needs FrSky-family.

Note

FBUS/S.Port master mode and the receiver's own RX protocol are independent: the master feature listens on its own dedicated UART, so it works alongside CRSF, ELRS, or any other receiver protocol. Only forwarding ties back to what the receiver link speaks.

A forwarded sensor shows on the radio under its own physical ID, as if it were plugged into the receiver: run Discover new on the radio's Telemetry page to add it. Its values are sent one after another, so a value the sensor sends often can't crowd out the others. A value the sensor sends only now and then (an RB's battery value, for example) is repeated about once a second, so the radio doesn't report it lost. If the sensor stops sending, the radio sees it go after about a second.

docs.title: Configuring forwarded devices from the radio
docs.text:
With a device on the FBUS master line forwarded, the radio can read and change its settings as if it were plugged into the receiver: FrSky's XAct tool for servos, the RB configuration pages, and other Device config pages on Ethos. Forward the device first: Ethos only offers a device's pages once it has seen the device's telemetry.

This only works on an FBUS master port with an F.Port2 or FBUS receiver, and not while armed.

Note

A device's settings change on the device itself, not in Gripora, so they are not part of a Gripora backup or diff.

docs.title: GPS
docs.text:
The GPS tab configures the GPS module and shows its live status (fix, satellite count, position, speed, a map).

On a car, GPS is optional. Its speed is used by speed attenuation when the motor has no RPM source (with an RPM source the wheel speed is used instead), and its position and speed go to telemetry and the Blackbox. Gripora has no GPS navigation or GPS rescue.

docs.title: When GPS is active
docs.text:
There is no GPS feature switch. GPS runs when the Protocol below matches a port on the Configuration tab:

Protocol Port needed NMEA or UBLOX a port set to GPS FBUS a port set to Bus: F.BUS Master or Bus: S.PORT Master CRSF a port set to Bus: CRSF Sensors MSP none

This tab appears as soon as any of those ports is set up, so you can pick the matching protocol here. The GPS BEEP SATELLITE COUNT mode and GPS telemetry only appear once the protocol and port match. Changes take effect after Save and Reboot.

docs.title: Module setup
docs.text:
Protocol selects how the GPS module talks to the controller: NMEA or UBLOX over a serial port, MSP (a companion device relaying GPS over MSP), FBUS (GPS from an FrSky FBUS/S.Port sensor), or CRSF (GPS from a CRSF Sensors accessory). For the last two, the signal-strength panel and the baud and config options don't apply, since both carry an already-processed fix rather than raw module output.

For NMEA and UBLOX modules, Auto Baud and Auto Config find the module's baud rate and configure it at start-up. Leave both on unless you have a reason to manage the module yourself. Auto Config sets a u-blox module to 10 Hz, or 5 Hz if the module refuses 10 Hz or the port is slower than 38400 baud. U-blox modules also have a Ground Assistance Type (SBAS region: EGNOS, WAAS, MSAS, GAGAN, auto-detect or none) and Use Galileo (swaps the QZSS constellation for Galileo, since a module only tracks so many constellations at once).

Only u-blox modules report 3D speed; for the others the ground speed is used.

Set Home Point Once controls when the home point is captured (shown as Dist to Home): off (the default) resets it on every arm; on captures it only on the first arm after power-up.

Wiring and configuring a u-blox or NMEA module by hand is covered in GPS Hardware and Module Setup.

docs.title: Diagnostics
docs.text: With a serial GPS (NMEA or UBLOX) and firmware that supports it, a Diagnostics panel under Status shows the GPS port and its pins, whether it opened and at what baud rate, the GPS state, and the byte, packet, error and timeout counters. A badge in its header gives the state at a glance (for example Receiving, No data or Bad data). When something is wrong, a line says what to do: no port set to GPS, nothing received (wiring or power), or data arriving but no valid messages (baud rate or protocol). In Expert Mode the panel also shows the last bytes received from the module. For the raw data and a baud rate scan, use the CLI command serialdebug; see GPS Hardware and Module Setup.

docs.title: Gyro
docs.text:
The Gyro tab configures gyro filtering: removing vibration noise from the motor, the drivetrain and the chassis from the gyro signal before it reaches the steering loop, without adding so much delay that the filtering itself starts to hurt the steering.

There are four different tools here, each catching noise a different way. It's tempting to turn all of them up "to be safe," but every filter trades noise removal for delay, and that delay comes straight out of how sharp and locked-in the steering feels -- so the goal is the least filtering that keeps things cool and quiet, not the most.

docs.title: Which filter should I use?
docs.text:
• If you can read real motor RPM (bidirectional DShot, or an RPM/frequency sensor), turn on the RPM Filter first. It uses the motor's actual RPM (and the gear ratio set in the Motors tab's Drive panel) to place notches exactly on the noise it's currently producing, so it introduces far less delay than guessing at a fixed frequency. esc_sensor_protocol = FBUS or crsf_sensors_use_rpm = ON (CRSF Sensors) can technically feed this too (nothing stops you setting either), but those update far too slowly and infrequently for RPM Filter's notches to track real noise -- use at your own risk, not a supported RPM source for filtering. It needs bidirectional DShot or a dedicated RPM/frequency-pin sensor to actually work as intended.
  • If you don't have an RPM source -- the Dynamic Notch Filter is the next best option. It watches the gyro signal itself, hunts for noise peaks, and places notches on them automatically. More flexible, but reacts a beat slower than RPM Filter since it has to detect the peak first.
  • The Lowpass Filters are the safety net underneath either one -- they don't need to know anything about your setup, they just cut everything above a cutoff. Leave Lowpass 1 on at its default; it's doing useful work even alongside RPM/Dynamic Notch filtering.
  • The fixed Notch Filters are for one specific, known resonance you can see in a Blackbox log that the other three aren't already handling -- not a first thing to reach for.

docs.title: Quick troubleshooting
docs.text: What you're seeing Try Hot steering servo, high-frequency buzzing or growling Enable RPM Filter or Dynamic Notch; if already on, raise RPM Filter Strength or lower Dynamic Notch Q Steering feels mushy or laggy Filtering is too aggressive for the setup -- try a lower RPM Filter Strength, raise Dynamic Notch Q, or raise the Lowpass cutoff Steering twitches at a specific throttle or motor RPM despite otherwise clean filtering Look for a peak in Blackbox at that condition and target it with a fixed Notch Filter

docs.title: RPM Filter
docs.text: Uses the motor's real RPM (and configured gear ratio) to track exactly where vibration is coming from and notch it out, rather than guessing -- this introduces substantially less delay than any filter that has to infer noise from the gyro signal itself. It needs bidirectional DShot or an RPM/frequency sensor; ESC telemetry (esc_sensor_protocol = FBUS) and CRSF Sensors (crsf_sensors_use_rpm = ON) aren't fast or precise enough, even though nothing stops you enabling either. Strength (Low/Medium/High) trades more aggressive noise removal for more delay -- start at Medium and only go higher if you're still seeing heat or noise in Blackbox.

docs.title: Dynamic Notch Filter
docs.text: Tracks peak noise frequencies in the gyro signal and places notch filters on them automatically -- the best option when there's no RPM source available. Notch Count is 4-6 if this is the only filter running, or 2-4 if it's working alongside an RPM Filter (which is already handling the main, predictable noise). Notch Q controls how narrow/selective each notch is -- 2.0-4.0 is the recommended range; going below 2.0 makes notches much wider and adds significantly more delay. Min/Max Hz should bracket the actual noise band -- Min just below your lowest-RPM noise frequency (but never under 20 Hz), Max about 10-20% above the highest noise frequency you expect.

docs.title: Lowpass Filters
docs.text: Lowpass 1 is the one filter left on by default: a straightforward cutoff that attenuates everything above its frequency, 1st or 2nd order. It can also run in Dynamic mode, sliding its cutoff between a Min and Max frequency instead of sitting fixed, so it can stay tighter at low noise/RPM and open up (less delay) when there's less to filter. Lowpass 2 (expert mode) is a fixed second stage -- generally only needed around 100Hz if RPM Filter or Dynamic Notch is already doing the main work; without either of those, two second-order lowpass stages are the recommended setup.

docs.title: Notch Filters
docs.text: Two fixed notches for known, specific resonances that aren't already handled by RPM/Dynamic Notch filtering -- each has a Center Frequency (where attenuation is strongest) and a Cutoff Frequency (where the notch starts). For example, a Center of 260Hz with a Cutoff of 160Hz attenuates roughly 160-360Hz, strongest at 260Hz. Find the frequency to target from a Blackbox gyro FFT rather than guessing.

docs.title: LED Strip
docs.text:
The LED Strip tab configures an addressable RGB LED strip connected to the controller: the layout, the colors and what each LED shows (for example the arm state or a warning). The tab only appears with the LED strip feature on (Configuration tab). The LEDLOW mode turns the strip off from a switch.

LED types, wiring, the available functions and colors, and the CLI syntax are described in the LED Strip reference.

docs.title: Conditions
docs.text:
The Conditions tab exposes a small in-firmware logic engine: simple conditional rules (based on modes, RC channel values, sensor values, etc.) that gate mixer rules or feed other conditions. This is the tool to reach for when you need custom behaviour that isn't a built-in mode, for example an output that only works while a switch is on and the car is armed.

Define conditions here, then gate any Mixer rule on one from its Condition column -- a gated rule contributes nothing while its condition is false.

Each of the 16 condition slots is one operation applied to two operands. Operands aren't limited to fixed values -- they can also read an RC channel, whether a mode is active, a sensor (voltage, current, RPM, RSSI, battery percentage, mAh drawn, GPS speed, altitude and others), the active profile, or another condition's current result, which is what lets conditions chain into more complex logic than a single comparison. Beyond the basic comparisons (Equal, Greater/Lower Than, Approx Equal) and boolean combinators (And, Or, Xor, Not), a few are worth knowing specifically: Sticky latches true once triggered rather than following its input from moment to moment, Delay only reports true once its input has held steady for a set time (filtering out brief blips), and Edge reports true only briefly on a transition rather than for as long as the condition holds.

docs.title: Mixer
docs.text:
The Mixer tab decides what drives each output: which servo steers, which output is the ESC, and anything else you wire up. It also holds the steering throw, the steering invert and the gyro direction.

A rule's output is a servo (S1-S24) or a motor (M1-M4). It makes no difference whether a servo is wired to a PWM output or is a bus servo on an SBUS or F.Bus line: servo N is PWM output N and bus channel N alike, so one rule drives both. See Servos → Bus Servos.

docs.title: Model Type
docs.text:
Model Type is Car or Custom. Change Model Type switches between them.

  • Car builds the rules for you from a few options and shows a summary instead of the rule list. This is the default.
  • Custom shows the full rule list for a mix built by hand.

docs.title: The car setup
docs.text:
With Car, Edit Configuration opens the car options. These are always set:

  • Steering servo (front wheels) on S1, from the steering wheel through the gyro (Stabilized Steering).
  • ESC on M1, reversible: forward, brake and reverse (Stabilized Throttle).

Two options can be added:

  • Rear steering (4-wheel steering) puts a second steering servo on S2. Opposite to the front wheels gives tighter turns; Same direction as the front wheels gives crab steering. Amount (0-100%, default 50%) is how far the rear wheels turn compared with the front.
  • Second ESC (dual motor, or front and rear motors) on M2. It gets the same throttle as M1: forward, brake and reverse.

Apply replaces all current mixer rules with the car set. If the board doesn't have enough servo outputs for rear steering, the dialog says so; assign more outputs on the Remap FC tab or turn rear steering off.

The summary shows what the rules do, for example Steering on S1, ESC on M1. If the rules were changed by hand and no longer match a car setup, it says so; Edit Configuration rebuilds them.

If the wheels steer or drive the wrong way, reverse the servo on the Servos tab or the motor direction in the ESC. The mix stays as it is.

The car setup names the servos it uses: STEER, or F STEER and R STEER with rear steering. See Servos → Name.

More on the defaults, the channel order and the gyro direction: Car Mixer and Channels.

docs.title: Steering Throw, Gyro Direction and Steering Invert
docs.text:
• Steering Throw scales every rule that reads the steering (Stabilized Steering) by one percentage, 0-200% (100% is the servo's normal travel). It raises or lowers the throw of all steering servos together, without changing each rule's weight. Pair it with Steering Override below to set a target throw: enable the override, command a known percentage, measure the wheel angle, and adjust the throw until it matches.
  • Gyro Direction → Reverse gyro (steering) reverses only the gyro's correction of the steering, not the wheel. Turn it on if, with the wheels off the ground, turning the car by hand makes the steering turn with the movement instead of against it. Don't use servo reverse for this: that reverses your steering too. The CLI setting is yaw_gyro_reverse. Board orientation and the attitude display are not affected.
  • Steering Invert flips every rule that reads the steering, the wheel and the gyro correction together.

The gyro correction is turned round for reverse by the controller itself, so Gyro Direction is set once, driving forward. See Drive State.

docs.title: Steering Override
docs.text: Enable steering override forces a stabilized input to a fixed value (-100% to 100%) for setup, for example to center or measure the steering. It only works while disarmed, isn't saved, and is reset after a reboot. While an override is active, arming is blocked.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
With Custom, the rule list is shown. Each rule reads one input and writes it to one output, combined with what's already on that output by its Operator:

  • Set overwrites the output.
  • Add adds to what's already there.
  • Mul multiplies what's already there.

Rules run from top to bottom. The first rule for an output should normally be Set, and later rules for the same output Add: a later Set wipes out everything written before it. The Configurator flags both cases on the rule.

Other fields of a rule:

  • Input source: a stabilized input (Stabilized Steering for the steering, Stabilized Throttle for the ESC), a commanded input (the stick after rates, without the gyro), an RC input that bypasses everything (RC Steering (bypass), RC Throttle (bypass)), or any receiver channel, CH #N. The bypass and AUX inputs are labelled with the physical channel they come from in your channel order, for example CH #1 (Steering) or CH #3 (AUX 1). Stabilized Roll and Pitch are always zero on a car.
  • Weight: how strongly the input drives the output; 1000 is full. Reverse flips it.
  • Differential % reduces (positive) or boosts (negative) the negative side of the rule relative to the positive side, for example to give a steering servo less throw one way.
  • Offset adds a fixed amount to the output.
  • Speed limits how fast the rule's output can move.
  • Curve reshapes the input with a curve from the Curves tab before the weight.
  • Condition applies the rule only while a condition from the Conditions tab is true; a rule that is off is dimmed.
  • Role tags a rule, see below.

Feed the ESC from Stabilized Throttle

The drive aids (ABS and traction control) and the failsafe throttle act on Stabilized Throttle. A rule that feeds an ESC from the RC throttle (bypass) or a raw channel skips them, and the ESC then doesn't get the failsafe throttle either. Stabilized Throttle runs from -1000 (full brake/reverse) to 1000 (full forward), with 0 at neutral.

docs.title: Rule roles
docs.text: A Role is a label on a rule; the mixer itself never reads it. The firmware keeps two roles inherited from WingFlight, Flap Compensation and Differential Thrust Yaw, but both are aircraft mixes and a car doesn't use them. The role picker only offers None. A rule loaded with one of the old roles still shows it by name, so you can set it back to None. Their adjustment functions are hidden on the Adjustments tab.

docs.title: Motors
docs.text:
The Motors tab sets how the controller drives the ESC: the throttle protocol and range, ESC telemetry, the motor RPM source, and the Drive panel that tells the steering gyro which way and how fast the car is going. It also has a Throttle Override to test the motor from the bench.

Wheels off the ground

Put the car on a stand with the wheels off the ground before you use Throttle Override or change the throttle range. Throttle Override makes the motor run.

docs.title: Reversible ESCs
docs.text:
Every motor output is reversible (bidirectional) by default: the throttle runs from -100% (full brake or reverse) through 0 (neutral) to +100% (full forward). With PWM, neutral is the midpoint of Low Throttle and High Throttle: 1500 µs with the defaults of 1000 and 2000 µs. A stopped or disarmed motor gets neutral, never the bottom of the range, which a car ESC would read as full brake or reverse.

Calibrate the ESC to the controller with the throttle at neutral, as its manual describes, so the car neither creeps nor brakes at neutral. The Setup Wizard's ESC step walks you through it; see Set Up Your Car.

docs.title: Throttle
docs.text:
• Throttle Protocol: older and most car ESCs take PWM; others take a digital protocol like DShot, which needs no range calibration. Check what your ESC supports before you switch. SRXL2 and Castle Link are described below.
  • Unsyncronised ESC update and Update Frequency: with PWM, the ESC signal runs at its own rate rather than with the steering loop. The default is 50 Hz; use a higher rate only if your ESC supports it.

docs.title: Throttle Range (PWM)
docs.text:
Low Throttle (min_throttle, default 1000 µs) is full brake/reverse, High Throttle (max_throttle, default 2000 µs) is full forward, and neutral is halfway between them. Motor Off (min_command) is not used for a reversible output.

Get these wrong and the motor can run with the throttle at neutral, even disarmed. Use Live Update, which applies changes at once, with Throttle Override to check the result before trusting the values.

docs.title: SRXL2 ESC
docs.text:
Spektrum SRXL2 ESCs (Smart ESCs) take their throttle and send their telemetry on one signal wire, which goes to a serial port, not to the motor output.

To use one, set a spare UART to ESC: SRXL2 on the Configuration tab. That's all that's needed: Throttle Protocol, Telemetry Protocol and Half-Duplex are then set to match and locked (shown disabled, with a tooltip saying why). The firmware forces the same values on save whatever is shown here. To go back to another ESC protocol, change the port's function on the Configuration tab.

The protocol list only offers SRXL2 once a port has that function, since without one the ESC gets no signal. The Setup Wizard's ESC step does the port assignment for you.

With an SRXL2 ESC there are two more settings:

  • SRXL2 Telemetry Interval: every how many throttle frames the ESC is asked for telemetry. 0 turns telemetry polling off. Default 7.
  • SRXL2 Motor 2 Channel: for dual-motor Smart ESCs (e.g. the Spektrum SPMXAE1020), the SRXL2 channel that carries the second motor, 2 to 32. Motor 1 is always channel 1. With a channel set, the motor count becomes 2 and the mixer's second motor output (M2) drives it: turn on Second ESC in the Mixer car setup, or add a rule for M2. Leave it Off for a single motor (the default). CLI: srxl2esc_motor2_channel.

Both take effect after Save and Reboot. Dual-motor Smart ESCs report no RPM, so RPM filtering and the speed from RPM are not available with them.

docs.title: Castle Link
docs.text: Castle Link uses the motor output, like PWM. The ESC's telemetry comes back on the same wire, so it needs no serial port and no telemetry protocol. See Castle ESC Telemetry.

docs.title: ESC Telemetry
docs.text:
Telemetry Protocol reads voltage, current, temperature, consumption and RPM from an ESC that sends telemetry. Connect the ESC's telemetry wire to the controller and set its port to ESC: Telemetry on the Configuration tab. Half-Duplex and Pin Swap set the wiring; Detect Wiring tries each combination until a valid frame arrives (save first, ESC powered, car disarmed). Sensor Correction scales the voltage, current and consumption the ESC reports.

With FrSky F.BUS as the protocol, telemetry comes over the F.Bus port instead; see FBUS/S.Port Sensors.

docs.title: RPM
docs.text:
Motor RPM is what lets the controller know the car's speed and when it has stopped. It comes from Dshot RPM Telemetry (bidirectional DShot, with a compatible ESC such as AM32, Bluejay or BLHeli32 32.7 or later), from ESC telemetry, or from the RPM Sensor (frequency) input. Set the motor's pole count (the number of magnets on the motor bell, not the stator teeth) so electrical RPM becomes motor RPM.

The same RPM feeds the RPM filter on the Gyro tab, which needs a fast source: bidirectional DShot or the RPM sensor input.

docs.title: Drive
docs.text:
The Drive panel sets what the controller needs to work out which way the car is travelling and how fast, from the throttle it sends to the ESC and the motor RPM. It uses this to keep the steering gyro correcting the right way in reverse, and to fade the gyro out when the car is nearly stopped.

  • ESC behaviour: what your ESC does below neutral. Automatic picks from the protocol: with DShot the ESC reverses directly, as AM32 does by default; with PWM it brakes first and reverses after the throttle returns to neutral, like most car ESCs. The others are Brake, then reverse, Reverse directly and Forward and brake only. An AM32 with RC car reverse turned on needs Brake, then reverse.
  • Speed from motor RPM: Tyre diameter (outside diameter of the driven tyres, default 100 mm) and Gear ratio (motor turns per wheel turn, the final drive ratio: for 10.4 : 1 enter 104 : 10), per motor. The panel shows the resulting formula. Speed attenuation on the Profiles tab uses this speed too, in place of GPS speed. The gear ratio is also used by the RPM filter and applies after the save and restart.
  • Steering gyro: Gyro starts at and Gyro fully on at (default 2.0 and 6.0 km/h). Below the start speed the gyro doesn't correct the steering, so at a standstill the steering follows the wheel alone; the correction rises to full at the second speed. Both need motor RPM: without it the gyro is always fully on. Gyro in reverse (on by default) and Reverse gyro gain (default 50%) set the correction while reversing.
  • Live shows the ESC behaviour in use, the ESC state (Neutral, Forward, Braking, Reverse), the direction, the speed and the gyro correction.

If no RPM source is set up, the panel says so: the controller can't tell when the car has stopped, so the gyro stays fully active at a standstill.

How the drive state works, and what each setting does in detail: Drive State.

docs.title: Throttle Override
docs.text: Throttle Override sets the throttle output to a value for setup and testing: -100% to +100% on a reversible output. It only works while disarmed, isn't saved, and resets after a reboot. While it is on, arming is blocked.

docs.title: Power
docs.text:
The Power tab configures battery voltage and current monitoring: cell count detection/limits, voltage divider scaling, and current sensor scaling if fitted.

Accurate voltage readings here feed the low-voltage warnings/beeper and any SmartFuel, so it's worth calibrating against a real multimeter reading rather than trusting default scale values.

docs.title: Meter source
docs.text:
Voltage and current can each be read from Battery ADC (the board's own onboard voltage divider / current shunt), ESC Telemetry, a FrSky Sensor, or a CRSF Sensor -- or left None if not fitted. Only ADC sources need the Scale and Divider fields below calibrated for your hardware; the other sources already report a computed value, so there's nothing to scale. Changing the source itself needs a reboot to remap hardware pins -- the rest of this tab applies live.

CRSF Sensor needs a UART assigned the CRSF Sensors port function first -- see the CRSF Sensors tab, including which decoded frame type actually feeds the voltage reading when more than one is present.

docs.title: Battery profiles
docs.text:
There are six battery profiles, and each one carries its own capacity, cell count and Min / Warn / Full / Max cell voltages. This lets one car switch between, for example, a 2S LiPo and a 3S LiPo pack. Click a profile's name to make it the active profile; the active row is highlighted.

A cell count of 0 detects the cell count automatically when the battery is connected. Within each profile the voltages must be ordered Min ≤ Warn ≤ Full ≤ Max -- a profile that is not ordered is reset to the defaults when the configuration is loaded.

Battery monitoring, the low-voltage warnings and SmartFuel all use the active profile. If the profile is changed while armed (for example with an adjustment), the change is applied as soon as the car is disarmed.

Firmware that predates per-profile cell settings shows the older layout: a single set of cell count and cell voltages shared by all profiles, with only the capacity set per profile.

docs.title: Calibration Manager
docs.text: Rather than computing a voltage divider or current-shunt scale by hand, plug in a battery (wheels off the ground), measure its actual voltage/current with a multimeter, and type those true values into the Calibration Manager -- it back-computes the corrected Scale for you from the difference between what it's currently reading and what you measured. Only available for ADC meter sources, and only meaningful if the Divider/Offset fields are already roughly right first (leaving a value at 0 skips calibrating it).

docs.title: SmartFuel
docs.text: A fuel-gauge charge estimate, more informative than raw voltage alone: Voltage mode estimates remaining charge from pack voltage, Current mode integrates measured mAh drawn against the configured battery capacity, and Combined reports whichever of the two is more pessimistic at any given moment (so an optimistic voltage reading under load can't mask a pack that's actually further depleted). New configurations default to Current. Until mAh used and the pack capacity are both known, Current mode uses the voltage estimate instead, so it also works without a current sensor. Every mode needs a battery voltage source; SmartFuel stays inactive until one is set. Voltage Drop Rate and Charge Drop Rate cap how fast the voltage-based estimate is allowed to fall, and Sag Gain compensates for voltage sag under load -- raise it if SmartFuel reads too pessimistic under load, lower it if too optimistic. Sag Gain is entered in volts per cell at full throttle (0.40 V by default), and the compensation follows the motor output, in either direction.

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text:
The Profiles tab holds the PID profiles: the steering stabilizer's tune, how it changes with throttle and speed, the drive aids and the drift settings. Each profile is a complete set, so a profile can be a tune for one track or surface.

Up to six profiles can be stored (fewer on boards with little memory). Pick the one to edit from the profile selector at the top; the loaded profile is shown there. Copy profile copies the current one to another, and Reset to defaults resets it. Switch profiles while driving with the Profile Selection function on the Adjustments tab.

Gripora stabilizes the steering only, so the tab shows the steering values. The controller measures the car's turn rate (yaw rate) with the gyro and steers so that it follows the rate the steering wheel asks for (set on the Rates tab).

docs.title: Driving Feel
docs.text:
Driving Feel is where to start tuning. One value per column, with a guide beside the table saying what each one does:

Column What it changes Raise it if... Lower it if... Master Gain [%] How hard the car fights unwanted turning The car wanders or feels soft, or twitches out of line on bumps or under power The steering wobbles, buzzes or oscillates at speed I-Term Decay [s] How long it holds its line after a bump You want it more locked in It feels too locked in; shorter is freer and suits drifting I-Term Relax (1-10) How firmly it stops at the end of a fast turn or slide The car kicks back the other way when you centre the wheel Long, sustained turns lose rate

The Throttle and Speed rows change the gain with throttle and speed, see Gain attenuation.

Every column is also an Adjustments function, so you can turn it on a knob while driving. The Setup Wizard can put Master Gain on a knob for you. A value under live adjustment shows the value being commanded.

docs.title: Master Gain
docs.text:
Master Gain scales the P, I and D terms together, live, without changing the stored gains. 100% (the default) is the tune as configured. F and B are not scaled. The range is 0-200%; 0 turns the gyro correction off.

A gain curve can shape it by steering deflection, so the gain tapers in or out towards full lock; see Gain Curves. A CURVE badge on Master Gain shows when one is shaping it.

docs.title: I-Term Decay
docs.text:
Master Gain sets how hard the car pushes back against a disturbance; I-Term Decay sets how long it holds on to that correction before letting it go. Anything faster than the decay time (a bump, a grip change) is corrected and the car returns to its line. Anything slower (a slow drift, a trim offset) is let go, so the controller doesn't keep pulling the car back towards where it was a few seconds ago.

The default is 0.60 s, the range 0.01-1.00 s. Shorter feels freer and suits drifting; longer feels more locked in but can start to hold trim errors. I-Term Decay and I gain overlap: under a steady load, a longer decay holds more I, much as a higher I gain would. Set I for how firmly a disturbance is corrected, then I-Term Decay for how long.

The CLI setting is iterm_decay_time (in 0.01 s). Its maximum bleed rate, I-Term Decay Max Rate (default 35°/s, iterm_decay_limit), is under PID Controller Settings; leave it at the default.

docs.title: I-Term Relax
docs.text:
While you steer quickly, I-Term Relax stops the I-term building up from your own input, so the car doesn't kick back the other way when you centre the stick. I-Term Decay deals with what the controller remembers after a turn; I-Term Relax stops it collecting the turn in the first place.

It is a score from 1 to 10, default 5. Higher means more relax and less bounce-back; lower keeps more hold through long, sustained turns. Most cars end up between 5 and 9. If the car kicks back at the end of a turn, raise it a step at a time.

The CLI setting is iterm_relax. It sets the I-term relax filter cutoff, from 50 Hz at 1 to 3 Hz at 10, with 5 = 10 Hz. The relax level (default 22°/s, lower is stronger, iterm_relax_level) is under PID Controller Settings; leave it at the default unless I-Term Relax alone doesn't remove the kick-back.

docs.title: PID Controller Gains
docs.text:
The PID gains table holds the steering loop's P, I, D, F (feedforward) and B (boost): the stored tune, which Master Gain scales.

  • P is how tightly the car tracks the steering wheel and corrects a bump or grip change right now. Too little and it feels loose and wanders; too much and the steering overshoots or oscillates, quickly.
  • I holds the turn rate over time against steady influences: a camber, uneven grip, a car that pulls to one side, a long sweeping corner. Too much and the car keeps rotating after a quick steering input is released.
  • D damps any change in turn rate, from your input or from a bump. It reduces overshoot from a high P, but is by far the most sensitive term to gyro noise; check Gyro filtering before adding it.
  • F steers from the stick alone, without waiting for an error: a sharper response to steering input. Too little feels slow and delayed; too much overshoots and kicks back at the end of a steering input.
  • B adds feedforward from how fast the stick moves, for a sharper start and stop, without the drawbacks of a high P or F.

The defaults are P 190, I 45, D 0, F 65 and B 35. F can't be set below 50, in the Configurator, the CLI, the Lua scripts or an adjustment: F sets most of the steering for a commanded rate, and P and I only correct what is left.

The Effective PID Gains preview shows the gains in use after Master Gain and the gain attenuation, so you can see the effect on the bench.

docs.title: Quick troubleshooting
docs.text: What you see Try Loose, wanders off line, twitches on bumps Raise Master Gain or P Steering oscillates or wobbles, worse at speed Lower Master Gain or P; use the Throttle or Speed row to lower it at speed Buzzing servo, hot servo Lower D, check Gyro filtering Steering feels slow or delayed Raise F Kicks back the other way after a quick input Raise I-Term Relax; if it overshoots the input itself, lower F Keeps rotating after a quick input is released Lower I or shorten I-Term Decay Doesn't hold a long corner or pulls to one side Raise I or lengthen I-Term Decay

docs.title: PID Controller Bandwidth and Settings
docs.text:
Expert settings, best left at their defaults until you need them:

  • Steering Bandwidth (PID loop bandwidth, Hz), Steering D-term Cutoff and Steering B-term Cutoff.
  • I-Term Decay Max Rate and I-Term Relax Level, above.
  • Error Limit for Steering Axis: a hard limit on the angle error in the loop, so the I-term can never grow past it.

docs.title: Gain attenuation
docs.text: Two rows in Driving Feel scale the steering's P, D, F and B (not I) with throttle and with speed. Together they never take the gains below 25%. GYRO OFF is not affected.

docs.title: Throttle
docs.text: The Throttle row (fw_tpa_gain, 25-200%, default 100%) scales the gains by a percentage, optionally shaped by a gain curve evaluated on throttle, 0-100%. The curve sees the size of the throttle, so brake and reverse count the same as forward. 100% with no curve means no change. Use it, for example, to reduce the gain at high throttle if the steering wobbles under power.

docs.title: Speed (speed attenuation)
docs.text:
The Speed row (fw_spa_gain, 25-200%, default 100%) scales the gains by the car's speed, on top of the Throttle row. Steering gets more effective as speed rises, so a tune that is right at low speed can wobble on a fast straight. Speed reduces the gain as the car goes faster.

  • It does nothing until a Speed curve is assigned in Gain Curves.
  • The curve's X axis runs from 0 to the speed curve range (fw_spa_speed_max, 10-300 km/h, default 60), the km/h value beside the Speed curve in the Gain Curves panel. Faster than that uses the curve's last point.
  • The speed is the wheel speed from the motor RPM when the motor has an RPM source (see the Drive panel on the Motors tab), otherwise GPS speed. GPS needs a fix.
  • If the speed is lost (no RPM source and no GPS fix), the gain holds for 3 seconds, then eases back to 100%. When Speed engages it eases in rather than jumping.

The Configurator's help text on the Speed row still says it needs a GPS; with an RPM source it doesn't.

A typical start: a curve that stays at 100% up to a moderate speed and falls to 60-70% at your top speed, with the speed curve range set a little above it. To see it while driving, log debug_mode = GAIN_ATTEN with Blackbox.

docs.title: Gain Curves
docs.text: Gain curves are assigned in the Gain Curves panel (advanced): one slot each for Steering (by steering deflection), Throttle and Speed. The Speed line also holds the speed curve range in km/h. The shapes themselves are edited on the Curves tab. "-" means no curve. Whenever a curve shapes Master Gain, its cell in Driving Feel shows a CURVE badge.

docs.title: Drive aids
docs.text:
The Drive aids panel holds ABS, traction control and launch control. They shape the throttle and brake you give before they reach the ESC:

  • ABS pulses the brake when you brake hard, so the wheels keep turning and the car keeps steering instead of locking up and sliding. It works only while the ESC is braking a car that is still rolling, and never pushes the throttle past neutral into reverse.
  • Traction control limits how fast the forward throttle may rise, so the wheels don't spin up when you pull the trigger hard. Letting off is instant, and the brake and reverse are never touched.
  • Launch control caps the throttle for a standing start, staged with the LAUNCH mode, and ramps it to full: Start throttle and Ramp time.

All are Off by default. They belong to the profile selected at the top: each profile has its own, and switching profile switches them. A Live box shows whether the aids are on, what ABS, traction control and launch control are doing, and the throttle from the transmitter next to the throttle to the ESC.

The aids are off while disarmed, in failsafe, and while the DRIVE AIDS OFF mode is on (Modes tab). The ESC's mixer rule must take Stabilized Throttle, as the car mixer preset does; a rule fed straight from the RC throttle bypasses them.

What each setting does, and which ESC setups ABS can't run on: Drive Aids.

docs.title: Drift
docs.text:
