The Drift panel sets up the DRIFT mode. While DRIFT is on (put it on a switch on the Modes tab), the steering wheel steers the wheels directly, as with GYRO OFF, and the gyro only counter-steers when the car rotates faster than the allowed rate. There is no heading hold.

Setting Default Range What it does Counter-steer gain 100 % 0-200 % How hard the gyro counter-steers past the allowed rate. 100 % gives full lock 360 °/s past it; 0 % turns the counter-steer off. Allowed turn rate 30 °/s 0-720 °/s Turn rate the gyro leaves alone, so the car can hold a slip angle. Raise it to hold more angle. Counter-steer limit 100 % 10-100 % The most lock the gyro adds, as a share of full lock. Lower it if the counter-steer snaps the car straight.

The line under the settings shows where the counter-steer starts and the turn rate at which it reaches full lock, or its limit. The settings belong to the profile selected at the top and are saved and reverted with it. The panel is hidden on firmware without drift mode.

How DRIFT works with GYRO OFF, failsafe and the drive state, and how to tune it: DRIFT.

docs.title: Rates
docs.text:
The Rates tab sets the steering response: how fast the car is asked to turn (its turn rate, or yaw rate) at full steering, and how much expo softens the steering around center.

Rates are separate from the PID tune on the Profiles tab: rates turn the steering wheel into a commanded turn rate, and the profile decides how closely the car follows it. The Setup Wizard's Driving style step sets a starting point (Beginner, Sport or Drift); see Set Up Your Car.

Up to six rate profiles can be stored and switched between from the profile selector at the top of the page, copied from one to another, or reset. The live curve chart and preview update immediately, so you can compare a change before saving it. Switch rate profiles while driving with the Rate Profile Selection function on the Adjustments tab.

docs.title: Rate, Shape and Expo
docs.text:
The steering row has three values:

  • Rate sets the top speed: the turn rate, in °/s, the car is asked for at full steering. It's shown in the Max Vel column, and it's the only one of the three that changes it.
  • Expo softens the response around center, for finer small corrections, without changing the top rate. At 0% Expo the response is a straight line from center to full lock.
  • Shape sets how sharply the curve bends within the softened region: how much of the rate increase is saved for the last part of the steering travel. Shape only does anything if Expo is above 0%.

A car can only turn as fast as its speed and grip allow. When the steering asks for more rate than the car can give, for example armed on a stand, the stabilizer keeps adding steering, so held steering creeps towards full lock. That is normal. With an RPM source, the Drive panel fades the gyro out at low speed and at a standstill, so the steering then follows the wheel alone.

docs.title: Quick troubleshooting
docs.text: What you feel Try Not enough steering at full lock, the car won't turn tight enough Raise Rate Too much at full lock, the car spins or snaps round Lower Rate Small corrections near center feel twitchy Raise Expo Numb around center, hard to make small corrections Lower Expo Flat, linear feel all the way, no extra towards full lock Raise Shape Changing Shape does nothing Check Expo isn't at 0%

docs.title: Dynamics
docs.text:
Extra steering shaping options under Dynamics (expert mode):

  • Response Time smooths the steering input before it becomes a setpoint. Larger values smooth more (and add lag); 0 turns it off.
  • Setpoint Boost Gain and Cutoff sharpen the steering input from how fast the stick moves, for a snappier feel. This acts on the stick signal, per rate profile, before it reaches the PID loop, unlike the B term on the Profiles tab.
  • Dynamic Ceiling Gain reduces how much stick travel is needed to reach the top rate while the stick moves quickly towards full lock.
  • Dynamic Deadband Gain and Filter widen the steering deadband for a moment while the stick moves quickly back through center, to smooth a wobble on a fast return to center.

docs.title: Receiver
docs.text: The Receiver tab sets how the controller talks to your receiver: the protocol and its signal options, the channel order, the channel range and deadband, telemetry, and any backup receivers. Live bars show every channel.

docs.title: Protocol and signal options
docs.text:
Receiver Protocol in the Primary Receiver box picks the protocol (serial protocols such as CRSF, S.BUS, FBUS, SRXL2 and others, or PWM/PPM and SPI receivers where the board has them). With a serial protocol, three signal switches appear. Get the wrong one and you see no signal at all, not a subtle problem:

  • Inverted flips the signal polarity. Turn it on for F.Port and F.Bus. Leave it off for Futaba S.BUS and S.BUS2: the controller already allows for S.BUS being inverted; turn it on only for a receiver that outputs non-inverted S.BUS. Not supported on F4-based boards.
  • Half-Duplex uses the Tx pin for both sending and receiving. Required for SBUS2, F.Port, SRXL and SRXL2. Plain S.BUS leaves it off.
  • Pin Swap swaps the Rx and Tx pins, for wiring that comes in reversed. Not supported on F4-based boards.

Detect Wiring tries every combination of the three switches for the saved protocol and stops at the first one that gives a signal. The transmitter must be on and bound, the car disarmed, and the tab saved first. Nothing is kept until you save.

For Futaba receivers, use Futaba S.BUS2 if the receiver has an S.BUS2 port (control and telemetry on one wire), or Futaba S.BUS if it doesn't (control only). The receiver must be set to output the same one.

For FrSky receivers set to F.Bus or F.Port2, pick FrSky FBUS. They are the same protocol at two speeds, and the controller finds the speed the receiver uses and keeps it once good frames arrive; telemetry starts after that. Changing the receiver between F.Bus and F.Port2 needs no change here.

docs.title: ExpressLRS switch mode
docs.text:
ExpressLRS receivers use the TBS CRSF protocol.

Warning

Gripora only supports the ExpressLRS Full Res 16ch Rate/2 switch mode, at the 100Hz Full or 333Hz Full packet rate. It sends all 16 channels at full (10-bit) resolution, including channel 5, at half the packet refresh rate.

The other switch modes send channel 5 (ExpressLRS AUX1) only as a two-position arm switch. Gripora uses channel 5 as a normal full-resolution channel (AUX 3 in the car channel order), so in those modes it can only be fully one way or the other.

When the protocol is TBS CRSF, the Receiver tab and the Setup Wizard's receiver step show this warning.

docs.title: SRXL2 full-size receivers
docs.text:
Some Spektrum full-size receivers (e.g. the AR6610T) need to see a valid SRXL2 handshake within about 200 ms of power-on, or they switch their receiver port to plain PWM instead of SRXL2, which can be too fast for the normal handshake to win during boot. When the controller's own SRXL2 unit ID is set to 0 (bus master), it sends the first handshake packets very early during boot, then carries on with the normal handshake.

This is CLI-only: set srxl2_unit_id = 0. The default is 1, so set it explicitly for a receiver that needs it.

docs.title: Channel Range
docs.text:
• Channel Center is the channel value with the steering wheel and the throttle trigger at neutral, usually 1500 µs (1520 µs on some Futaba radios).
  • Channel Travel is how far the channel moves from center at full steering lock or full throttle.
  • Steering Deadband is how far the steering channel must move from center, in µs, before the car steers (default 5 µs, range 0-100). It keeps a wheel that rests slightly off center from steering on its own. The CLI setting is yaw_deadband. roll_deadband and pitch_deadband still exist in the CLI but have no use on a car.

docs.title: Throttle neutral
docs.text: The throttle is centered like the steering: above neutral drives forward, below it brakes and reverses. Throttle Neutral shows the neutral the controller uses: the Channel Center, with a small fixed deadband around it. The car only arms with the throttle at neutral, and a receiver failsafe returns the throttle to neutral.

docs.title: Channel Assignment
docs.text:
Channel Order picks which receiver channel drives the steering, the throttle and AUX 1-4. The default is Car (CH1 steering, CH2 throttle), as car and pistol-grip radios (Futaba, Sanwa, Spektrum, FrSky, Radiomaster and most others) send them: CH1 steering, CH2 throttle, CH3-CH6 AUX 1-4. Pick Custom order, or change a channel in the list, if your radio differs. A custom order is one letter per channel from CH1: S steering, T throttle, 1-4 AUX 1-4, - not used, for example TS1234 for throttle on CH1 and steering on CH2. See Car Mixer and Channels.

The live bars next to each channel let you check that the order matches your radio before you set up the Mixer: turn the wheel and the Steering bar moves, pull the trigger and the Throttle bar moves.

Up to 24 channels are shown. Most receiver protocols carry 16 or 18; FrSky F.Bus in its 24-channel mode carries all 24. Channels beyond the four AUX channels can be used for modes, adjustments, failsafe and as Mixer inputs. Every channel picker in the Configurator names a channel CH #N, with its role where it has one, for example CH #3 (AUX 1).

RSSI can be read from AUTO (reported by the receiver protocol, if the link supports it), the board's analog RSSI input (ADC), or a spare channel (CH #5 onward) that your receiver puts an RSSI value on.

Virtual radio (desktop app only) simulates channel input for bench testing without a transmitter. Bind Receiver sends a bind request to receivers that support it.

docs.title: Telemetry
docs.text: Telemetry settings for the receiver link: the telemetry signal options and, for CRSF/ELRS, Custom Telemetry (Gripora's own sensor set, decoded by a Lua script on the radio) with its Telemetry Packet Rate and Telemetry Packet Ratio, which must match the ELRS settings on the transmitter.

docs.title: Telemetry Sensors
docs.text:
Selects which telemetry values are sent back to your transmitter, and for protocols with a fixed transmission sequence (e.g. Smart Port), in what order: values earlier in the list update more often. The sensors on offer depend on what the protocol and the firmware support (e.g. RPM only appears with a configured RPM source).

New configurations start with the sensors the Gripora Lua suites use, including System Status and System Config in the Status group. These two carry the controller's status (arm state, receiver links, failsafe, GPS, profiles and more) for the radio's callouts and dashboard alerts. See Telemetry for the default list and what each status bit means.

docs.title: Primary Receiver / Backup Receiver 1 and 2
docs.text:
The main receiver's protocol box is labelled Primary Receiver. Its title bar always shows a Link badge for the main receiver's own signal, whether or not a backup port is set up.

If a serial port is set to Receiver: Backup 1 on the Configuration tab, a second box, Backup Receiver 1, appears below it; a port set to Receiver: Backup 2 adds a Backup Receiver 2 box. Each has:

  • A Protocol list (None, Futaba S.BUS, FrSky FBUS, FrSky F.PORT, Jeti EXBUS or TBS CRSF). None, the default, means the port is assigned but not decoding anything yet. FrSky FBUS also covers F.Port2 receivers, as on the main receiver.
  • Inverted, Half-Duplex and Pin Swap, with the same meaning as on the main receiver but set separately, since this is a different UART. OFF always means "this protocol's normal wiring": S.BUS is naturally inverted, the others aren't.
  • Link and Active Source badges in its title bar. Active Source names the receiver in control: Main RX, Backup 1 or Backup 2.

Changes to these fields need Save and Reboot.

Once a backup protocol is set and receiving, every channel in Channel Assignment gets a smaller bar per backup under the main one, showing that backup's value for the channel, so you can check a bound backup gives sane values before relying on it. See Backup RX Input for what the feature does, including the failover order.

docs.title: Remap FC
docs.text: The Remap FC tab changes what each pin of the board does: a motor output, a servo output, a serial port, the LED strip, the frequency (RPM) input and so on. Add another ESC output or an extra servo, or move a function to a free pin, without a soldering iron.

docs.title: Using it
docs.text:
1. Read FC reads the board's pins and their current use through the CLI. The tab shows the MCU and the board design it found.
  2. Click a pin to see what it does, and choose what it should do. Picking a function moves it to this pin from wherever it was; picking the pin's own default puts it back. A pin that is hard-wired can't be remapped.
  3. The tab suggests fixes for conflicts, for example swapping two functions or moving one to a free pin. Changes can't be sent while two functions share a pin, or while the motor or servo numbering has a gap.
  4. Save and Reboot sends the changes as CLI resource, timer and dma commands and saves them.

Where the board has a configuration in gripora-targets, the tab uses its pin defaults.

The car setup on the Mixer tab tells you when the board has too few servo outputs for rear steering; this is the tab to add one.

Take a backup first. A pin change is saved with the rest of the configuration (diff all includes the resource lines).

docs.title: Sensors
docs.text: The Sensors tab shows live raw sensor data (gyro, accelerometer and, where fitted, magnetometer and barometer), to diagnose a sensor that seems to be misbehaving or to compare noise levels before and after a filtering change. The gyro's yaw axis (the turn rate) is the one the steering uses.

docs.title: Servos
docs.text:
The Servos tab configures each servo: center point, travel limits, direction (reverse), speed and trim, on top of whatever mixer rules send input to it.

There are 24 servos. Servo N is sent on PWM output N, where the board has one, and on channel N of a bus output (SBUS, F.Bus) when one is set up, so a servo is set up the same way however it is wired. The table lists the servos in use; see Bus Servos.

Set the limits conservatively at first. It's easier to increase travel once you've checked the steering doesn't bind at full lock than to find a stalled, straining servo afterwards. The Setup Wizard's Binding limits step helps with this.

docs.title: Name
docs.text:
Each servo can have a short Name, such as STEER, so you can tell the servos apart without counting outputs. A name is up to 8 characters (letters, digits, spaces and punctuation). It is saved on the controller and kept in a CLI backup, but nothing while driving uses it. The column only shows with firmware that supports names.

The Mixer tab, the Setup Wizard, Servo Override and Balance show the name with the servo number, for example Servo #1 (STEER). When a mixer setup (the Mixer tab's car setup or the Setup Wizard's model step) assigns the servos, it names them for you: STEER for a single steering servo, F STEER and R STEER with rear steering. A name it gave earlier to a servo the new mix no longer uses is cleared; a name you typed is kept.

The Ethos Lua suite shows and edits the names too. The EdgeTX scripts show them but can't edit them.

docs.title: Endpoints and scale
docs.text:
Min/Max cap the servo's pulse-width travel, to keep the steering off its mechanical stops at full lock. Scale Neg/Scale Pos are a separate pair of per-side scaling factors (500μs by default) -- adjust these instead of Min/Max specifically to correct a servo that throws noticeably further on one side than the other.

The limits are the same for every servo, on a PWM output and on a bus:

Field Range Default Center 1000-2000 µs 1500 µs Min / Max down to 880 µs / up to 2159 µs 600 µs either side of Center Scale Neg / Scale Pos 50-1000 µs 500 µs

880-2159 µs is everything an SBUS or F.Bus channel can carry. Narrow-band servos (760 µs center) are not supported.

docs.title: PWM update rate
docs.text:
PWM update rate, above the table, is how often every PWM output is updated. It is one setting for all of them:

  • Standard (50 Hz) -- the default, and safe for any servo.
  • High speed (333 Hz) -- responds faster, but is for digital servos only. It can damage an analog servo, so check the data sheet first.

It only takes effect after Save and reboot, since the rate is set up at boot time, not applied live like most other fields here. It doesn't affect bus outputs, which run at their own frame rate. The CLI setting is servo_pwm_rate, 25-333 Hz; a value other than 50 or 333 is shown here as it is.

docs.title: Speed and Reverse
docs.text:
Speed limits how fast the servo is allowed to move, expressed as milliseconds needed for a 60° rotation; 0 means unlimited. It slows one output, separately from the Mixer rule's own Speed limit on the same output.

Reverse flips the direction if the wheels steer the wrong way for the stick. It reverses the stick and the gyro correction together. If only the gyro corrects the wrong way, use Gyro Direction on the Mixer tab instead, not Reverse here.

docs.title: Balance Curve
docs.text:
When two servos drive the same steering (dual steering servos) and don't quite track each other, a per-servo balance curve trims one servo's travel to match its partner. Balance curves are edited on the Curves tab, not here. Any servo with a non-flat curve shows a curve icon in its row; click it to jump straight to that servo's curve.

Note

The Geometry Correction switch that older Configurator versions showed on this tab has been removed from the Configurator, so the correction can no longer be turned on or off from here.

docs.title: Trim
docs.text:
Trim never changes a servo's Mid. Each servo has a separate Trim value in µs, added to its output on top of Mid. Mid and the Min/Max end stops you set on the bench stay where you put them, however much you trim.

The Trim column holds two kinds of trim:

  • Saved trim: set by a Stepped Servo Trim adjustment, or by typing it in here. It is saved like any other setting (on disarm, or with Save on this tab).
  • Live trim: set by a Mapped Servo Trim adjustment (a knob or a trim channel from the radio). It follows the channel, is never saved, and starts from zero every time the controller boots.

Both together are limited to 20% of the servo's Scale (the larger of Scale Neg and Scale Pos, so ±100 µs at the default 500 µs). The output also stays inside the servo's Min/Max, so trim can never drive the steering past the end stops you set.

How the column shows it:

  • No Servo Trim adjustment for this servo: the saved trim, editable.
  • A Servo Trim adjustment covers this servo: read-only, showing the trim in use (saved plus live), so it moves as you press the trim. Hover over it to see the two parts. A badge beside it shows the adjustment, highlighted while active with its channel.

The Signal column's full-stick estimate allows for the saved trim: trim uses up travel on one side and gives it back on the other.

docs.title: Clear trims and Move trims into Center
docs.text:
Above the table:

  • Clear trims sets every saved trim to 0.
  • Move trims into Center adds each servo's saved trim to its Mid and sets the trim to 0. The servo doesn't move, but Min/Max are measured from Mid, so the end stops move with it. Use it once the car drives straight and you want the result to become the new center, and check the end stops afterwards.

Both count as unsaved changes until you press Save.

docs.title: Trimming from the transmitter
docs.text:
Map Servo Trim Steering on the Adjustments tab to trim from the transmitter. The Setup Wizard's Trim and gain step sets this up for you:

  • Stepped (trim buttons): each press moves the saved trim by one Step. A quick tap counts. Hold the button and it starts repeating after half a second. Only the first step of each press beeps. The trim is saved when you disarm.
  • Mapped (a trim channel or knob): sets the live trim directly, within the adjustment's range. It is never saved, so the radio keeps the trim.

Trimming the steering moves every servo whose Mixer rule takes its input from the steering (Stabilized Steering), front and rear. Each servo's Reverse, its rule's weight sign and the Steering Invert are taken into account. Servos fed by a raw RC channel, an override or a logic condition aren't touched. When any servo on the steering reaches its trim limit, the trim stops for all of them, so a pair of steering servos never get pulled out of line.

Because a Mapped trim is never saved, a channel that is misread (for example one that isn't valid yet just after power-up) can move the steering by at most the trim limit and leaves nothing behind once the reading is right again. The firmware also ignores a trim channel until the receiver link has been there for a full second (at power-up and after a brief link drop).

Stepped trims work on the bench too: the Trim column follows each press, and Save keeps the result.

Keep the radio's own steering trim off the steering channel when the controller trims. A trim left on the stick is read as steering input, which the gyro holds against.

docs.title: Trim buttons on one channel
docs.text:
The radio's steering trim buttons can drive a Stepped trim on one spare channel. The Setup Wizard's Trim and gain step sets this up (Trim buttons on one channel), with Ethos as the example; on other radios (EdgeTX, OpenTX and so on) set up the same mix and weights. By hand:

  1. Model → Trims: leave the steering trim enabled, with Audio on so each press clicks.
  2. Model → Mixes: keep the steering trim off the steering channel. An Ethos car model's Steering mix has no trim switch: add a Free mix with Source Steering and Output the steering channel (CH1), then delete the Steering mix.

  3. Add a Free mix named TRIM: always on, Source Maximum, Operation Add, Output a spare channel. Add an action for each steering trim button, with the trim position as its active condition, setting the mix weight:

    Trim button Weight Channel Adjustment T1 CW 40% about 1680-1730 µs Servo Trim Steering, up T1 CCW 30% about 1630-1680 µs Servo Trim Steering, down

  4. On the Adjustments tab, add Servo Trim Steering as Stepped, always on, on that channel, with those two windows and a Step of 2 µs.

T1 is the steering trim on the radio the wizard was written against; use your own steering trim buttons with the same weights. Each weight puts its own value on the channel (100% is 2012 µs). With no button pressed, the channel reads outside both windows.

Upgrading from older firmware

Older firmware wrote Stepped trims straight into Mid. Anything trimmed that way stays in Mid after the upgrade, and the new saved trims start at 0. In the CLI, servo trim lists the saved trims and servo trim <servo> <µs> sets one; diff and dump include them.

docs.title: Bus Servos
docs.text:
For FrSky XACT servos on one F.Bus wire, see FrSky Servos and the XACT Servo Programming tab.

Enabling SBUS Output or FBUS Master on a serial port (see Configuration) sends the servos down that UART too, for digital bus servos wired to it instead of individual PWM wires. Servo N is channel N on the bus. It is the same servo as PWM output N, with the same Center, Min/Max, Scale, Trim, Speed and Reverse, so one Mixer rule and one row in the table drive both.

The table lists the servos in use: servo 1 up to the board's PWM output count or the bus channel count (see Bus output channel count), whichever is larger. A note above the table says which servos the bus sends and which are also on a PWM output. On a board with four PWM outputs and a 12-channel bus, for example, servos 1-12 are listed, all twelve go down the bus, and servos 1-4 are on the PWM outputs as well.

To send something on the bus that isn't on a PWM output, give it a servo number the board has no PWM output for.

docs.title: Bus output channel count
docs.text:
How many channels each bus output sends is set with F.Bus output channels and SBUS output channels, above the table. Each appears only when a port has that output assigned. A change applies straight away, the table resizes to match, and it is saved with the rest of this tab. The CLI settings are fbus_master_channels and sbus_out_channels:

Output Channel counts Default Frame F.Bus 8, 12, 16, 24 24 8 uses the 8-channel frame, 12 and 16 the 16-channel frame, 24 the 24-channel frame SBUS 8, 12, 16 16 Always the 16-channel SBUS frame

Channels past the count are sent at center. Pick 16 or less for F.Bus if anything on the bus only accepts the 16-channel frame.

SBUS and F.Bus output can run at the same time, each with its own count. Servo N is channel N on both, and the table follows the larger of the two counts.

With a count of 16, channels 17 and 18 are also sent as on/off channels, driven by servos 17 and 18: on when that servo's output is at 1500 µs or above. Both are listed in the table. The 24-channel F.Bus frame has no on/off channels.

With a 24-channel F.Bus receiver, receiver channels 19-24 are available too (see Receiver), so they can be mixed straight to servos 19-24.

Upgrading from older firmware

Older firmware had separate PWM servos (S1-S8) and bus servos (S9 and up), with a Clone PWM outputs to bus servos switch, and a Rate for each servo. All of that is gone. Servo and mixer rule settings reset to their defaults on the upgrade. In a backup made before it, a line that names servo 9 or above meant a bus channel 8 lower than it does now: the Configurator leaves those lines out when it restores such a backup, and they must not be pasted back into the CLI as they are. Set those servos up again by hand.

docs.title: Maintenance
docs.text:
The Maintenance tab, in the Diagnostics group, holds the one-off actions on the controller: calibration, saving, resetting and rebooting.

Button What it does Calibrate Accelerometer Put the car (or the board) on a level surface and keep it still while it calibrates. Calibrate Magnetometer Only with a magnetometer: turn the car at least 360° about every axis within 30 seconds. Save Settings Writes the current settings to the controller's memory. Reset Settings Restores every setting to its default, after a confirmation. Take a backup first. Boot Loader / DFU Reboots into the boot loader, for flashing firmware. Mass Storage Mode Reboots so the controller shows up as a USB drive, for copying Blackbox logs. System Reboot Reboots and reinitialises the controller.

The accelerometer is used for the board orientation and for which way is level. The Setup Wizard's first step calibrates it too, see Set Up Your Car.

A reset sets the car defaults: steering servo on S1, ESC on M1, CH1 steering and CH2 throttle. See Car Mixer and Channels.

docs.title: Status
docs.text:
The Status tab is the first view after connecting. It shows a live summary of the controller: whether it can arm and, if not, why; the battery; a 3D car that follows the controller's attitude; and the receiver channels.

Use it as the first check after connecting: a sensor that isn't detected or a flag that blocks arming shows up here before you go any further.

The Info box shows the car name, firmware, board and whether the configuration has been changed from the defaults, with the run count and run time. Below the arming and battery boxes, the Instruments row shows what the car is doing, and the 3D car shows heading, pitch and roll; Reset Z axis zeroes the heading shown on it.

docs.title: Instruments
docs.text:
• Steering: a dial with two needles. Stick is your steering wheel; Output is the steering command the controller sends, worked back from the steering servo's pulse, so it includes the gyro correction. With the car still and the stick centred they sit together; the gap between them is what the gyro adds. If no servo is driven by steering in the mixer, the dial says so.
  • Throttle and brake: two bars around neutral, Transmitter (what you give) and To ESC (what reaches the ESC after the drive aids). The ABS, Traction and Launch badges are lit while that aid is ready (launch: staged) and highlighted while it acts. Aids off shows while the drive aids pass the throttle through: disarmed, in failsafe or with DRIVE AIDS OFF.
  • Speed: the wheel speed from motor RPM (or No RPM source), the travel direction, the ESC state (neutral, forward, brake, reverse) and the gyro correction from the drive state.
  • Turn rate: the yaw rate from the gyro, left or right, on a scale to 360 °/s each way.
  • Body roll and pitch: the car's tilt from the attitude estimate, with a small drawing of the car from behind and from the side. The steering loop doesn't use it; it is a check that the board orientation is right.

Firmware that doesn't report the drive state shows a note in the speed card; without the drive aids status only the transmitter throttle is shown.

docs.title: Enable Arming
docs.text: Enable Arming lets the car arm while the Configurator is connected, which it normally can't (the MSP flag below). The Configurator asks you to confirm. Never drive the car with the Configurator connected, and put the car on a stand with the wheels off the ground before you enable it.

docs.title: Arming disable flags
docs.text:
When the car won't arm, the Status tab lists each active arming-disable flag; hover one for a plain-language explanation. The ones you'll meet most often on a car:

  • THROTTLE: the throttle isn't at neutral. A car only arms with the trigger at neutral (the channel center, with a small deadband).
  • MSP: the Configurator is connected. Use Enable Arming above for a bench test.
  • RX_FAILSAFE: no valid receiver signal.
  • CALIBRATING: the gyro is still calibrating; keep the car still after power-up.
  • ANGLE: the attitude estimate isn't ready yet.
  • SETUP: a setup tool, such as the Setup Wizard or a servo, mixer or motor override, is holding the outputs. Arming works again once it lets go.
  • BACKUP_RX: a backup receiver is configured but hasn't linked yet, so the first arm of the session is blocked until every configured backup does. Check the backup receiver's power, binding and wiring, or power-cycle it, then confirm its Link badge on the Receiver tab comes up.

The full list of flags, and what clears each one, is in Arming and Stick Commands.

docs.title: XACT Servo Programming
docs.text:
The XACT Servo Programming tab programs FrSky XACT servos on an F.Bus line from the Configurator. XACT servos are configured over the same F.Bus wire that drives them, so no separate programming connection is needed. The tab only appears when a serial port is set to Bus: F.BUS Master on the Configuration tab.

For wiring and the whole setup of XACT steering servos, see FrSky Servos.

docs.title: Programming a servo
docs.text:
1. Scan for Servos finds the XACT servos on the bus and lists them with their Physical ID, App ID and channel.
  2. Select one to edit it. The settings are:
    • Physical ID: the servo's bus address (00-1A). Every servo on the bus needs its own.
    • App ID: tells servos of the same model apart. Give each servo on the bus a different value.
    • Channel: the bus channel (CH1-CH24) the servo follows. Bus channel N carries servo N, so the steering servo on S1 listens to CH1.
    • Range (120°, 90° or 180° of total travel), Direction, Pulse Type (leave it at 1500 µs), Data Rate and Center.
    • Advanced: Holding Strength, Operation Smoothing and Deadband. Series 65 servos (firmware 40 and later) add Working Mode and Max Angle.
  3. Save writes the values to the servo.

One servo at a time

Servos ship with the same IDs. Two servos sharing a Physical ID collide on the bus and show as one, and a save addressed by App ID can reach both. The tab warns about duplicates and blocks a save that would keep a duplicate App ID. Connect each new servo on its own, give it its own IDs, then join it to the bus.

The servo's settings are stored in the servo itself, not in Gripora, so they are not part of a Gripora backup or diff.

docs.title: Boards with an FBUS mux
docs.text: On boards that switch their outputs between PWM and F.Bus with an FPGA, an FBUS mux outputs section lets you put F.Bus on one output alone, so a scan or write only reaches the servo plugged in there. Arming is blocked while one output is selected. Auto program gives the servo on each F.Bus output its own Physical ID, App ID and channel and sets its range to 180°.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text:
Gripora is open source, and contributions -- code, documentation, and testing -- are welcome. Gripora is stability-control firmware for RC cars, forked from WingFlight (itself a fork of Rotorflight and Betaflight). The car conversion is in progress, so some inherited code and naming still comes from the fixed-wing firmware; see the Developer Guide for what that means for a change.

  • Documentation (this site) lives in gripora-project/gripora-docs. Every page has an Edit this page link for quick fixes. User and developer documentation both live here, not in the firmware repository's docs/.
  • Firmware lives in gripora-project/gripora-firmware -- see Building the Firmware.
  • Configurator lives in gripora-project/gripora-configurator.

See the Developer Guide for the repositories and general contribution guidance, Code Guidelines and Testing and Coding Style for how to write the code, and the Technical Reference for the internals. Use the issue tracker to discuss larger changes before starting.

docs.title: Building the Firmware
docs.text: Gripora firmware is built with the same ARM GCC toolchain and Makefile structure as Rotorflight and Betaflight. Run every command below from the root of a gripora-firmware checkout. make help lists all the options.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A Linux, macOS, or WSL environment (native Windows builds of board firmware are not supported directly; the SITL simulator target is the exception, see below)
  • make, git and python3

docs.title: Installing the toolchain
docs.text:
The ARM toolchain does not need to be installed by hand:

make arm_sdk_install

downloads the version the Makefile expects into tools/. Run it once.

docs.title: Targets
docs.text:
Gripora builds unified targets: one firmware per MCU family, listed in make/targets_list.mk:

Target MCU family STM32F405 STM32F405 STM32F411 STM32F411 STM32F7X2 STM32F722 / F7x2 STM32F7X2M STM32F7X2 variant with the FBUS mux FPGA STM32F745 STM32F745 STM32G47X STM32G47x STM32H730 STM32H730 STM32H743 STM32H743

Board-specific pin mappings and defaults are not in the firmware repository. They live in gripora-targets and are applied as a configuration on top of the unified firmware when it is flashed. The only other target is SITL, below.

docs.title: Building
docs.text:
Build one target, for example the one preferred for test builds:

make TARGET=STM32F7X2

or every unified target, as the project's CI does:

make unified

The firmware files are written under obj/. Extra defines go in OPTIONS, for example make TARGET=STM32F7X2 OPTIONS="USE_SOMETHING"; see Customizing the Build.

docs.title: Version string
docs.text: The version comes from src/main/build/version.h. CI adds a suffix with FC_VER_SUFFIX (a snapshot tag, or on a feature branch the feature/<name> slug plus the short git SHA). FC_VERSION_STRING must stay under 30 bytes, so a long suffix fails the build with fc_version_string_too_long. Keep feature branch names short. Never change the version numbers themselves in a pull request; see the Developer Guide.

docs.title: Unit tests
docs.text:
make test

builds and runs the unit tests in src/test/unit natively, with no board. See Code Guidelines and Testing.

docs.title: Flashing a locally built firmware
docs.text: A locally built .hex file can be flashed the same way as an official build, from the Configurator's Firmware Flasher, using Load Firmware [Local] instead of the online build list. Then apply your board's configuration from gripora-targets.

docs.title: Simulator (SITL)
docs.text:
TARGET=SITL builds Gripora as a native executable that exchanges sensor and output packets with an external simulator over UDP, so the firmware can run without a board. Unlike the ARM builds, it can be built natively on Windows:

make mingw_sdk_install    # Windows only, once: installs MinGW-w64 GCC
make TARGET=SITL          # produces obj/main/gripora_SITL.elf

On Linux, macOS and WSL the system gcc is used. RC input arrives over MSP, and the CLI and the Configurator can connect over TCP (ports 5761 and up, one per UART). Settings are kept in eeprom.bin in the working directory. A few features that need real hardware (ADC, PWM receiver input, serial receivers, LED strip and similar) are not built, so SITL has fewer CLI settings than a board.

The simulator bridge and models that SITL was developed with live in the wingflight-sitl-hitl repository and model an aircraft, not a car. See the SITL README in the firmware repository (src/main/target/SITL/README.md) for ports, packets and eeprom.bin handling.

docs.title: Code Guidelines and Testing
docs.text: Guidance for firmware changes. For layout and formatting rules, see Coding Style.

docs.title: General principles
docs.text:
1. Name everything well.
  2. Strike a balance between simplicity and not repeating code.
  3. Functions that start with find can return null. Functions that start with get should not.
  4. Keep functions short. It makes them easier to test.
  5. Don't be afraid of moving code to a new file. It reduces test dependencies.
  6. Avoid noise words in names, like data or info. Think about what you are naming, and don't be afraid to rename anything.
  7. Avoid comments that describe what the code is doing. The code should describe itself. Comments are useful for the big picture and for documenting what a variable holds.
  8. Document a variable at its declaration. Don't copy the comment to the extern usage, since it will rot.
  9. Seek advice from other developers.
  10. Be professional. Humor, or criticism of existing code, in the code itself is not helpful to whoever has to change it next.
  11. There is always more than one way to do something, and code is never final, but it does have to work.

docs.title: Changing steering, mixer and arming code
docs.text:
Mixer, mode, PID, drive-state and drive-aids changes are safety-critical: they decide what the steering servo and the ESC do. Treat changes in src/main/flight/mixer.c, src/main/pg/mixer.c, src/main/flight/pid.c, src/main/flight/drive.c and src/main/flight/drive_aids.c as high risk, and check the arming and override behaviour in src/main/fc/core.c too. Before you change them, read Steering Control Dynamics. It records the signal chain, sign conventions and the design rationale, and lists known defects that can look intentional.

  • Do not renumber the permanent mode (BOX) IDs. Keep MSP and CLI compatible where you can.
  • Saved settings live in parameter groups. Follow the parameter group rules, and bump the group version whenever you change the group, including its defaults or ranges.
  • Never change the MSP API or firmware version numbers; see the Developer Guide.
  • Check the change on the bench with the wheels off the ground before driving.

docs.title: Unit testing
docs.text:
Ideally, any new code has a test. The codebase is old and was not designed for testing, so this can be hard. Focus on the smallest change that lets you add a test.

Tests live in src/test/unit and use GoogleTest. They are written in C++, linked with the firmware's C code, and built and run natively on your development machine, so you need no board. To run them from the root of the firmware repository:

make test

make junittest does the same. Each *_unittest.cc file becomes one executable in obj/test. make -k test carries on with the next test after a failure. Test reports are also written by the run.

Tests exist for the PID, setpoint, curves, maths, speed attenuation, the drive state (drive_unittest.cc), the drive aids (drive_aids_unittest.cc), servos and telemetry status, among others. Some test files are disabled by their .cc.txt extension, for example the mixer, IMU, failsafe and arming-prevention tests, and need reviving before they can run. So the mixer, failsafe and fc/core.c arming paths have no running tests: changes there need extra care and, where possible, a new test.

docs.title: Pull requests
docs.text:
• Keep a pull request to one thing. It is easier to review and test.
  • Fork the repository, create a branch for each change, and open the pull request against master. Never open a pull request from your own master.
  • Don't rewrite history on a branch after you have opened the pull request.
  • Firmware pull requests should build with make unified and pass make test.
  • If your change affects what a user sees, update the matching page on this site, and say so in the pull request.
  • Keep the description short: What, Compatibility and Testing, as described in the Developer Guide.

docs.title: General
docs.text:
This document overrides the original Baseflight style that was referenced before. This document has taken inspiration from that style, from Eclipse defaults and from Linux, as well as from some Cleanflight and Betaflight developers and existing code.

There are not so many changes from the old style, if you managed to find it.

docs.title: Indentation
docs.text: 1TBS (based K&R) indent style with 4 space indent, NO hard tabs (all tabs replaced by spaces).

docs.title: Tool support
docs.text:
Any of these tools can get you pretty close:

Eclipse built in "K&R" style, after changing the indent to 4 spaces and change Braces after function declarations to Next line. 

astyle --style=kr --indent=spaces=4 --min-conditional-indent=0 --max-instatement-indent=80 --pad-header --pad-oper --align-pointer=name --align-reference=name --max-code-length=120 --convert-tabs --preserve-date --suffix=none --mode=c

indent -kr -i4 -nut
(the options for these commands can be tuned more to comply even better)

Note: These tools are not authorative. Sometimes, for example, you may want other columns and line breaks so it looks like a matrix.

Note2: The Astyle settings have been tested and will produce a nice result. Many files will be changed, mostly to the better but maybe not always, so use with care.

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
Functions shall have the opening and closing braces at the beginning of the next line, and followed by a line break. 

int function(int x)
{
    body of function
}

docs.title: Opening braces
docs.text: All non-function statement blocks (i.e. if, switch, for, as well as any others) shall have the opening brace last on the same line, with the following statement on the next line.

docs.title: Closing braces
docs.text:
Closing braces shall be but on the line after the last statement in the block. 

if (x is true) {
    we do y
    ...
}


switch (action) {
case ADD:
    return "add";
case REMOVE:
    return "remove";
case CHANGE:
    return "change";
default:
    return NULL;
}

If the closing brace is followed by an else or else if that shall be on the same line, again with the opening brace on the same line. 

if (x is true) {
    we do y
    ...
} else {
    we do z
    ...
}

docs.title: Braces are required
docs.text: Omission of "unnecessary" braces in cases where an if or else block consists only of a single statement is not permissible in any case. These "single statement blocks" are future bugs waiting to happen when more statements are added without enclosing the block in braces.

docs.title: Spaces
docs.text:
Use a space after (most) keywords. The notable exceptions are sizeof, typeof, alignof, and attribute, which look somewhat like functions (and are usually used with parentheses). So use a space after these keywords: 

if, switch, case, for, do, while
but not with sizeof, typeof, alignof, or attribute. E.g., 
s = sizeof(struct file);
When declaring pointer data or a function that returns a pointer type, the preferred use of '*' is adjacent to the data name or function name and not adjacent to the type name. Examples: 
char *linux_banner;
memparse(char *ptr, char **retptr);
char *match_strdup(substring_t *s);
Use one space around (on each side of) most binary and ternary operators, such as any of these: 
=  +  -  <  >  *  /  %  |  &  ^  <=  >=  ==  !=  ?  :
but no space after unary operators: 
&  *  +  -  ~  !  sizeof  typeof  alignof  __attribute__  defined
no space before the postfix increment & decrement unary operators: 
++  --
no space after the prefix increment & decrement unary operators: 
++  --
and no space around the '.' and "->" structure member operators.

'*' and '&', when used for pointer and reference, shall have no space between it and the following variable name.

docs.title: typedef
docs.text:
enums that do not have a count or some other form of terminator element shall have a comma after their last element:

typedef enum {
    MSP_RESULT_ACK = 1,
    MSP_RESULT_ERROR = -1,
    MSP_RESULT_NO_REPLY = 0,
    MSP_RESULT_CMD_UNKNOWN = -2,
} mspResult_e;

This ensures that, if more elements are added at a later stage, only the additional lines show up in the review, making it easier to review.

enums with a count should have that count declared as the last item in the enumeration list, so that it is automatically maintained, e.g.: 

typedef enum {
    PID_CONTROLLER_MW23 = 0,
    PID_CONTROLLER_MWREWRITE,
    PID_CONTROLLER_LUX_FLOAT,
    PID_COUNT
} pidControllerType_e;
It shall not be calculated afterwards, e.g. using PID_CONTROLLER_LUX_FLOAT + 1;

typedef struct definitions should include the struct name, so that the type can be forward referenced, that is in: 

typedef struct motorMixer_s {
    float throttle;
...
    float yaw;
} motorMixer_t;
the motorMixer_s name is required.

docs.title: Naming
docs.text:
Generally, descriptive lowerCamelCase names are preferred for function names, variables, arguments, etc. For configuration variables that are user accessible via CLI or similar, all_lowercase with underscore is preferred.

Variable names should be nouns.

Simple temporary variables with a very small scope may be short where it aligns with common practice. Such as "i" as a temporary counter in a for loop, like for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++). Using "temporaryCounter" in that case would not improve readability.

docs.title: Declarations
docs.text:
Avoid global variables.

Variables should be declared at the top of the smallest scope where the variable is used. Variable re-use should be avoided - use distinct variabes when their use is unrelated. One blank line should follow the declaration(s).

Hint: Sometimes you can create a block, i.e. add curly braces, to reduce the scope further. For example to limit variable scope to a single case branch.

Variables with limited use may be declared at the point of first use. It makes PR-review easier (but that point is lost if the variable is used everywhere anyway).

docs.title: Initialisation
docs.text:
The pattern with "lazy initialisation" may be advantageous in the Configurator to speed up the start when the initialisation is "expensive" in some way. In the FC, however, it’s always better to use some milliseconds extra before arming than to use them while driving.

So don't use "lazy initialisation".

An explicit "init" function, is preferred.

docs.title: Data types
docs.text:
Be aware of the data types you use and do not trust implicit type casting to be correct.

Angles are sometimes represented as degrees in a float. Sometimes as decidegrees in a uint8_t. You have been warned.

Avoid implicit double conversions and only use float-argument functions.

Check .map file to make sure no conversions sneak in, and use -Wdouble-promotion warning for the compiler

Instead of sin() and cos(), use sin_approx() and cos_approx() from common/math.h.

Float constants should be defined with "f" suffix, like 1.0f and 3.1415926f, otherwise double conversion might occur.

docs.title: Naming
docs.text:
Methods that return a boolean should be named as a question, and should not change any state. e.g. 'isOkToArm()'.

Methods should have verb or verb-phrase names, like deletePage or save. Tell the system to 'do' something 'with' something. e.g. deleteAllPages(pageList).

Non-static functions should be prefixed by their class. Eg baroUpdate and not updateCompass .

Groups of functions acting on an 'object' should share the same prefix, e.g. 

float biQuadFilterApply(...);
void biQuadFilterInit(...);
boolean biQuadIsReady();
rather than 
float applyBiQuadFilter(...);
void newBiQuadLpf(...);
boolean isBiQuadReady();

docs.title: Parameter order
docs.text:
Data should move from right to left, as in memcpy(void *dst, const void *src, size_t size). This also mimics the assignment operator (e.g. dst = src;)

When a group of functions act on an 'object' then that object should be the first parameter for all the functions, e.g.: 

float biQuadFilterApply(biquad_t *state, float sample);
void biQuadNewLpf(biquad_t *state, float filterCutFreq, uint32_t refreshRate);
rather than 
float biQuadFilterApply(float sample, biquad_t *state);
void biQuadNewLpf(float filterCutFreq, biquad_t *state, uint32_t refreshRate);

docs.title: Declarations
docs.text:
Functions not used outside their containing .c file should be declared static (or STATIC_UNIT_TESTED so they can be used in unit tests).

Non-static functions should have their declaration in a single .h file.

Don't make more than necessary visible for other modules, not even types. Pre-processor macros may be used to declare module internal things that must be shared with the modules test code but otherwise hidden.

In the .h file: 

#ifdef MODULENAME_INTERNALS_
… declarations …
#endif
In the module .c file, and in the test file but nowhere else, put #define MODULENAME_INTERNALS_ just before including the .h file.

Note: You can get the same effect by putting the internals in a separate .h file.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
Keep functions short and distinctive. Think about unit test when you define your functions. Ideally you should implement the test cases before implementing the function.

Never put multiple statements on a single line. Never put multiple assignments on a single line. Never put multiple assignments in a single statement.

Defining constants using pre-processor macros is not preferred. Const-correctness should be enforced. This allows some errors to be picked up at compile time (for example getting the order of the parameters wrong in a call to memcpy).

A function should only read data from the HW once in each call, and preferably all at one place. For example, if gyro angle or time is needed multiple times, read once and store in a local variable.

Use for loops (rather than do or while loops) for iteration.

The use of continue or goto should be avoided. Same for multiple return from a function and multiple break inside a case. In general, they reduce readability and maintainability. In rare cases such constructs can be justified but only when you have considered and understood the alternatives and still have a strong reason.

In expressions, parentheses should only be used where they are required, i.e. where operator precedence will not evaluate in the right order, or where a compiler warning is triggered without parentheses. This brings all expressions into a canonical form, and avoids the problem of different developers having different ideas of what 'easy to read' expressions are.

One exception to this rule is the ternary conditional operator

pidStabilisationEnabled = (pidControllerState == PID_STABILISATION_ON) ? true : false

Here, the condition shall be enclosed in braces, to make the ternary operator easier to spot when reading left to right.

docs.title: Includes
docs.text:
All files must include their own dependencies and not rely on includes from the included files or that some other file was included first.

Do not include things you are not using.

#pragma once (see wiki) is preferred over #include guards to avoid multiple includes.

docs.title: Documentation comments
docs.text:
All new code files, structs, enums, and functions should include a comment at its top describing its purpose. All PRs that modify existing items should add a comment if not already present, and update it if applicable due to changes made by the PR. These comments may be ommitted if the item is trivial or self-explanatory.

Example file-level comment:

/* This file contains code used to send DSHOT commands using the STM timer's burst DMA functionality.
* It uses DMA to alter timer PWM duty cycle. For an alternative approach, see `drivers/dshot_bitbang.c` 
for a DSHOT implementation that uses GPIO bitbanging.
*/

Example enum-level comment: 

/* 
* Describes allocation of ELRS telemetry packets, and is associated with time between telemetry
* packet transmission.
* See [ELRS: Telemetry Bandwidth](https://www.expresslrs.org/1.0/info/telem-bandwidth/) for more information.
*/
typedef enum {
    TLM_RATIO_NO_TLM = 0,
    // ..

docs.title: Other details
docs.text:
No trailing whitespace at the end of lines or at blank lines.

Stay within 120 columns, unless exceeding 120 columns significantly increases readability and does not hide information. (Less is acceptable. More than 140 makes it difficult to read on Github so that shall never be exceeded.)

Take maximum possible advantage of compile time checking, so generally warnings should be as strict as possible.

Don't call or reference "upwards". That is don't call or use anything in a software layer that is above the current layer. The software layers are not that obvious in Betaflight, but we can certainly say that device drivers are the bottom layer and so should not call or use anything outside the device drivers.

Target specific code (e.g. #ifdef CC3D) is not permissible outside of the src/main/target directory.

typedef void handlerFunc(void); is easier to read than typedef void (*handlerFuncPtr)(void);.

Code should be spherical. That is its surface area (public interfaces) relative to its functionality should be minimised. Which is another way of saying that the public interfaces shall be easy to use, do something essential and all implementation should be hidden and unimportant to the user

Code should work in theory as well as in practice. It should be based on sound mathematical, physical or computer science principles rather than just heuristics. This is important for test code too. Tests shall be based on such principles and real-world properties so they don't just test the current implementation as it happens to be.

Guidelines not tramlines: guidelines are not totally rigid - they can be broken when there is good reason.

docs.title: Developer Guide
docs.text: General guidance for contributing to Gripora's firmware, configurator and radio scripts.

docs.title: Repositories
docs.text:
Gripora is split across several repositories under gripora-project:

Repository Purpose gripora-firmware Controller firmware (C) gripora-targets Board configurations (custom defaults) applied on top of the unified targets gripora-configurator Desktop/web app for flashing and configuring the controller over MSP (Svelte/Vite) gripora-blackbox Blackbox Explorer for analysing logs gripora-lua-edgetx Transmitter Lua scripts for EdgeTX gripora-lua-ethos-suite Lua suite for FrSky Ethos gripora-docs This documentation site (MkDocs) gripora-website Project website and logo/branding assets

The firmware's release and dev-build workflows also publish firmware binaries to gripora-artifacts, which the web Configurator downloads from.

docs.title: Where the project stands
docs.text:
Gripora was forked from WingFlight, a fixed-wing firmware, and the car conversion is in progress. Keep these in mind when changing anything:

  • Only yaw (steering) is stabilised. Roll and pitch keep their slots in the per-axis arrays, PID and rate profiles, MSP messages and Blackbox fields, but always hold zero.
  • Throttle is signed, -1..1 around rc_center: forward above neutral, brake or reverse below it. "Throttle off" (arming, auto-disarm, failsafe) means the throttle trigger at neutral.
  • Removed aircraft features keep their ids. Attitude hold, angle/leveling, acro trainer, GPS rescue and navigation, thrust vectoring, the governor, auto trim, the tune advisor and the MANUAL and TRADITIONAL modes are gone, but their mode (BOX), adjustment, parameter group, debug and MSP ids are kept as reserved so later ids do not move. Never reuse or renumber them.
  • The aircraft mixer concepts are gone. The control-surface presets, the aircraft model types and the WINGFLIGHT_AIRPLANE build marker have been removed; the model types are CAR and CUSTOM, and there is no build-time fork marker. Inherited comments and receiver-protocol channel names may still say aileron or elevator. Don't add new aircraft concepts.
  • Car features go under src/main/flight/ (the directory name is inherited) until a reorganisation is agreed: drive.c (drive state), drive_aids.c (ABS, traction control and launch control), speed_atten.c; DRIFT is pidApplyDrift() in pid.c.
  • WingFlight fixes can be pulled in from the upstream remote (WingFlight/wingflight-firmware). Keep diffs to inherited code small so that stays easy.

docs.title: Firmware changes
docs.text: See Building the Firmware to get a local build working first, and Code Guidelines and Testing before changing steering, mixer or arming code.

docs.title: Keep stable interfaces stable
docs.text:
• Do not renumber permanent mode (BOX) ids. GYRO OFF is 12, DRIVE AIDS OFF 66, LAUNCH 67 and DRIFT 68.
  • Keep MSP and CLI backward compatible where you can. If a setting is renamed, keep an alias where practical and record it in the firmware's Changes.md.

docs.title: Never bump the MSP API or firmware version
docs.text:
The maintainers bump these by hand when a release is made, so a pull request must not change them:

  • the MSP API version, API_VERSION_MAJOR / API_VERSION_MINOR in src/main/msp/msp_protocol.h (currently 33.0);
  • the firmware version, FC_VERSION_MAJOR / FC_VERSION_MINOR / FC_VERSION_PATCH_LEVEL in src/main/build/version.h.

MSP changes made between releases belong to the upcoming API version. List them in the pull request under Compatibility, so the release bump covers them and the Configurator can pick them up.

The firmware identifies itself over MSP as Gripora / GRPA. The Configurator, the Ethos suite and the EdgeTX scripts check that identifier and the API version, so an MSP change affects all of them. Gripora-specific MSP2 messages are named MSP2_GRIPORA_*.

docs.title: Bump the parameter group version
docs.text: Parameter groups are the exception to "don't bump versions": whenever a group changes (fields added, removed, reordered or resized, array lengths, default values or value ranges), bump its version, the last argument of PG_REGISTER*, in the same change. Stored settings from older builds then reset to the current defaults instead of being misread. The version is 4 bits (0-15). See Parameter Groups.

docs.title: Dev builds from a feature branch
docs.text: Feature-branch dev builds embed FC_VER_SUFFIX, made from the feature/<name> branch slug plus the short git SHA. src/main/build/version.h requires FC_VERSION_STRING to stay under 30 bytes, so a long branch name makes the workflow fail with fc_version_string_too_long. That is a real compile failure, not a superseded run: keep feature branch names short (or change .github/workflows/dev-build.yml to truncate the suffix).

docs.title: Configurator changes
docs.text: The Configurator is a Vite + Svelte app. See its repository's README for local dev setup (pnpm install, pnpm start). Its tabs live in src/tabs/ and its English text in locales/en/messages.json; user-facing names in these docs follow that text.

docs.title: Docs changes
docs.text:
This site is built with MkDocs Material. Every page is plain Markdown under docs/; the site nav is defined in mkdocs.yml. To preview locally:

pip install -r requirements.txt
mkdocs serve

User-facing documentation (setup, Configurator tabs, driving modes, CLI reference) and the developer material under Contributing both live here. The firmware repository's docs/ holds only a pointer to this site; source code that depends on a document links to it by URL. When a firmware pull request changes behaviour a user sees, note in it which page here needs updating.

docs.title: Issues and pull requests
docs.text:
Maintainers and users read these, so keep them short and precise.

Issues

  • Title: the symptom in one line.
  • Body: firmware version and target, steps to reproduce, expected and actual behaviour. Attach the CLI diff all output or a Blackbox log when relevant.

Pull requests

  • Title: imperative, under about 70 characters (for example "Fix steering I-term windup in GYRO OFF").
  • Body, a few lines each:
    • What: the change and why it is needed. Link the issue (Fixes #123).
    • Compatibility: MSP, CLI or setting changes, and whether the Configurator or these docs need updating.
    • Testing: what was built and run (unit tests, SITL, bench, driving).
  • One topic per pull request. Leave out file-by-file change lists and generated summaries.

docs.title: Technical Reference
docs.text: Internals for people working on the firmware, the Blackbox tools or the Configurator. Most users will not need these pages.

docs.title: How the firmware is built and stored
docs.text:
• Parameter Groups -- how settings are grouped, and the rules for changing them safely.
  • Configuration Format -- how the configuration is laid out in flash and on the wire.
  • Atomic Barrier -- how the atomic-block macros keep the compiler from reordering accesses.
  • Customizing the Build -- building with different features enabled.
  • Custom Board Configuration -- mapping pins on a custom board with the CLI.

docs.title: Logs and estimators
docs.text:
• Blackbox Log Format -- the frame types, predictors and encodings of the log.
  • SmartFuel Internals -- how the charge estimator works, and its MSP interface.

docs.title: Debugging
docs.text:
• Hardware Debugging -- debug adapters and how to use them.
  • Hardware Debugging with VS Code and J-Link

docs.title: Steering control and wiring design
docs.text:
• Steering Control Dynamics -- the signal chain from the receiver to the steering servo and the ESC, sign conventions, the rationale behind each stage, and the known defects and limitations. Read it before changing the PID, mixer, drive state or drive aids code.
  • RX serial wiring auto-detect and ESC telemetry signalling auto-detect -- the design of the live trial that finds the right inversion, half-duplex and pin-swap settings.

docs.title: Protocols
docs.text:
• MSP over Telemetry -- how the radio scripts carry MSP over S.Port, F.Port, FBUS and CRSF, and what limits the speed.

The firmware identifies itself over MSP as Gripora / GRPA and speaks MSP API 33.0. Gripora's own MSP2 messages are named MSP2_GRIPORA_* (ids 0x5Fxx, in src/main/msp/msp_protocol.h). The Configurator and both radio suites check the identifier and accept API 33.x only, so a change to an MSP message affects all of them. See also MSP Overview.

docs.title: Atomic Barrier implementation
docs.text:
static int markme_bar = 0;
static int markme = 0;

markme++;
// (1) markme is read into register, but not changed
markme_bar++;
// markme_bar is read from memory and incremented
ATOMIC_BLOCK_NB(NVIC_PRIO_TIMER) {
   ATOMIC_BARRIER(markme_bar);
// start of ATOMIC_BLOCK_NB scope:
//  markme_bar is stored into memory (it is input/output - "+m" output operand - of asm volatile)
//  BASEPRI is saved into temporary variable
//  BASEPRI_MAX is decremented to NVIC_PRIO_TIMER (if it is higher than NVIC_PRIO_TIMER or zero; lower number means higher priority on ARM)
   markme++;
// nothing happens, markme value is not needed yet
   markme_bar++;
// (2) markme_bar re-read from memory (ATOMIC_BARRIER marked it as modified - "+m" output operand of asm volatile)
//  and incremented

// end of ATOMIC_BLOCK_NB scope:
//  markme_bar is stored into memory (cleanup function from ATOMIC_BARRIER) / input "m" operand), but kept for later use in register
//    (actually markme_bar+1 is stored and pre-increment value kept in register)
// BASEPRI value is restored
};

markme++;
// register value read in (1) is incremented by 3
markme_bar++;
// register value read in (2) is incremented (actually +=2, because register contains pre-increment value)

// markme and markme_bar are stored into memory

docs.title: Atomic Barrier Warning
docs.text:
The ATOMIC_BLOCK/ATOMIC_BARRIER construction is dependent on gcc extensions. I relies on gcc cleanup function (attribute ((cleanup))) and assumes that cleanup handler is called, when leaving block, even when associated variable is eliminated.

There is (a bit paranoid) safeguard warning to make sure that generated assembly is hand-checked on new gcc version. It is assumed that only major gcc version versions need to be checked.

If GCC is upgraded and a warning appears when compiling then the generated asm source must be verified.

e.g. 

%% serial_softserial.c
warning "Please verify that ATOMIC_BARRIER works as intended"

To perform the verification, proceed as per discusson on issue #167 which reads:

I hope it's enough to check that optimized-away variable still has cleanup code at end of scope.

static int markme=0;
markme++;
ATOMIC_BLOCK_NB(0xff) {
   ATOMIC_BARRIER(markme);
   markme++;
};
markme++;

pass -save-temps=obj (or -save-temps=cwd, but lots of files will end up in same directory as makefile) to gcc link step (LTO is in use), find resulting *.ltrans*.ltrans.s (grep for markme, on linux it ends up in /tmp) and check that generated assembly sequence is:

                 MSR basepri_max, r3
# (possibly markme address load)
                # barier (markme) start

# (increment markme, load and store to memory)
        ldr     r2, [r3]
        adds    r0, r2, #1
        str     r0, [r3]

                # barier(markme)  end
                MSR basepri, r3

# (markme value should be cached in register on next increment)

The # barrier(markme) must surround access code and must be inside MSR basepri instructions .

Similar approach is used for ATOMIC_BLOCK in avr libraries, so gcc should not break this behavior.

IMO attribute(cleanup) and asm volatile is defined in a way that should guarantee this.

attribute(cleanup) is probably safer way to implement atomic sections - another possibility is to explicitly place barriers in code, but that can (and will eventually) lead to missed barrier/basepri restore on same path creating very hard to find bug.

The 'MEMORY_BARRIER()' code can be omitted when 'ATOMIC_BLOCK' (with full memory barriers) is used, but it is better to explicitly state what memory is protected by barrier. gcc 5 can use this knowledge to greatly improve generated code.

docs.title: Blackbox logging internals
docs.text:
The Blackbox is designed to record the raw internal state of the controller at near-maximum rate. By logging the raw inputs and outputs of the control loop, the Blackbox log aims to allow the offline bench-top simulation, debugging, and testing of control algorithms using data collected from real runs. The format was designed for flight controllers (Cleanflight), and the text below keeps its original wording.

A typical logging regime might capture 30 different state variables (for an average of 28 bytes per frame) at a sample rate of 900Hz. That's about 25,000 bytes per second, which is 250,000 baud with a typical 8-N-1 serial encoding.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
Please refer to the source code to clarify anything this document leaves unclear:

  • The firmware's Blackbox logger: blackbox.c, blackbox_io.c, blackbox_fielddefs.h
  • The Gripora Blackbox Explorer, which decodes the logs, is linked from the Gripora GitHub organization.

The encodings and predictors below are the same as in the original Cleanflight/Betaflight format. The field names and the flight-mode fields differ: the firmware source is the reference for which fields a Gripora log contains.

docs.title: What is specific to a Gripora log
docs.text:
The rest of this page is the inherited format specification. These points are where a Gripora log differs from what that text suggests (checked against src/main/blackbox/blackbox.c):

  • Firmware type is Gripora; Firmware revision is Gripora <version> (<git short sha>) <target>.
  • Throttle is signed. rcCommand[4] is the throttle command x1000 around neutral (rc_center): positive is forward, negative is brake or reverse. rcCommand[0..2] are the roll, pitch and yaw sticks (-500..500), and rcCommand[3] is a zero placeholder kept so the field group's encoding does not change.
  • Only yaw (steering) is stabilised. The roll and pitch entries of setpoint, mixer and axisP/I/D/F/B are kept for layout but are always zero. setpoint[3] and mixer[3] are zero placeholders. mixer[2] is the stabilized yaw input, which the car mixer preset sends to the steering servo (S1).
  • Motor fields are signed, so brake/reverse output to a bidirectional motor logs as a negative value.
  • Gripora headers record the active profile's settings: fw_tpa (gain, curve), fw_spa (gain, curve, speed max in km/h), drive_abs (mode, freq, floor, hold, trigger, dyn freq, dyn hold, corner freq, corner hold, in the order of the drive_abs_* CLI settings) and drive_tc (mode, ramp time in ms), along with master_gain, gain_curve, iterm_decay and iterm_relax_level.
  • Debug modes DRIVE (drive state) and DRIVE_AIDS (ABS and traction control) log the car-specific state; their fields are listed in the firmware's Changes.md.

docs.title: Logging cycle
docs.text: Blackbox is designed for flight controllers that are based around the concept of a "main loop". During each main loop iteration, the flight controller will read some state from sensors, run some flight control algorithms, and produce some outputs. For each of these loop iterations, a Blackbox "logging iteration" will be executed. This will read data that was stored during the execution of the main loop and log this data to an attached logging device. The data will include algorithm inputs such as sensor and RC data, intermediate results from flight control algorithms, and algorithm outputs such as motor commands.

docs.title: Log frame types
docs.text: Each event which is recorded to the log is packaged as a "log frame". Blackbox only uses a handful of different types of log frames. Each frame type is identified by a single capital letter.

docs.title: Main frames: I, P
docs.text:
The most basic kind of logged frames are the "main frames". These record the primary state of the flight controller (RC input, gyroscopes, flight control algorithm intermediates, motor outputs), and are logged during every logging iteration.

Each main frame must contain at least two fields, "loopIteration" which records the index of the current main loop iteration (starting at zero for the first logged iteration), and "time" which records the timestamp of the beginning of the main loop in microseconds (this needn't start at zero, on Cleanflight it represents the system uptime).

There are two kinds of main frames, "I" and "P". "I", or "intra" frames are like video keyframes. They can be decoded without reference to any previous frame, so they allow log decoding to be resynchronized in the event of log damage. "P" or "inter" frames use an encoding which references previously logged frames in order to reduce the required datarate. When one interframe fails to decode, all following interframes will be undecodable up until the next intraframe.

docs.title: GPS frames: G, H
docs.text:
Because the GPS is updated so infrequently, GPS data is logged in its own dedicated frames. These are recorded whenever the GPS data changes (not necessarily alongside every main frame). Like the main frames, the GPS frames have their own intra/inter encoding system.

The "H" or "home" frame records the lat/lon of a reference point. The "G" or "GPS" frame records the current state of the GPS system (current position, altitude etc.) based on the reference point. The reference point can be updated (infrequently) during the flight, and is logged whenever it changes.

To allow "G" frames to continue be decoded in the event that an "H" update is dropped from the log, the "H" frame is logged periodically even if it has not changed (say, every 10 seconds). This caps the duration of unreadble "G" frames that will result from a single missed "H" change.

docs.title: Slow frames: S
docs.text:
Some flight controller state is updated very infrequently (on the order of once or twice a minute). Logging the fact that this data had not been updated during every single logging iteration would be a waste of bandwidth, so these frames are only logged when the "slow" state actually changes.

All Slow frames are logged as intraframes. An interframe encoding scheme can't be used for Slow frames, because one damaged frame causes all subsequent interframes to be undecodable. Because Slow frames are written so infrequently, one missing Slow frame could invalidate minutes worth of Slow state.

On Cleanflight, Slow frames are currently used to log data like the user-chosen flight mode and the current failsafe state.

docs.title: Event frames: E
docs.text:
Some flight controller data is updated so infrequently or exists so transiently that we do not log it as a flight controller "state". Instead, we log it as a state transition . This data is logged in "E" or "event" frames. Each event frame payload begins with a single byte "event type" field. The format of the rest of the payload is not encoded in the flight log, so its interpretation is left up to an agreement of the writer and the decoder.

For example, one event that Cleanflight logs is that the user has adjusted a system setting (such as a PID setting) using Cleanflight's inflight adjustments feature. The event payload notes which setting was adjusted and the new value for the setting.

Because these setting updates are so rare, it would be wasteful to treat the settings as "state" and log the fact that the setting had not been changed during every logging iteration. It would be infeasible to periodically log the system settings using an intra/interframe scheme, because the intraframes would be so large. Instead we only log the transitions as events, accept the small probability that any one of those events will be damaged/absent in the log, and leave it up to log readers to decide the extent to which they are willing to assume that the state of the setting between successfully-decoded transition events was truly unchanged.

docs.title: Log field format
docs.text:
For every field in a given frame type, there is an associated name, predictor, and encoding.

When a field is written, the chosen predictor is computed for the field, then this predictor value is subtracted from the raw field value. Finally, the encoder is used to transform the value into bytes to be written to the logging device.

docs.title: Field predictors
docs.text:
The job of the predictor is to bring the value to be encoded as close to zero as possible. The predictor may be based on the values seen for the field in a previous frame, or some other value such as a fixed value or a value recorded in the log headers. For example, the battery voltage values in "I" intraframes in Cleanflight use a reference voltage that is logged as part of the headers as a predictor. This assumes that battery voltages will be broadly similar to the initial pack voltage of the flight (e.g. 4S battery voltages are likely to lie within a small range for the whole flight). In "P" interframes, the battery voltage will instead use the previously-logged voltage as a predictor, because the correlation between successive voltage readings is high.

These predictors are presently available:

docs.title: Predict zero (0)
docs.text: This predictor is the null-predictor which doesn't modify the field value at all. It is a common choice for fields which are already close to zero, or where no better history is available (e.g. in intraframes which may not rely on the previous value of fields).

docs.title: Predict last value (1)
docs.text: This is the most common predictor in interframes. The last-logged value of the field will be used as the predictor, and subtracted from the raw field value. For fields which don't change very often, this will make their encoded value be normally zero. Most fields have some time-correlation, so this predictor should reduce the magnitude of all but the noisiest fields.

docs.title: Predict straight line (2)
docs.text: This predictor assumes that the slope between the current measurement and the previous one will be similar to the slope between the previous measurement and the one before that. This is common for fields which increase at a steady rate, such as the "time" field. The predictor is history_age_2 - 2 * history_age_1.

docs.title: Predict average 2 (3)
docs.text: This predictor is the average of the two previously logged values of the field (i.e. (history_age_1 + history_age_2) / 2 ). It is used when there is significant random noise involved in the field, which means that the average of the recent history is a better predictor of the next value than the previous value on its own would be (for example, in gyroscope or motor measurements).

docs.title: Predict minthrottle (4)
docs.text: This predictor subtracts the value of "minthrottle" which is included in the log header. In Cleanflight, motors always lie in the range of [minthrottle ... maxthrottle] when the craft is armed, so this predictor is used for the first motor value in intraframes.

docs.title: Predict motor[0] (5)
docs.text: This predictor is set to the value of motor[0] which was decoded earlier within the current frame. It is used in intraframes for every motor after the first one, because the motor commands typically lie in a tight grouping.

docs.title: Predict increment (6)
docs.text: This predictor assumes that the field will be incremented by 1 unit for every main loop iteration. This is used to predict the loopIteration field, which increases by 1 for every loop iteration.

docs.title: Predict home-coord (7)
docs.text: This predictor is set to the corresponding latitude or longitude field from the GPS home coordinate (which was logged in a preceding "H" frame). If no preceding "H" frame exists, the value is marked as invalid.

docs.title: Predict 1500 (8)
docs.text: This predictor is set to a fixed value of 1500. It is preferred for logging servo values in intraframes, since these typically lie close to the midpoint of 1500us.

docs.title: Predict vbatref (9)
docs.text: This predictor is set to the "vbatref" field written in the log header. It is used when logging intraframe battery voltages in Cleanflight, since these are expected to be broadly similar to the first battery voltage seen during arming.

docs.title: Predict last main-frame time (10)
docs.text: This predictor is set to the last logged time field from the main frame. This is used when predicting timestamps of non-main frames (e.g. that might be logging the timing of an event that happened during the main loop cycle, like a GPS reading).

docs.title: Field encoders
docs.text:
The field encoder's job is to use fewer bits to represent values which are closer to zero than for values that are further from zero.
