Blackbox supports a range of different encoders, which should be chosen on a per-field basis in order to minimize the encoded data size. The choice of best encoder is based on the probability distribution of the values which are to be encoded. For example, if a field is almost always zero, then an encoding should be chosen for it which can encode that case into a very small number of bits, such as one. Conversely, if a field is normally 8-16 bits large, it would be wasteful to use an encoder which provided a special short encoded representation for zero values, because this will increase the encoded length of larger values.

These encoders are presently available:

docs.title: Unsigned variable byte (1)
docs.text:
This is the most straightforward encoding. This encoding uses the lower 7 bits of an encoded byte to store the lower 7 bits of the field's value. The high bit of that encoded byte is set to one if more than 7 bits are required to store the value. If the value did exceed 7 bits, the lower 7 bits of the value (which were written to the log) are removed from the value (by right shift), and the encoding process begins again with the new value.

This can be represented by the following algorithm:

while (value > 127) {
    writeByte((uint8_t) (value | 0x80)); // Set the high bit to mean "more bytes follow"
    value >>= 7;
}
writeByte(value);

Here are some example values encoded using variable-byte encoding:

Input value Output encoding 1 0x01 42 0x2A 127 0x7F 128 0x80 0x01 129 0x81 0x01 23456 0xA0 0xB7 0x01

docs.title: Signed variable byte (0)
docs.text:
This encoding applies a pre-processing step to fold negative values into positive ones, then the resulting unsigned number is encoded using unsigned variable byte encoding. The folding is accomplished by "ZigZag" encoding, which is represented by:

unsigned32 = (signed32 << 1) ^ (signed32 >> 31)

ZigZag encoding is preferred against simply casting the signed integer to unsigned, because casting would cause small negative quantities to appear to be very large unsigned integers, causing the encoded length to be similarly large. ZigZag encoding ensures that values near zero are still near zero after encoding.

Here are some example integers encoded using ZigZag encoding:

Input value ZigZag encoding 0 0 -1 1 1 2 -2 3 2147483647 4294967294 -2147483648 4294967295

docs.title: Neg 14-bit (3)
docs.text:
The value is negated, treated as an unsigned 14 bit integer, then encoded using unsigned variable byte encoding. This bizarre encoding is used in Cleanflight for battery pack voltages. This is because battery voltages are measured using a 14-bit ADC, with a predictor which is set to the battery voltage during arming, which is expected to be higher than any voltage experienced during flight. After the predictor is subtracted, the battery voltage will almost certainly be below zero.

This results in small encoded values when the voltage is closely below the initial one, at the expense of very large encoded values if the voltage rises higher than the initial one.

docs.title: Elias delta unsigned 32-bit (4)
docs.text:
Because this encoding produces a bitstream, this is the only encoding for which the encoded value might not be a whole number of bytes. If the bitstream isn't aligned on a byte boundary by the time the next non-Elias Delta field arrives, or the end of the frame is reached, the final byte is padded with zeros byte-align the stream. This encoding requires more CPU time than the other encodings because of the bit juggling involved in writing the bitstream.

When this encoder is chosen to encode all of the values in Cleanflight interframes, it saves about 10% bandwidth compared to using a mixture of the other encodings, but uses too much CPU time to be practical.

The basic encoding algorithm is defined on Wikipedia. Given these utility functions:

/* Write `bitCount` bits from the least-significant end of the `bits` integer to the bitstream. The most-significant bit
 * will be written first
 */ 
void writeBits(uint32_t bits, unsigned int bitCount);

/* Returns the number of bits needed to hold the top-most 1-bit of the integer 'i'. 'i' must not be zero. */
unsigned int numBitsToStoreInteger(uint32_t i);

This is our reference implementation of Elias Delta:

// Value must be more than zero
void writeU32EliasDeltaInternal(uint32_t value)
{
    unsigned int valueLen, lengthOfValueLen;

    valueLen = numBitsToStoreInteger(value);
    lengthOfValueLen = numBitsToStoreInteger(valueLen);

    // Use unary to encode the number of bits we'll need to write the length of the value
    writeBits(0, lengthOfValueLen - 1);

    // Now write the length of the value
    writeBits(valueLen, lengthOfValueLen);

    // Having now encoded the position of the top bit of value, write its remaining bits
    writeBits(value, valueLen - 1);
}

To this we add a wrapper which allows encoding both the value zero and MAXINT:

void writeU32EliasDelta(uint32_t value)
{
    /* We can't encode value==0, so we need to add 1 to the value before encoding
     *
     * That would make it impossible to encode MAXINT, so use 0xFFFFFFFF as an escape 
     * code with an additional bit to choose between MAXINT-1 or MAXINT.
     */
    if (value >= 0xFFFFFFFE) {
        // Write the escape code
        writeU32EliasDeltaInternal(0xFFFFFFFF);
        // Add a one bit after the escape code if we wanted "MAXINT", or a zero if we wanted "MAXINT - 1"
        writeBits(value - 0xFFFFFFFE, 1);
    } else {
        writeU32EliasDeltaInternal(value + 1);
    }
}

Here are some reference encoded bit patterns produced by writeU32EliasDelta:

Input value Encoded bit string 0 1 1 0100 2 0101 3 01100 4 01101 5 01110 6 01111 7 00100000 8 00100001 9 00100010 10 00100011 11 00100100 12 00100101 13 00100110 14 00100111 15 001010000 225 00010001100010 4294967292 000001000001111111111111111111111111111101 4294967293 000001000001111111111111111111111111111110 4294967294 0000010000011111111111111111111111111111110 4294967295 0000010000011111111111111111111111111111111

Note that the very common value of zero encodes to a single bit, medium-sized values like 225 encode to 14 bits (an overhead of 4 bits over writing a plain 8 bit value), and typical 32-bit values like 4294967293 encode into 42 bits, an overhead of 10 bits.

docs.title: Elias delta signed 32-bit (5)
docs.text: The value is first converted to unsigned using ZigZag encoding, then unsigned Elias-delta encoding is applied.

docs.title: TAG8_8SVB (6)
docs.text:
First, an 8-bit (one byte) header is written. This header has its bits set to zero when the corresponding field (from a maximum of 8 fields) is set to zero, otherwise the bit is set to one. The least-signficant bit in the header corresponds to the first field to be written. This header is followed by the values of only the fields which are non-zero, written using signed variable byte encoding.

This encoding is preferred for groups of fields in interframes which are infrequently updated by the flight controller. This will mean that their predictions are usually perfect, and so the value to be encoded for each field will normally be zero. This is common for values like RC inputs and barometer readings, which are updated in only a fraction of main loop iterations.

For example, given these field values to encode:

0, 0, 4, 0, 8

This would be encoded:

0b00010100, 0x04, 0x08

docs.title: TAG2_3S32 (7)
docs.text:
A 2-bit header is written, followed by 3 signed field values of up to 32 bits each. The header value is based on the maximum size in bits of the three values to be encoded as follows:

Header value Maximum field value size Field range 0 2 bits [-2...1] 1 4 bits [-8...7] 2 6 bits [-32...31] 3 Up to 32 bits [-2147483648...2147483647]

If any of the three values requires more than 6 bits to encode, a second, 6-bit header value is written in the lower bits of the initial header byte. This second header has 2 bits for each of the encoded values which represents how many bytes are required to encode that value. The least-significant bits of the header represent the first field which is encoded. The values for each possibility are as follows:

Header value Field size Field range 0 1 byte [-127...128] 1 2 bytes [-32768...32767] 2 3 bytes [-8388608...8388607] 3 4 bytes [-2147483648...2147483647]

This header is followed by the actual field values in order, written least-significant byte first, using the byte lengths specified in the header.

So bringing it all together, these encoded bit patterns are possible, where "0" and "1" mean bits fixed to be those values, "A", "B", and "C" represent the first, second and third fields, and "s" represents the bits of the secondary header in the case that any field is larger than 6 bits:

00AA BBCC,
0100 AAAA BBBB CCCC
10AA AAAA 00BB BBBB 00CC CCCC
11ss ssss (followed by fields of byte lengths specified in the "s" header)

This encoding is useful for fields like 3-axis gyroscopes, which are frequently small and typically have similar magnitudes.

docs.title: TAG8_4S16 (8)
docs.text:
An 8-bit header is written, followed by 4 signed field values of up to 16 bits each. The 8-bit header value has 2 bits for each of the encoded fields (the least-significant bits represent the first field) which represent the number of bits required to encode that field as follows:

Header value Field value size Field range 0 0 bits [0...0] 1 4 bits [-8...7] 2 8 bits [-128...127] 3 16 bits [-32768...32767]

This header is followed by the actual field values in order, written as if the output stream was a bit-stream, with the most-significant bit of the first field ending up in the most-significant bits of the first written byte. If the number of nibbles written is odd, the final byte has its least-significant nibble set to zero.

For example, given these field values:

13, 0, 4, 2

Choosing from the allowable field value sizes, they may be encoded using this many bits each:

8, 0, 4, 4

The corresponding header values for these lengths would be:

2, 0, 1, 1

So the header and fields would be encoded together as:

0b01010010, 0x0D, 0x42

docs.title: NULL (9)
docs.text: This encoding does not write any bytes to the file. It is used when the predictor will always perfectly predict the value of the field, so the remainder is always zero. In practice this is only used for the "loopIteration" field in interframes, which is always perfectly predictable based on the logged frame's position in the sequence of frames and the "P interval" setting from the header.

docs.title: Log file structure
docs.text:
A logging session begins with a log start marker, then a header section which describes the format of the log, then the log payload data, and finally an optional "log end" event ("E" frame).

A single log file can be comprised of one or more logging sessions. Each session may be preceded and followed by any amount of non-Blackbox data. This data is ignored by the Blackbox log decoding tools. This allows for the logging device to be alternately used by the Blackbox and some other system (such as MSP) without requiring the ability to begin a separate log file for each separate activity.

docs.title: Log start marker
docs.text: The log start marker is "H Product:Blackbox flight data recorder by Nicholas Sherlock\n". This marker is used to discover the beginning of the flight log if the log begins partway through a file. Because it is such a long string, it is not expected to occur by accident in any sequence of random bytes from other log device users.

docs.title: Log header
docs.text:
The header is comprised of a sequence of lines of plain ASCII text. Each header line has the format H fieldname:value and ends with a '\n'. The overall header does not have a terminator to separate it from the log payload (the header implicitly ends when a line does not begin with an 'H' character).

The header can contain some of these fields:

docs.title: Data version (required)
docs.text:
When the interpretation of the Blackbox header changes due to Blackbox specification updates, the log version is incremented to allow backwards-compatibility in the decoder:

H Data version:2

docs.title: Logging interval
docs.text: Not every main loop iteration needs to result in a Blackbox logging iteration. When a loop iteration is not logged, Blackbox is not called, no state is read from the flight controller, and nothing is written to the log. Two header lines are included to note which main loop iterations will be logged:

docs.title: I interval
docs.text:
This header notes which of the main loop iterations will record an "I" intraframe to the log. If main loop iterations with indexes divisible by 32 will be logged as "I" frames, the header will be:

H I interval: 32

The first main loop iteration seen by Blackbox will be numbered with index 0, so the first main loop iteration will always be logged as an intraframe.

docs.title: P interval
docs.text:
Not every "P" interframe needs to be logged. Blackbox will log a portion of iterations in order to bring the total portion of logged main frames to a user-chosen fraction. This fraction is called the logging rate. The smallest possible logging rate is (1/I interval) which corresponds to logging only "I" frames at the "I" interval and discarding all other loop iterations. The maximum logging rate is 1/1, where every main loop iteration that is not an "I" frame is logged as a "P" frame. The header records the logging rate fraction in numerator/denominator format like so:

H P interval:1/2

The logging fraction given by num/denom should be simplified (i.e. rather than 2/6, a logging rate of 1/3 should be used).

Given a logging rate of num/denom and an I-frame interval of I_INTERVAL, the frame type to log for an iteration of index iteration is given by:

if (iteration % I_INTERVAL == 0)
    return 'I';

if ((iteration % I_INTERVAL + num - 1) % denom < num)
    return 'P';

return '.'; // i.e. don't log this iteration

For an I-interval of 32, these are the resulting logging patterns at some different P logging rates.

Logging rate Main frame pattern Actual portion logged 1 / 32 I...............................I...............................I 0.03 1 / 6 I.....P.....P.....P.....P.....P.I.....P.....P.....P.....P.....P.I 0.19 1 / 3 I..P..P..P..P..P..P..P..P..P..P.I..P..P..P..P..P..P..P..P..P..P.I 0.34 1 / 2 I.P.P.P.P.P.P.P.P.P.P.P.P.P.P.P.I.P.P.P.P.P.P.P.P.P.P.P.P.P.P.P.I 0.50 2 / 3 I.PP.PP.PP.PP.PP.PP.PP.PP.PP.PP.I.PP.PP.PP.PP.PP.PP.PP.PP.PP.PP.I 0.66 5 / 6 I.PPPPP.PPPPP.PPPPP.PPPPP.PPPPP.I.PPPPP.PPPPP.PPPPP.PPPPP.PPPPP.I 0.81 1 / 1 IPPPPPPPPPPPPPPPPPPPPPPPPPPPPPPPIPPPPPPPPPPPPPPPPPPPPPPPPPPPPPPPI 1.00

docs.title: Firmware type (optional)
docs.text:
Because Blackbox records the internal flight controller state, the interpretation of the logged data will depend on knowing which flight controller recorded it. To accomodate this, the name of the flight controller should be recorded:

H Firmware type:Cleanflight

More details should be included to help narrow down the precise flight-controller version (but these are not required):

H Firmware revision:c49bd40
H Firmware date:Aug 28 2015 16:49:11

docs.title: Field X name (required)
docs.text:
This header is a comma-separated list of the names for the fields in the 'X' frame type:

H Field I name:loopIteration,time,axisP[0],axisP[1]...

The decoder assumes that the fields in the 'P' frame type will all have the same names as those in the 'I' frame, so a "Field P name" header does not need to be supplied.

docs.title: Field X signed (optional)
docs.text:
This is a comma-separated list of integers which are set to '1' when their corresponding field's value should be interpreted as signed after decoding, or '0' otherwise:

H Field I signed:0,0,1,1...

docs.title: Field X predictor (required)
docs.text:
This is a comma-separated list of integers which specify the predictors for each field in the specified frame type:

H Field I predictor:0,0,0,0...

docs.title: Field X encoding (required)
docs.text:
This is a comma-separated list of integers which specify the encoding used for each field in the specified frame type:

H Field X encoding:1,1,0,0...

docs.title: vbatref
docs.text: This header provides the reference voltage that will be used by predictor #9.

docs.title: minthrottle
docs.text: This header provides the minimum value sent by Cleanflight to the ESCs when armed, it is used by predictor #4.

docs.title: Additional headers
docs.text:
The decoder ignores headers that it does not understand, so you can freely add any headers that you require in order to properly interpret the meaning of the logged values.

For example, to create a graphical displays of RC sticks and motor percentages, the Blackbox rendering tool requires the additional headers "rcRate" and "maxthrottle". In order to convert raw gyroscope, accelerometer and voltage readings into real-world units, the Blackbox decoder requires the calibration constants "gyro.scale", "acc_1G" and "vbatscale". These headers might look like:

H rcRate:100
H maxthrottle:1980
H gyro.scale:0x3d79c190
H acc_1G:4096
H vbatscale:110

docs.title: Log payload
docs.text:
The log payload is a concatenated sequence of logged frames. Each frame type which is present in the log payload must have been previously described in the log header (with Frame X name, etc. headers). Each frame begins with a single capital letter to specify the type of frame (I, P, etc), which is immediately followed by the frame's field data. There is no frame length field, checksum, or trailer.

The field data is encoded by taking an array of raw field data, computing the predictor for each field, subtrating this predictor from the field, then applying the field encoders to each field in sequence to serialize them to the log.

For example, imagine that we are encoding three fields in an intraframe, are using zero-predictors for each field (#0), and are encoding the values using the unsigned variable byte encoding (#1). For these field values:

1, 2, 3

We would encode a frame:

'I', 0x01, 0x02, 0x03

Imagine that we are encoding an array of motor commands in an interframe. We will use the previous motor commands as a predictor, and encode the resulting values using signed variable byte encoding. The motor command values seen in the previous logged iteration were:

1430, 1500, 1470, 1490

And the motor commands to be logged in this iteration are:

1635, 1501, 1469, 1532

After subtracting the predictors for each field, we will be left with:

205, 1, -1, 42

We will apply ZigZag encoding to each field, which will give us:

410, 2, 1, 84

We will use unsigned variable byte encoding to write the resulting values to the log, which will give us:

'P', 0x9A, 0x03, 0x02, 0x01, 0x54

docs.title: Log end marker
docs.text:
The log end marker is an optional Event ("E") frame of type 0xFF whose payload is the string "End of log\0". The payload ensures that random data does not look like an end-of-log marker by chance. This event signals the tidy ending of the log. All following bytes until the next log-begin marker (or end of file) should be ignored by the log decoder.

'E', 0xFF, "End of log", 0x00

docs.title: Log validation
docs.text:
Any damage experienced to the log during recording is overwhelmingly due to subsequences of bytes being dropped by the logging device due to overflowing buffers. Accordingly, Blackbox logs do not bother to include any checksums (bytes are not expected to be damaged by the logging device without changing the length of the message). Because of the tight bandwidth requirements of logging, neither a frame length field nor frame trailer is recorded that would allow for the detection of missing bytes.

Instead, the decoder uses a heuristic in order to detect damaged frames. The decoder reads an entire frame from the log (using the decoder for each field which is the counterpart of the encoder specified in the header), then it checks to see if the byte immediately following the frame, which should be the beginning of a next frame, is a recognized frame-type byte (e.g. 'I', 'P', 'E', etc). If that following byte represents a valid frame type, it is assumed that the decoded frame was the correct length (so was unlikely to have had random ranges of bytes removed from it, which would have likely altered the frame length). Otherwise, the frame is rejected, and a valid frame-type byte is looked for immediately after the frame-start byte of the frame that was rejected. A rejected frame causes all subsequent interframes to be rejected as well, up until the next intraframe.

A frame is also rejected if the "loopIteration" or "time" fields have made unreasonable leaps forward, or moved at all backwards. This suffices to detect almost all log corruption.

docs.title: Configuration Format
docs.text:
The configuration format and external protocol use some of the same concepts as SAE J1939. A parameter group (PG) is a set of parameters belonging to the same topic and are stored and sent together. A parameter group instance has a unique parameter group number (PGN). Each parameter also has a suspect parameter number (SPN) which can be used to get or set a parameter directly.

When used as on-wire formats structures should be packed to give the same in storage, in memory, and on-wire format. However care must be taken over memory alignment issues when packing structures.

The PGs can be defined on a system-wide basis on a profile specific basis. profiles can be activated on the fly.

The storage consists of a header, zero or more PGs, a footer and a checksum. To keep the RAM usage low, the parameters are written directly to flash which means that things that are only known at the end, such as the size are stored in the footer. The checksum is written after the footer.

The header holds:

  • The format number. This is bumped on incompatible changes.

Each stored PG holds:

  • The size of this record
  • The PGN
  • Version number
  • Profile number
  • Flags
  • The record format. This is bumped on incompatible changes.
  • The PG data

The footer holds:

  • A zero to mark the end of data

The checksum is based on the header, PGs, and footer.

The PG registrations hold similar but not identical information (e.g. the profile number is not known until it is stored).

docs.title: Initialisation function.
docs.text: All fields are reset to 0 upon initialisation and then if a reset function is defined for the group then initial settings can be defined by the system.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text:
Upgrades are done at the PG level. pgLoad() (src/main/pg/pg.c) first resets the group to its defaults, then restores the stored data only if the stored version matches the registered one, copying no more than the smaller of the two sizes. A version mismatch keeps the defaults for that whole group.

Gripora bumps the PG version on every change to a group, including new fields, defaults and ranges, so an upgrade resets a changed group to its defaults instead of mixing old and new data. See Parameter Groups.

docs.title: Downgrading
docs.text: Downgrades are done at the PG level. Any trailing, unrecognised fields will be silently dropped on load. Saving the config back to flash will discard these unrecognised fields.

docs.title: Incompatible changes
docs.text: An incompatible change is where a field is inserted, deleted from the middle, reordered, resized (including changing the size of a contained array), or has the meaning changed. Such changes should be handled by bumping the PG version field or allocating a new PGN.

docs.title: Custom Board Configuration Using CLI
docs.text:
Warning: this is beyond the normal use case. Use a pre-made board configuration for a controller board that has been tested, from the gripora-targets repository.

Gripora can support a custom controller board, as long as it uses supported hardware. Before you start, check that your MCU and peripherals are supported, and test your hardware separately. Then flash the matching unified target (see Building the Firmware) and configure the pins from the CLI.

Use the resource command to map each peripheral to a pin:

  • # resource lists the current assignments
  • resource <resource> [<index>] <pin> assigns one, for example resource SERVO 1 B0
  • resource <resource> [<index>] none frees it

The timer and dma commands attach a timer or DMA channel to a pin. Servo and motor outputs, and some other functions such as battery voltage monitoring, need this:

  • # timer
  • timer <pin> AF(x) [1-3]
  • # dma
  • dma [SPI_TX|ADC|pin] [index|pin] [0|1]

Use save to store the configuration. For anything beyond this, use the pre-made board configurations as a reference.

docs.title: Create a Customized Version
docs.text:
Controller boards have limited flash and RAM, so the features built into the official firmware are a compromise. If you build your own firmware you can switch features on and off to save space or to enable something the official build leaves out.

Keep in mind that a firmware you build yourself is a piece of software that you are responsible for. It can have bugs that the official version does not, and enabling a feature that the developers left off may overload the processor or overflow flash or RAM. Do not drive with it before you have tested it on the bench, with the wheels off the ground.

This is for people who can already build the firmware from source. See Building the Firmware for the toolchain and targets, and Code Guidelines and Testing for contribution guidelines. Choose a unified target that matches your MCU:

make TARGET=STM32F405

The build ends with a size summary:

   text    data     bss     dec     hex filename

text + data is the flash used, and data + bss is the static RAM used. Keep them under the flash and RAM size of your MCU.

docs.title: Where features are chosen
docs.text:
• src/main/target/common_pre.h sets the features that are on or off for all targets, and often depends on the flash size of the MCU. This is the first place to look.
  • src/main/target/common_post.h and common_deprecated_post.h derive dependent settings after the target file has been read.
  • The unified target's own target.h (in src/main/target/STM32_UNIFIED/) covers what is specific to an MCU family.

A feature is a USE_ macro. To remove a feature you do not use, such as a receiver or telemetry protocol, remove or #undef its USE_ macro, and rebuild to see how much flash it saves.

You can also pass a macro on the command line without editing the files:

make TARGET=STM32F405 OPTIONS="USE_SOMETHING"

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Change one thing at a time and rebuild. Some features depend on others, and the build will tell you when something you removed is still in use.
  • Removing a receiver or telemetry protocol you never use is the safest way to gain space.
  • If you enable a feature that is commented out or disabled by default, keep an eye on the CPU load, which you can see with the CLI tasks command.

docs.title: ESC telemetry wiring auto-detect — design
docs.text: Same mechanism as RX serial wiring auto-detect, applied to the ESC telemetry port (escSensorConfig) instead of the RX port(s). Read that doc first for the underlying rationale (why this needs a live re-init rather than just a configurator-side reboot loop, the general shape of the trial state machine, the UART invert/pin-swap latch bug it uncovered and fixed). This note only covers what's different here.

docs.title: What's different from the RX version
docs.text:
• No inverted bit. escSensorInit() (src/main/sensors/esc_sensor.c) always opens the port SERIAL_NOT_INVERTED - ESC telemetry protocols don't invert. So this is a 4-combo search (halfDuplex × pinSwap), not 8.
  • No baud confound. Every protocol here has a baud fixed by the protocol itself (115200/19200/38400 depending on which), not a user-configurable or negotiated one - CRSF's crsf_use_negotiated_baud had no analogue to worry about.
  • Graupner requires half-duplex to function at all (single-wire request/response - validateAndFixEscSensorConfig() already forces it on for exactly this reason), rather than merely ignoring the bit the way CRSF/GHST do for RX. Pinned rather than varied, same treatment either way.
  • Better signal-detection primitive. The RX version used rxIsReceivingSignal(), a boolean that decays after ~100ms without a fresh frame - fine for streaming protocols, but it flickered false between frames for anything slower than ~10Hz and produced a real false-negative on CRSF during bench testing. ESC telemetry already has a plain monotonic totalFrameCount counter, incremented by every protocol's own decode path only on a structurally/checksum-valid frame. Success is declared once that counter has advanced by ESC_SENSOR_TRIAL_MIN_FRAMES (2) since the combo was applied - a delta check, immune to the "gap between frames" flicker entirely, so no debounce timer was needed this time.
  • Some protocols don't have a UART to test at all: Castle Link (PWM edge timing, no serial port), FBUS and SRXL2 ESC telemetry (each reads via its own dedicated port function, not FUNCTION_ESC_SENSOR). All three are clean REJECTED cases, mirroring "no serial port assigned."
  • Settle timing split by decode mechanism, not per-protocol guesswork: protocols that go through the shared "rrfsm" (request/response) decode engine (HW5, Scorpion, OpenYGE, FLY, Graupner, XDFLY, ZTW, OMPHOBBY - see the dispatch switch in escSensorProcess()) poll the ESC rather than just listening to a continuous stream, so get the longer settle tier. BLHeli32, HW4, Kontronik, APD, and Record get the default (faster) tier.

docs.title: MSP
docs.text:
One new command, MSP2_GRIPORA_ESC_SENSOR_TRIAL (0x5F14 - 0x5F12/0x5F13 are claimed by the RX wiring auto-detect PR's MSP2_GRIPORA_RX_SERIAL_TRIAL/ MSP2_GRIPORA_RX_INPUT_BACKUP_TRIAL, deliberately skipped rather than colliding, since both branches were cut from master independently and each just grabbed the next free slot from its own starting point). Same start/poll/stop action-byte shape as the RX version and MSP2_GRIPORA_BOARD_AUTO_ALIGN. Response layout is one field shorter than the RX version's (no inverted byte):

U8 state, U8 comboIndex, U8 halfDuplex, U8 pinSwap, U16 elapsedMs

docs.title: Open items pending bench testing
docs.text: Same category as the RX version: the settle-time tiers are informed starting points (this time from which decode engine a protocol uses, not a guess at protocol identity alone), not measurements. Needs real ESCs on the bench across a few different telemetry protocols before trusting the timing, same as CRSF needed for the RX version.

docs.title: Steering Control Dynamics: Signal Chain, Design Rationale and Known Defects
docs.text:
This document describes how Gripora turns the driver's steering and throttle into steering-servo and ESC commands. It records why each stage is built the way it is, and lists the known defects and limitations. Read it before changing steering-control code: src/main/flight/{setpoint,pid,drive,drive_aids,speed_atten,mixer,servos,motors}.c, src/main/fc/rc.c, src/main/fc/core.c and src/main/flight/failsafe.c.

The page keeps its old address (contributing/tech/flight-dynamics/) because source comments and the firmware's AGENTS.md link to it. Directory and file names such as src/main/flight/ are inherited from the fixed-wing firmware Gripora was forked from (WingFlight).

Scope. Everything between the receiver and the servo/motor outputs: RC processing, setpoint shaping, the steering rate PID, the drive state, speed and throttle gain attenuation, GYRO OFF, DRIFT, the drive aids (ABS, traction control and launch control), the mixer, servo and motor output, and the arming and failsafe logic that overrides them.

Basis. A static read of the firmware source at the time of writing, checked against the unit tests where they exist. Nothing here was verified by driving. Where a statement depends on behaviour that can only be observed on a car, it says so.

docs.title: 1. Conventions
docs.text:
These are easy to get wrong.

Item Convention Where Axes Only yaw (steering) is stabilised. Roll and pitch keep their slots in every per-axis array, PID and rate profile, MSP message and Blackbox field, but their setpoints and PID outputs are always zero. setpointUpdate() zeroes roll/pitch setpoints; pidResetRollPitch() in pid.c Yaw sign RC yaw (steering stick) is clockwise-positive; gyro yaw is negative for the same motion. setpoint.c negates the RC yaw once, and everything downstream keeps that sign. GYRO OFF negates the raw channel the same way, so the steering direction is the same with and without the gyro. setpointUpdate(), mixerUpdateInputs() Pitch sign attitude.values.pitch / attitude.raw[PITCH] are positive nose-down (inherited Betaflight convention). Nothing in the steering loop uses pitch; it matters for attitude telemetry and the Blackbox attitude field. imu.c Throttle Signed, -1..1 around rc_center: forward above, brake/reverse below. Inputs within 10 µs of centre are neutral (RC_THROTTLE_NEUTRAL_DEADBAND). "Throttle off" for arming, auto-disarm and failsafe is the stick within 15 µs of centre (isThrottleOff(): that deadband plus RC_THROTTLE_DEADBAND, 5 µs). fc/rc.c Channel order Default map RT1234AE: CH1 steering, CH2 throttle, CH3-CH6 AUX1-4. Roll and pitch are unused and parked on CH7/CH8. pg/rx.c (rcmap) PID output The PID sum is a unitless steering command: ±1.0 is the full stabilized-yaw mixer input, which the default rule sends to S1 at weight 1000, i.e. full servo scale. pidSum into MIXER_IN_STABILIZED_YAW; limits ±1000 in pg/mixer.c Units Setpoint and gyro rate in °/s. axisError (the I accumulator) in degrees, limited by error_limit (degrees). Drive speeds in km/h (settings in 0.1 km/h). pid.c, drive.c Loop timing pid.dT comes from gyro.targetLooptime. With pid_process_denom > 1, taskMainPidLoop() in core.c spreads setpoint → PID → mixer → servo across consecutive ticks. activePidLoopDenom cases

docs.title: Signal chain
docs.text:
RX (rx.c) ─► rcInput ─► rc.c: deadbands, ±1 deflection; throttle signed -1..1 around rc_center
                              │
                              ▼
        setpoint.c: yaw sign ─► smoothing ─► yaw dynamic deadband/ceiling
                    ─► response/accel limit (sp.deflection) ─► boost ─► rates curve (sp.setpoint)
                    roll and pitch setpoints forced to 0
                              │
                              ▼
        pid.c: driveUpdate() + speedAttenUpdate(), yaw I cleared on a direction change
               yaw gyro × (yaw_gyro_reverse ? -1 : 1) × travel direction (±1)
               P, D: Kp/Kd · masterGain · gainCurve · atten · corr
               I:    Ki · masterGain · corr · axisError
               F, B: Kf/Kb · atten            (atten = max(TPA · SPA, 0.25), corr = drive correction scale)
               DRIFT: P = counter-steer(gyro past drift_allow) · atten · corr, D as above,
                      I = 0, F = raw steering deflection, B = 0
                              │
                              ▼
        mixer.c inputs: STABILIZED_YAW = pidSum   (GYRO OFF: raw steering channel instead)
                        STABILIZED_THROTTLE = driveAidsApply(throttle)   (failsafe: failsafe_throttle instead)
                              │
                        rule table (default: STABILIZED_YAW → S1, STABILIZED_THROTTLE → M1)
                              │
              servos.c (curve, speed, reverse, scale, trim, travel)      motors.c (bidirectional: 0 = neutral)

drive.c reads the stabilized throttle the mixer sent on the previous loop (failsafe included) as its command input, so the drive state follows what the ESC is actually told to do.

docs.title: 2. Subsystems: what they do and why
2.1 RC processing — fc/rc.c
docs.text: Each stick is centred on rc_center, a per-axis deadband is removed (roll_deadband, pitch_deadband, yaw_deadband; the throttle uses a fixed 10 µs), and the result is scaled to ±1 by rc_deflection. The throttle is that same signed deflection: there is no 0..1 throttle any more. getThrottle() returns it; the Blackbox logs it x1000 as rcCommand[4]. AUX channels are passed on as rcInput − rc_center.

docs.title: 2.2 Setpoint shaping — flight/setpoint.c
docs.text:
Order of operations: yaw negation, smoothing (cutoff derived from the measured RX frame interval), yaw dynamic deadband/ceiling, response-time and acceleration limit (→ sp.deflection), setpoint boost, rates curve (→ sp.setpoint). Roll and pitch are computed and then set to zero; their stick deflection is still available to mixer rules through the RC inputs.

  • Smoothing tied to the RX frame rate. Inherited from Rotorflight: it removes stair-stepping from slow link updates without a fixed lag.
  • Rates. rcRates × 5 °/s at full stick on the default curve. The default yaw rate is 150 °/s (pg/rates.c); the Configurator's setup wizard driving styles set 90 (Beginner), 150 (Sport) or 300 °/s (Drift).
  • Yaw dynamic deadband is on by default (yaw_dynamic_deadband_gain 10), inherited.

docs.title: 2.3 Steering rate PID — flight/pid.c
docs.text:
error = setpoint − gyroRate, on yaw only (pid_mode 1; any value other than 0 runs mode 1). Before the error is formed, the yaw gyro rate is negated if yaw_gyro_reverse is on, and multiplied by the travel direction from the drive state (§2.4). Terms:

Term Formula Notes P Kp · masterGain · gainCurve · atten · corr · error I Ki · masterGain · corr · axisError Not attenuated by TPA or SPA. Accumulation is also scaled by corr. D Kd · masterGain · gainCurve · atten · corr · d/dt(−gyro) Gyro-only D (no setpoint kick). Default D = 0. F Kf · atten · setpoint Carries the steady stick response. Not scaled by corr, so the stick always steers. B Kb · atten · d/dt(setpoint) Feedforward boost. Not scaled by corr.

atten = max(TPA × SPA, 0.25) (PID_ATTENUATION_MIN); corr is driveGetCorrectionScale() (§2.4).

Default authority (defaults from pg/pid.c, scale constants from flight/pid.h): yaw P 190, I 45, D 0, F 65, B 35, error_limit 60°.

Quantity Value P at 100 °/s error 190 × 6.67e-6 × 100 ≈ 0.13 of full travel I ceiling (Ki · error_limit) 45 × 2e-4 × 60 = 0.54 of full travel F per °/s 65 × 2.5e-5 = 0.0016, so 615 °/s of setpoint is full travel from F alone F at full stick, default 150 °/s ≈ 0.24 of full travel

Design decisions:

  • Gyro reversed for reverse travel, stick unchanged. The yaw response to a steering angle is proportional to the signed speed (yaw rate ≈ v · tan(steer) / wheelbase), so reversing flips its sign and a forward tune becomes positive feedback. The stick keeps meaning "wheel angle" in both directions, so correcting in reverse is exactly negating the gyro rate the loop sees: P, I and D all follow, F and B are untouched (pid.c pidApplyGyroRate(), drive.c header comment).
  • yaw_gyro_reverse (PID config PG v4) negates only this loop's yaw gyro, for when the gyro corrects the wrong way (typically a reversed steering channel fixed with a servo reverse). Board orientation and the attitude estimate are unchanged. It is in MSP_MIXER_CONFIG as an optional trailing byte.
  • Correction scale on P, I and D only. At a standstill there is no yaw response to correct with, so P and D would only push the steering and I would wind up; F and B carry the stick and must always steer the wheels.
  • I-term cleared on a direction change, because it was accumulated for the other sign of the plant.
  • I held at zero while disarmed (yaw only): on the bench the car cannot respond, and whatever built up would arrive as a steering bump on arming. P and D still act while disarmed so the setup wizard's gyro-direction check (turn the car by hand, the wheels steer against it) works.
  • Throttle gain attenuation (fw_tpa_gain, fw_tpa_curve). A baseline scale times an optional curve from the shared gain-curve pool, evaluated on |throttle| (0..1), mirroring master_gain + gain_curve. Applied to P, D, F and B, not I.
  • Speed attenuation (fw_spa_gain, fw_spa_curve, fw_spa_speed_max), flight/speed_atten.c. A car's yaw response to a steering angle grows with speed, so a tune that is right at moderate speed can oscillate flat out; TPA cannot see that when the throttle is closed at speed. Same shape as TPA, with the curve evaluated at speed / fw_spa_speed_max (default 60 km/h, range 10-300). Multiplied with TPA.
    • Speed source: the RPM wheel speed from the drive state when there is an RPM source, otherwise GPS (max(speed3d, groundSpeed); only u-blox reports 3D speed).
    • Filtering: low-passed at 1 Hz (FW_SPA_SPEED_CUTOFF_HZ).
    • Speed loss (no RPM source and no GPS fix): hold the last scale for 3 s, then slew back to 1.0 at 0.2/s. Engaging (first speed, speed regained, profile change) slews onto the curve at the same rate.
    • With no curve SPA is exactly 1.0. Per PID profile, in PG_FW_SPA_CONFIG (v1). Unit-tested in speed_atten_unittest.
  • Master gain applied at the point of use, not baked into coef[], so live adjustments stay correct whichever adjustment last touched a coefficient.
  • I-term relax (iterm_relax, the "bounceback" score 1-10, default 5, and iterm_relax_level, default 22 °/s): a high-pass of the setpoint scales I accumulation down during fast steering input. pidItermRelaxCutoff() maps the score to the setpoint low-pass cutoff (50, 30, 20, 15, 10, 8, 7, 6, 5, 3 Hz). Always on.
  • I-term decay (iterm_decay_time, default 60 = 0.6 s time constant, range 1-100; iterm_decay_limit, default 35 °/s): I bleeds continuously, so a stale I-term does not hold the steering off centre.
  • Anti-windup: accumulation stops only when the stabilized-yaw mixer input is saturated and the error would push further into saturation (pidAxisSaturated()). Servo travel clipping also raises saturation (mixerSaturateServoOutput()), so trim-induced clipping is covered. Saturation flags last MIXER_SATURATION_TIME (5) ticks.
  • I held in GYRO OFF. While GYRO OFF drives the steering (mixerStabilizationBypassed(), false once failsafe is active) the gyro is not tracking the setpoint, so I is not integrated; decay still runs.
  • Gyro overflow (gyroOverflowDetected()): pidReset() zeroes all PID state and outputs.

Mode 0 (pid_mode = 0) outputs F only: a stick-proportional command with no gyro. DRIFT (§2.6) replaces mode 1 only; in mode 0 it does nothing.

docs.title: 2.4 Drive state — flight/drive.c, PG_DRIVE_CONFIG
docs.text:
The drive state estimates the travel direction and the wheel speed for the steering loop and the drive aids.

  • Inputs. The stabilized throttle sent to the ESC (failsafe included), and the motor RPM when motor 1 has an RPM source (DShot telemetry, ESC telemetry or a frequency sensor), averaged with motor 2 if it has one too. RPM is a magnitude: no source reports a direction, so the direction comes from what the ESC was commanded to do. Wheel speed = motor RPM ÷ motor1_gear_ratio × π × drive_wheel_diameter, filtered at 10 Hz. Stopped = below 1 km/h for 0.1 s.
  • ESC model, drive_esc_mode. The commanded state (neutral, forward, brake, reverse) follows the ESC's own rules. A command within 5 % of neutral is neutral.
    • FWD_BRK_REV: below neutral brakes after forward; back to neutral (held at least 50 ms, DRIVE_NEUTRAL_DWELL_S), then below again, reverses. A brake or reverse carries on while the stick stays below neutral. Reverse is also the first below-neutral command after arming.
    • FWD_REV: below neutral reverses, braking or coasting first while RPM shows the car still rolling forward.
    • FWD_BRK: below neutral only ever brakes.
    • AUTO: FWD_REV on a DShot protocol (the AM32 default), FWD_BRK_REV otherwise. An AM32 with "RC car reverse" on needs FWD_BRK_REV set by hand.
  • Direction with RPM changes only at zero speed: an RPM-confirmed standstill, or the moment the wheels pass through zero (the unfiltered speed shows it). Braking while rolling forward is never taken for reverse. Wheels speeding up from zero under a below-neutral command are taken as reverse in every mode that can reverse, and under an above-neutral command as forward, so a reversal the model did not expect (a sensored ESC, an AM32 reversing at its own threshold) is still caught.
  • Direction without RPM follows the command at once (forward +1, reverse −1; brake and neutral keep it). The ESC may brake or coast for a while before it really changes direction, so on each change the correction scale drops to zero and fades back in over 1 s (DRIVE_DIR_CHANGE_RAMP_S).
  • Correction scale = speed factor × reverse factor × ramp factor:
    • speed factor (RPM only): 0 below drive_gyro_min_speed (default 2.0 km/h, never below 1.0 km/h, the stop speed, so the correction is faded out before the direction can flip), rising linearly to 1 at drive_gyro_full_speed (default 6.0 km/h, always above the minimum). Without RPM it is 1.
    • reverse factor: 1 forward; in reverse drive_gyro_reverse_gain % (default 50), or 0 with drive_gyro_reverse OFF.
    • ramp factor: the 1 s fade after an unconfirmed direction change.
  • Disarmed the state is held at neutral and forward, the ramp is complete and the speed factor is not applied, so the gyro corrects on the bench (with I held at zero, §2.3). Every arming starts from neutral and forward.
  • Debug mode DRIVE: throttle command x1000, commanded state, direction, speed x10, speed known, correction scale x1000, motor 1 RPM, stopped. Unit-tested in drive_unittest.

docs.title: 2.5 GYRO OFF — flight/mixer.c
docs.text:
BOXPASSTHROUGH, shown as GYRO OFF (permanent id 12). While it is on and failsafe is not active, the stabilized-yaw mixer input is replaced by the steering channel's deflection, negated to keep the stabilized sign (§1): no rates, no expo, no PID. It is written directly (mixerSetBypassInput()), so the stabilized-yaw input's min/max limits do not apply; the input rate and the servo's own limits still do. While disarmed, a bench override or a wiggle still wins over the switch.

Only the steering is bypassed. The throttle still goes through the drive aids (§2.7); DRIVE AIDS OFF is the separate switch for those.

docs.title: 2.6 DRIFT — flight/pid.c pidApplyDrift(), PG_DRIFT_CONFIG
docs.text:
BOXDRIFT, permanent id 68. While it is on and failsafe is not active (mixerDriftActive()), and pid_mode is not 0, pidApplyDrift() runs on yaw instead of mode 1:

Term Formula Notes F −getRcDeflection(YAW) The steering wheel straight through, negated as in GYRO OFF (§1). No rates, no expo, not attenuated, not scaled by corr. P clamp(−drift_gain/100 · excess / 360, ±drift_limit/100) · atten · corr The counter-steer. excess is the gyro rate (sign and travel direction as in §2.3) beyond ±drift_allow, zero inside it. DRIFT_FULL_RATE = 360 °/s. D Kd · masterGain · atten · corr · d/dt(−gyro) As in mode 1, but without the master gain curve. I 0 axisError is held at zero. B 0 The rate setpoint is still computed (for the log) and fed to the B filter.

Design decisions:

  • Wheel angle, not turn rate, from the stick. In a drift the front wheels point against the rotation, so a rate setpoint from the stick would ask for the wrong sign. The driver sets the wheel angle; the gyro only adds counter-steer once the rotation passes an allowance, which holds a slip angle and catches over-rotation.
  • No I-term. Heading hold would fight the drift. Holding axisError at zero also means leaving DRIFT starts mode 1 clean.
  • The counter-steer is the P term, so it is logged as axisP[2] and scaled by atten and corr exactly as P is in mode 1: none at a standstill with RPM, reduced in reverse, faded after an unconfirmed direction change.
  • Master gain and Kp don't scale the counter-steer; drift_gain alone sets it.
  • Through the stabilized-yaw input, unlike GYRO OFF: the input's min/max limits apply. pidSum is not clamped in pid.c; the input limits (±1000) hold it to full travel.
  • Precedence: GYRO OFF's bypass is written after the PID output in mixerUpdateInputs(), so GYRO OFF wins over DRIFT; failsafe turns both off.

Settings per PID profile (drift_gain 100 %, 0-200; drift_allow 30 °/s, 0-720; drift_limit 100 %, 10-100), in PG_DRIFT_CONFIG (1030), copied and reset with the profile. MSP MSP2_GRIPORA_DRIFT_CONFIG / SET (0x5F42/0x5F43); Blackbox header drift. Unit-tested in pid_unittest.

docs.title: 2.7 Drive aids (ABS, traction control, launch control) — flight/drive_aids.c, PG_DRIVE_AIDS_CONFIG
docs.text:
The driver's throttle/brake command passes through driveAidsApply() before it becomes STABILIZED_THROTTLE. An aid only ever moves the command towards neutral, never past it and never into the opposite direction. Failsafe replaces the result afterwards, so a failsafe throttle is never shaped. The aids pass the command through unchanged while disarmed, in failsafe and with DRIVE AIDS OFF (permanent id 66). A mixer rule fed from the RC throttle input instead of STABILIZED_THROTTLE bypasses them. Every aid is OFF by default. The settings are per PID profile (copied and reset with the profile).

  • ABS (timed). Runs only while the drive state has the ESC braking (state BRAKE) and the car is not RPM-confirmed stopped, and the brake is past drive_abs_trigger. Each cycle (1 / drive_abs_freq) holds the brake command for half the cycle plus drive_abs_hold (at most 85 % of the cycle), then eases it to drive_abs_floor % of the command. DYNAMIC moves the rate towards drive_abs_dyn_freq, the floor towards 60 % of drive_abs_floor and the hold towards drive_abs_dyn_hold as the brake deepens from the trigger to full. drive_abs_corner_freq adds rate and drive_abs_corner_hold moves the hold with steering-stick deflection; where both a dynamic and a steering hold apply, the shorter wins. The rate is limited to 2-33 Hz.
  • 10 % minimum release. A brake-then-reverse ESC that sees neutral in the middle of a brake reverses on the next pull, so the released brake never drops below 10 % brake (DRIVE_ABS_MIN_BRAKE). The command stays on the brake side of neutral, and the drive state stays BRAKE with it.
  • Traction control (RAMP). A forward command may only rise at a limited rate, zero to full in drive_tc_ramp_time (50-2000 ms, default 500); letting off is instant. It shapes only a forward command, never a brake (including a command above neutral while the ESC brakes a car rolling backwards) or reverse. While it, or the aids, are off the limit follows the command, so turning it on with the trigger held never cuts the throttle.
  • Timing only. Both use the sticks and time, no wheel-slip sensing.
  • Debug mode DRIVE_AIDS: throttle in and out x1000, flags, ABS rate x10 (or TC limit x1000 when driving forward with TC on), floor x1000, hold ms, cycle phase ms, steering x1000. Unit-tested in drive_aids_unittest.

docs.title: 2.8 Mixer — flight/mixer.c, pg/mixer.c
docs.text:
A rule table: output (SET/ADD/MUL) = (offset + weight · curve(input · rate)) / 1000, with a separate negative weight, an optional slew (speed) and an optional logic-condition gate. model_type is CAR (0) or CUSTOM (1). The default (car) rules are SET STABILIZED_YAW → S1 (steering) and SET STABILIZED_THROTTLE → M1 (reversible ESC); rear steering and a second ESC are added by the Configurator's car preset as further rules. The stabilized throttle input range is −1000..1000.

  • Saturation flags last 5 ticks and gate the PID's anti-windup.
  • Overrides and wiggle apply only while disarmed. The wiggle (ready, armed, arming-error patterns, wiggle_* settings) moves only the steering (yaw) input (flight/wiggle.c).
  • Non-finite guard. A NaN or infinity at a mixer input, a rule output or an accumulated output is replaced by zero (and counted as saturation at the input).
  • Live-adjustable rule weights keep the configured polarity in mixerRuleSign[], because a live magnitude passes through 0, which has no sign.

docs.title: 2.9 Servo output — flight/servos.c
docs.text:
Order: mixer output (or a bench override) → geometry correction → balance curve → non-finite guard → speed limit (each servo on its own) → reverse → rpos/rneg scale → trim (saved + runtime) → travel limit → mid.

  • There are 24 servos; servo N goes to PWM output N where the board has one and to channel N of an SBUS/F.Bus output, from one output stage. Every servo has the signal range 880-2159 µs and one PWM update rate (servo_pwm_rate).
  • Trim never edits mid, so min/max (offsets from mid) stay where they are. Saved and runtime trim are added before the travel limit, so the output stays inside min/max.

docs.title: 2.10 Motor output — flight/motors.c, drivers/
docs.text: Every motor defaults to motor_control_mode bidirectional, with min_throttle 1000 and max_throttle 2000. A zero command to a bidirectional motor is neutral: on PWM, SRXL2 and SITL the midpoint of min_throttle..max_throttle, never min_command, which a car ESC reads as full brake/reverse and many learn as their neutral at power-up. On DShot zero is the motor-stop command, positive commands use the forward range and negative ones the reverse range.

docs.title: 2.11 Attitude estimator — flight/imu.c
docs.text: The inherited Mahony quaternion filter still runs on all three axes (gyro integration corrected by the accelerometer, plus magnetometer or GPS course when available). Accelerometer readings are only used within 0.9-1.1 g; the gain is x10 while disarmed, with a quick re-convergence after a disarm. Nothing in the steering loop or the drive aids uses the attitude: it feeds the arming check (§2.12), telemetry and the Blackbox.

docs.title: 2.12 Arming, running latch, failsafe — fc/core.c, flight/failsafe.c, rx/rx.c
docs.text:
• Arming is blocked unless the throttle is at neutral (ARMING_DISABLED_THROTTLE) and the attitude estimate is established (isAttitudeEstimateReady(), which does not check that the car is level), among the other arming-disable flags. While armed with the throttle at neutral the armed beeper sounds; with stick arming, auto_disarm_delay (default 5 s) at neutral disarms.
  • Running latch (INFLIGHT_MODE, the telemetry RUNNING bit): set once armed and |throttle| > 0.1, held through stops, cleared on disarm. There is no airborne detection any more. A disarm while running, after at least rearm_min_armed_seconds (5 s) armed, opens a rearm_grace_seconds (10 s) window in which re-arming skips the throttle and attitude checks, so an accidental disarm can be recovered while the car is moving.
  • Receiver signal loss (rx.c): bad channels hold their last value for 300 ms, then each channel takes its rxfail value. The default (AUTO) puts roll, pitch and steering at centre and the throttle at neutral (getFailsafeThrottle() returns the throttle centre); other channels hold their last value.
  • Failsafe (failsafe.c) is monitoring from start-up and runs its state machine:
    • Armed with the throttle at neutral for at least failsafe_throttle_low_delay (10 s) before the link drops: disarm straight away ("just disarm").
    • Otherwise, after failsafe_delay (1.5 s) without a valid signal, failsafe_procedure runs: DROP (default) disarms at once; AUTO-LAND holds failsafe_throttle (default 1500 µs, neutral) for failsafe_off_delay (1 s), then disarms.
    • While a procedure is active, failsafe_throttle replaces the drive aids' output on the stabilized throttle, and GYRO OFF and DRIFT are ignored. Re-arming needs failsafe_recovery_delay (1 s) of valid signal.
    • A FAILSAFE mode switch acts as stage 1 (default), KILL (disarm at once) or STAGE2 (failsafe_switch_mode).

docs.title: 3. Decision log (Gripora)
docs.text:
Gripora was forked from WingFlight 0.0.43 in November 2026. The fixed-wing history (attitude hold, thrust vectoring, GPS navigation, the governor and so on) is in the WingFlight repository; none of that code remains.

Commit Decision Why 6a4250e76 Remove the aircraft features (attitude hold, trainer, angle/leveling, GPS nav and rescue, airborne detection, auto trim, trim monitor, thrust vectoring, hold engine, governor, tune advisor); stabilise yaw only; signed throttle around rc_center; bidirectional neutral; ids kept reserved Car conversion, step 1; reserved ids keep MSP, BOX and saved-profile layouts valid 24ab3af49 Car mixer preset (S1 steering, M1 ESC), steering-only wiggle, yaw_gyro_reverse A gyro that corrects the wrong way must be fixable without reversing the driver's steering 6a94592d0 Drive state: gyro negated in reverse, correction faded with speed and reduced in reverse Reversing turned the correction into positive feedback; at a standstill I wound up and slammed the steering 4dff3f73b Default channel order CH1 steering, CH2 throttle Car radios 36fdb2256 Gyro corrects on the bench (no speed fade disarmed); yaw I held at zero disarmed The setup wizard's gyro-direction check needs a correction with the car still; no I bump on arming f67886c8f MSP API 33.0; MSP2_GRIPORA_* names Gripora's protocol is its own from here d5e28efef Timed ABS, per PID profile; DRIVE AIDS OFF mode First drive aid; a profile switch changes it with the tune 259d57c55 fw_spa_speed_max default 60 km/h, range 10-300 Car speeds 8afcd9c4d Timed traction control (ramp) Second drive aid 167f8dbb2 Launch control: the LAUNCH mode stages a capped, ramped standing start Third drive aid 987dc46bd DRIFT mode: steering wheel direct, gyro counter-steer past drift_allow, no I-term, per PID profile; WINGFLIGHT_AIRPLANE removed A rate loop asks for the wrong wheel angle in a drift; the marker was tested nowhere

docs.title: 4. Known defects and limitations
docs.text: Confirmed = follows directly from the code. Needs verification = depends on behaviour that can only be observed on a car.

docs.title: High
docs.text:
H-1. Without an RPM source there is no low-speed fade. Confirmed. The speed factor is 1 without RPM (driveSpeedFactor()), so armed at a standstill the full P and I correction runs. Holding steering off centre on a stopped car then makes P push and I wind up towards full lock, because the car cannot yaw at the commanded rate. The Configurator says so on the Motors tab. Fix: an RPM source (DShot telemetry, ESC telemetry or a frequency sensor).

H-2. FWD_REV with no RPM: braking is taken for reverse, and ABS never runs. Confirmed. Without RPM, driveNextState() cannot know the car is still rolling, so every below-neutral command is REVERSE. The travel direction flips at once: the gyro rate is negated during what is physically still a forward brake, softened only by the 1 s correction fade-in, and the yaw I-term is cleared. ABS needs state BRAKE, so it never runs. The Configurator warns on the drive aids panel. Fixes: an RPM source, or FWD_BRK_REV if the ESC supports it.

docs.title: Medium
docs.text:
M-1. The ESC model can disagree with the ESC. Needs verification. Without RPM the direction is only what the model predicts. FWD_BRK_REV reverses after 50 ms at neutral (DRIVE_NEUTRAL_DWELL_S); a real ESC may need a longer or shorter neutral, or have its own reverse threshold. With RPM, a reversal the model missed is caught when the wheels speed up from zero; without RPM it is not.

M-2. Default steering authority from F is small. Confirmed arithmetic; needs verification on a car. With the defaults (yaw F 65, 150 °/s at full stick) feedforward gives about 24 % of full travel at full stick. With an RPM source and the car below drive_gyro_min_speed, P, I and D are scaled to zero, so F and the transient B are all the steering there is: an armed, stopped car may not reach full lock until it moves. Whether this matters in practice, and whether F or the default rate should change, has not been checked on a car.

M-3. Wheel speed is driven-wheel speed. Inferred, not verified. Speed comes from motor RPM through the gear ratio, so it reads the driven wheels. Wheelspin or locked wheels under braking make it differ from ground speed, which affects the low-speed gyro fade, the "stopped" detection (which gates ABS) and speed attenuation.

M-4. Drive aids act on the stick, not on the wheels. Confirmed (by design). ABS and traction control are timed from the stick and the clock. The ABS "steering" adjustments use the steering-stick deflection, not the actual wheel angle. There is no slip detection; sensor-based modes are planned as separate modes.

docs.title: Low
docs.text:
• L-1. GYRO OFF bypasses the stabilized-yaw input limits. Confirmed, intentional. mixerSetBypassInput() writes the input directly, so a tightened mixer input min/max on stabilized yaw does not apply in GYRO OFF. Servo min/max still do.
  • L-2. GYRO OFF does not bypass the drive aids. Confirmed. Only the steering is raw; ABS and traction control still shape the throttle unless DRIVE AIDS OFF is on. User-facing text that says the throttle "passes straight" in GYRO OFF is describing the steering only.
  • L-3. Arming does not check that the car is level. Confirmed. isAttitudeEstimateReady() only checks that the attitude estimate is established. ARMING_DISABLED_ANGLE keeps its name because it is user-visible.
  • L-4. First IMU update integrates over a huge dt. Confirmed. previousIMUUpdateTime starts at 0, so the first step is long. Inherited from Betaflight; converges quickly, happens once per boot.
  • L-5. Accelerometer accepted at 0.9-1.1 g with no correction for cornering or acceleration. Confirmed. Only attitude telemetry and the arming check depend on it.

docs.title: Fixed in the inherited code and still in place
docs.text:
• Failsafe state machine runs. The inherited Rotorflight code had failsafeStartMonitoring() commented out, so failsafe never ran; WingFlight re-enabled it, and it is called from core.c. (Older notes that say "stage 2 is disabled" are out of date.) There is still no running automated test (flight_failsafe_unittest.cc.txt).
  • Non-finite guard at the mixer inputs, rule outputs and the servo boundary.
  • Each servo is speed-limited on its own (the inherited helicopter code scaled all cyclic servos together).

docs.title: Not reviewed
docs.text: Dynamic notch and RPM filters, gyro/accelerometer drivers and calibration, logic_condition.c, Blackbox, MSP and CLI plumbing.

docs.title: 5. Test coverage
docs.text:
Running unit tests (make test, src/test/unit) cover the PID (pid_unittest), setpoint, curves, maths, speed attenuation, the drive state (drive_unittest), the drive aids (drive_aids_unittest), servos and telemetry status. The mixer, IMU, failsafe and arming-prevention tests exist but are disabled (flight_mixer_unittest.cc.txt, flight_imu_unittest.cc.txt, flight_failsafe_unittest.cc.txt, arming_prevention_unittest.cc.txt), so the mixer, failsafe and fc/core.c arming paths have no running tests.

Worth adding, cheapest first:

  1. Drive state with the real ESC (M-1): Blackbox the DRIVE debug mode while braking, reversing and re-reversing with and without RPM, and compare the commanded state and direction with what the car did.
  2. Standstill steering (H-1, M-2): armed, stopped, full steering, with and without RPM; record mixer[2] and the servo output.
  3. Failsafe: revive flight_failsafe_unittest for the just-disarm, DROP and AUTO-LAND paths with a signed neutral throttle.
  4. Mixer: revive flight_mixer_unittest for GYRO OFF, the drive aids hand-off and the failsafe throttle replacement.

Nothing in this document has been verified by driving.

docs.title: Hardware Debugging with VSCode and JLink
docs.text: This page sets up Gripora firmware debugging in VS Code. It was written for Rotorflight (from which Gripora inherits its build), so the example board is a Rotorflight-era one.

docs.title: Assumptions and Prerequisites
docs.text:
• JLink: This guide assumes JLink. ST-Link/OpenOCD should be possible. but unverified.
  • Flydragon V2: Other controllers should be very similar.
  • SWD wiring: SWDIO, SWCLK, 3.3V, GND are required. SWO pin is optional for advanced topic.\
  • Linux build environment.
  • VSCode workspace connected to the build environment.
  • JLink, VSCode and build environment can be on 3 different hosts.
  • Optionally, use the Gripora Configurator to flash your built firmware once, to load board config.

docs.title: JLink host
docs.text: (Skip if JLink and build environment are on the same host): 1. Install JLink software. 2. Run "JLink Remote Server" and start the server.\

docs.title: Build environment
docs.text:
1. Install JLink software too.
  2. Install a recent version of arm-none-eabi-gdb. In my case, it is under /usr/bin/arm-none-eabi-gdb.
  3. Run make clean once, in case you have some cached .o and .elf without debug info.

docs.title: VSCode
docs.text:
1. Open your gripora-firmware workspace.
  2. Install extension Cortex-Debug.
  3. Add these settings to .vscode/settings.json: 
        "cortex-debug.armToolchainPath": "${workspaceRoot}/tools/gcc-arm-none-eabi-9-2020-q2-update/bin/",
    "cortex-debug.gdbPath": "/usr/bin/arm-none-eabi-gdb",
  4. Create .vscode/tasks.json (or merge) with the following content: 
    {
    "version": "2.0.0",
    "tasks": [
        {
            "type": "shell",
            "label": "build STM32F7X2",
            "command": "make",
            "args": ["STM32F7X2", "DEBUG=INFO"],
            "problemMatcher": [],
            "options": {
                "cwd": "${workspaceFolder}"
            },
            "presentation": {
                "close": true
            },
        }
    ]
}
  5. Create .vscode/launch.json (or merge) with the following content: 
    {
  "version": "0.2.0",
  "configurations": [
    {
      "name": "Launch STM32F7X2 JLink",
      "cwd": "${workspaceRoot}",
      "executable": "${workspaceRoot}/obj/main/gripora_STM32F7X2.elf",
      "request": "launch",
      "type": "cortex-debug",
      "servertype": "jlink",
      "serverpath": "JLinkGDBServerCLExe",
      "ipAddress": "xxx.yyy.aaa.bbb", // Replace with your JLink host. Remove if run locally.
      "device": "STM32F722RE",
      "runToEntryPoint": "main",
      "serverArgs": [
        "-speed", "6000" // Optional: in case your jlink doesn't auto detect optimal speed for you
      ],
      "swoConfig": {
        "enabled": true,
        "source": "probe",
        "swoFrequency": 2000000,
        "cpuFrequency": 216000000,
        "decoders": [
          {
            "port": 0,
            "type": "console",
            "label": "SWO output",
            "encoding": "ascii"
          }
        ]
      },
      "preLaunchTask": "build STM32F7X2"
    }
  ]
}
  6. Now go to Run and Debug panel, select the configuration you just created, and click the green play button.\ \ VSCode will build, download and start a debug session.
  7. JLink by default only erases affected sections. Therefore, the configuration will preserve. In case you did not pre-load board config in the prerequisite steps, you can still load your board's configuration from gripora-targets in the CLI.

docs.title: Attach to a running target
docs.text:
Use this Launch configuration: 

    {
      "name": "Attach STM32F7X2 JLink",
      "cwd": "${workspaceRoot}",
      "executable": "${workspaceRoot}/obj/main/gripora_STM32F7X2.elf",
      "request": "attach",
      "type": "cortex-debug",
      "servertype": "jlink",
      "serverpath": "JLinkGDBServerCLExe",
      "ipAddress": "xxx.yyy.aaa.bbb", // Replace with your JLink host. Remove if run locally.
      "device": "STM32F722RE",
      "serverArgs": [
        "-speed", "6000" // Optional: in case your jlink doesn't auto detect optimal speed for you
      ],
      "swoConfig": {
        "enabled": true,
        "source": "probe",
        "swoFrequency": 2000000,
        "cpuFrequency": 216000000,
        "decoders": [
          {
            "port": 0,
            "type": "console",
            "label": "SWO output",
            "encoding": "ascii"
          }
        ]
      }
    }
(Changes: launch->attach, remove runToEntryPoint and preLaunchTask)

docs.title: SWO
docs.text:
SWO is an optional debug pin can be used for various purposes (https://kb.segger.com/SWO).

On Flydragon, the SWO pin (PB3) is not exposed as a pad but connects to the buzzer (through a driver circuit). You will need to carefully solder a wire to this tiny resistor:\ \

And also unmap the pin from buzzer: 

Resource BEEPER 1 NONE

docs.title: SWO terminal
docs.text:
You can utilize high speed SWO terminal to print debug strings. First, add this piece of code to any (linked) .c file: 

int _write(int file, char *ptr, int len)
{
    (void) file;
    int i;
    for (i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        ITM_SendChar(*ptr++);
    }
    return len;
}

Comment out this line from src/main/common/platform.h which prevents us to compile printf. 

#pragma GCC poison sprintf snprintf

Now you can printf anywhere in the code and the output will be shown in the "TERMINAL" -> "SWO:SWO console":\

docs.title: SWO graphing
docs.text: You can send values to different ITM channels and plot a graph. This is useful to track multiple variables or state machines. Refer to https://github.com/Marus/cortex-debug/wiki/SWO-Output#output-graphing-graphing.

docs.title: SWO trace
docs.text: SWO trace is currently not supported by Cortex-Debug extension. I suggest to use SEGGER Embedded Studio for this task -- "An externally built executable for a Cortex-M processor" project.

docs.title: Hardware debugging
docs.text:
The code can be compiled with debugging information, you can then upload a debug version to a board via a JLink/St-Link debug adapter and step through the code in your IDE.

A guide for setting up VS Code with a J-Link can be found in Hardware Debugging with VSCode and JLink.

A guide for visual studio can be found here: http://visualgdb.com/tutorials/arm/st-link/

This video is also helpful in understanding the proces: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kjvqySyNw20

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Various debugging hardware solutions exist, the Segger J-Link clones are cheap and are known to work on Windows with both the Naze and Olimexino platforms.

docs.title: J-Link devices
docs.text:
Segger make excellent debuggers and debug software.

The Segger J-Link GDB server can be obtained from here.

http://www.segger.com/jlink-software.html

docs.text: https://www.segger.com/j-link-edu.html

docs.text: http://www.hotmcu.com/usbminijtag-jlink-jtagswd-debuggeremula%E2%80%8Btor-p-29.html?cPath=3_25&zenid=fdefvpnod186umrhsek225dc10

docs.text: https://www.olimex.com/Products/ARM/JTAG/ARM-JTAG-20-10/ http://uk.farnell.com/jsp/search/productdetail.jsp?sku=2144328

docs.title: STLink V2 devices
docs.text: STLink V2 devices can be used too, via OpenOCD.

docs.title: CEPark STLink V2
docs.text: http://www.goodluckbuy.com/cepark-stlink-st-link-v2-emulator-programmer-stm8-stm32-downloader.html

docs.title: Compilation options
docs.text:
1. Use make DEBUG=INFO ... to build with debug information for gdb to load, without affecting the code optimization.
  2. Use make DEBUG=GDB ... to build with reduced optimization to preserve debugging (-Og).

You may find that if you compile all the files with DEBUG=GDB on that the program is too big to fit on the target device. If this happens you have some options:

  • Compile all files with normal optimization (make clean, make DEBUG=INFO ...), then re-save or touch the files you want to be able to step though and then run make DEBUG=GDB .... This will then re-compile the files you're interested in debugging with debugging symbols and you will get a smaller binary file which should then fit on the device.
  • You could use a development board such as an PORT103R, development boards often have more flash rom.

docs.title: Install OpenOCD via Brew
docs.text:
ruby -e "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/master/install)"

brew install openocd

docs.title: Windows
docs.text: Run the Launch the J-Link GDB Server program and configure using UI.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
STM32F103 targets

"C:\Program Files (x86)\UTILS\openocd-0.8.0\bin-x64\openocd-x64-0.8.0.exe" -f interface/stlink-v2.cfg -f target/stm32f1x_stlink.cfg

STM32F30x targets

"C:\Program Files (x86)\UTILS\openocd-0.8.0\bin-x64\openocd-x64-0.8.0.exe" -f scripts\board\stm32f3discovery.cfg

docs.title: OSX/Linux
docs.text:
STM32F30x targets

  openocd -f /usr/share/openocd/scripts/board/stm32vldiscovery.cfg

docs.title: MSP over Telemetry
docs.text:
The Ethos suite and the EdgeTX scripts configure the controller through MSP carried on the telemetry link: FrSky S.Port, F.Port, FBUS (F.Port2), or CRSF. This page follows one request from the radio to the firmware and back, names the code that handles each hop, and shows what bounds the speed. It is written for people working on the firmware side or on the Lua transports.

The FrSky transports are the slow ones and get most of the attention here. CRSF carries up to 57 MSP bytes per frame and is covered only for comparison.

docs.title: The path
docs.text:
radio Lua  --push frame-->  RF module  --RF downlink-->  receiver  --bus-->  FC
radio Lua  <--pop frame--   RF module  <--RF uplink---   receiver  <--bus--  FC
Hop S.Port (telemetry port) FBUS / F.Port2 (RX port) F.Port Request reaches the FC receiver transmits it on the bus addressed to physical ID 0x0D downlink frame to ID 0x0D, frame ID 0x30 telemetry-request frame, frame ID 0x30 FC may transmit only when polled on ID 0x1B when polled on 0x1B or 0x0D after each telemetry request Reply frame 0x1B, frame ID 0x32 uplink written under 0x1B, frame ID 0x32 0x00, frame ID 0x32 Firmware driver src/main/telemetry/smartport.c src/main/rx/fbus.c src/main/rx/fport.c

All three feed the same assembler, src/main/telemetry/msp_shared.c, which also serves CRSF.

docs.title: Frame format
docs.text:
A FrSky frame carries 6 bytes of MSP: a status byte and 5 bytes of message. The status byte is

Bits Meaning 7 error (replies only) 6-5 MSP version: 01 v1, 10 v2 4 start of a message 3-0 sequence number, modulo 16

The message is the MSP frame without its $M< prefix and without a CRC, since the telemetry frame has its own. The firmware accepts three layouts and answers in the one the request used:

Version bits Header Used by 11 compact command (16 bit), length (8 bit; 0xFF then a 16-bit length for longer messages) Ethos suite, EdgeTX scripts 10 MSPv2 flags, command (16 bit), length (16 bit) older WingFlight and Rotorflight Lua 01 MSPv1 length, command (8 bit), CRC byte at the end older EdgeTX scripts, commands below 256

The compact header is 3 bytes, so the first frame carries 2 bytes of payload and every later frame carries 5. The MSPv2 header is 5 bytes and fills the first frame on its own:

compact: frames = 1 + ceil((payload - 2) / 5)
MSPv2:   frames = 1 + ceil(payload / 5)
Message compact frames MSPv2 frames read request, no payload 1 1 11-byte reply 3 4 12-byte write 3 4 52-byte write (MSP_TELEMETRY_CONFIG) 11 12 81-byte reply 17 18 448-byte reply (mixer rule pool) 91 91

A frame is lost, not retransmitted, when the sequence breaks. The firmware drops the rest of a request whose chunk went missing and answers nothing, and the radio drops the rest of a reply.

docs.title: Assembly and chunking
docs.text:
msp_shared.c keeps one request buffer (192 bytes) and one reply buffer (640 bytes). A request bigger than the buffer is answered with an error; a reply that overflows the buffer is replaced by an error reply rather than sent truncated. The reply is handed back one chunk at a time by sendMspReply().

A request that arrives while a reply is still going out replaces that reply, and the new reply starts with its own START frame. The radio relies on this: it resends as soon as it sees a sequence break instead of waiting for the old reply to drain.

After MSP_EEPROM_WRITE the FC answers the next 5 polls with empty frames before sending the reply, to keep the bus quiet while flash is written.

docs.title: S.Port on the telemetry port
docs.text:
handleSmartPortTelemetry() runs from the telemetry task at 250 Hz. It reads the bytes the receiver put on the bus, and smartPortDataReceive() recognises two things: a poll of 0x1B, which makes the FC clear to send, and a frame addressed to 0x0D, which is a request chunk.

Each poll of 0x1B sends one frame. A pending MSP reply chunk always wins over sensor data. After the last chunk the FC sends no sensor data for 250 ms (SMARTPORT_MSP_SILENCE_US), which gives the receiver's uplink buffer time to drain the reply before sensor frames compete for it.

The FC cannot use the 0x0D slot on S.Port: the receiver transmits in that slot when it has a request to deliver, and the FC has no way to know in advance whether it will.

docs.title: FBUS and F.Port2
docs.text:
The receiver streams control frames and follows each with a downlink frame that polls one physical ID. fbus.c queues frames from the UART interrupt and frameStatus() sorts them. A downlink to 0x0D with frame ID 0x30 carries a request chunk; a downlink with frame ID 0x10 asks for data; 0x00 is a null poll that is answered with an empty frame.

The FC answers no earlier than 500 µs after the downlink frame and not at all after 3 ms. The RX task is woken for it by rxFrameCheck() in the scheduler loop, so the answer normally goes out within the first millisecond. The reply chunk is written under the common ID 0x1B whichever ID was polled, which is what both Lua transports filter on.

Data polls of 0x0D carry pending reply chunks too, not only the polls that brought a request. Sensor data is only ever sent on 0x1B. Measured on an X20S with an FBUS receiver, this takes an 81-byte reply from 0.48 s to 0.39 s and leaves an 11-byte reply at 0.12 s, even though the receiver turns many of the extra polls into null polls while its uplink is busy.

docs.title: F.Port
docs.text: fport.c answers telemetry-request frames on the control line. A request chunk arrives as a telemetry request with frame ID 0x30; data and null requests are answered with the next reply chunk or sensor frame. The timing constants match FBUS.

docs.title: What bounds the speed
docs.text:
For a round trip of one read request and one reply:

  1. The radio pushes the request frame. The Ethos suite pushes one frame per background wakeup and keeps a frame the module refuses for the next wakeup. The EdgeTX scripts ask the module whether it has room first.
  2. The RF downlink carries the frame to the receiver. This is the slowest hop for writes and is set by the RF protocol, not by anything in this repository.
  3. The receiver delivers it on the next poll of 0x0D.
  4. The FC answers the next poll of 0x1B (or, on FBUS, 0x0D) with the first chunk, and one more chunk per poll after that. On S.Port a poll slot is 12 ms, and the receiver cycles through the IDs it has seen answer, so each extra answering ID lengthens the gap between polls of 0x1B.
  5. The receiver uplinks each frame to the radio. The uplink has its own rate and a small buffer; when polls outrun it, frames are dropped and the radio sees a sequence break.
  6. The radio pops the frames on its next wakeups and reassembles the reply.

Worked example on S.Port, FC the only sensor: a 40-byte reply is 9 frames at one per 12 ms, about 110 ms after the first chunk, plus the two RF hops and the wakeup latency at each end. A page that reads ten such settings spends over a second in replies alone.

A lost frame costs more than its own slot. The Ethos suite resends on the next wakeup after a sequence break, which costs one round trip, and only waits its full retry window (0.8 s) when nothing at all comes back, which is what a lost request frame or a lost START frame looks like.

docs.title: Measuring
docs.text:
Set debug_mode = FBUS and read the debug fields in the Configurator sensors tab or a Blackbox log:
