Field Value 0 microseconds between downlink polls of 0x1B 1 microseconds between downlink polls of 0x0D 2 frame ID of the last poll of 0x1B 3 frame ID of the last poll of 0x0D 4 MSP request chunks received 5 MSP reply chunks sent 6 frames rejected by the checksum or type checks 7 microseconds from the end of the downlink frame to the FC's uplink

Fields 0 and 1 are the ceiling on reply throughput: 5 payload bytes per poll. Field 3 shows whether a receiver polls 0x0D with data requests between MSP requests, which is what lets the FC use that slot for reply chunks.

On the radio, the Ethos suite's Developer → MSP Speed tool reports the round-trip time of a read over a chosen period, and its MSP log (Developer settings) records every frame with a SEQ line for each sequence break, including the gap since the previous wakeup, which separates frames lost on the link from frames lost to a full queue on the radio.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
• The link sets the rate for long replies. On an FBUS receiver the FC is polled on 0x1B and 0x0D every 21 ms each, and 30 to 40% of those polls become null polls while a reply streams, because the receiver's RF uplink to the radio is busy. Loss-free medians from one bench session, 120 s runs on an X20S, for a 81-byte and an 11-byte read:

    Firmware Lua framing 81-byte read 11-byte read replies on 0x1B only MSPv2 0.484 s 0.117 s replies on 0x1B only compact 0.470 s 0.115 s replies on 0x1B and 0x0D MSPv2 0.385 s 0.116 s replies on 0x1B and 0x0D compact 0.382 s 0.101 s

Answering 0x0D polls is worth 20% on long replies; the compact header is worth one frame, which shows on the short read only once the 0x0D polls make frames cheap enough for it to matter. - A request chunk lost on the way to the FC is never acknowledged; the radio only finds out when its retry window expires. - A reply bigger than 640 bytes cannot be sent at all; the FC answers with an error. - The 250 ms sensor silence after a reply stalls dashboard sensors while a page is loading.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
'Parameter Groups' is the name of the pattern, inherited from Betaflight, used to store (and at a later point transfer) firmware configuration data.

With parameter groups, parameters are combined in logical groups (e.g. all the parameters for one particular device / feature go into one parameter group). These groups are modelled as data structures in the firmware.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
The following rules have to be taken into consideration when dealing with parameter groups in code:

  1. Each feature or group of related features, hardware driver or group of related hardware drivers should use a parameter group of its own;
  2. A parameter group of any given ID and version shall be identical across all targets and build configurations - this means that nothing that is contained in a parameter group directly or indirectly can be conditional. The finest granularity for parameters to be available on a given target is by having or not having support for a given parameter group;
  3. The only exception to 2. are parameter group arrays. For parameter group arrays, it is permissible to have the length of the array defined conditionally. Because the length of the struct defining the array elements is fixed for any given version, and the overall size of the array is stored with the array, the length of the array can be calculated when reading it. This consideration only applies to parameter group arrays declared with PG_DECLARE_ARRAY, and the length supplied in the declaration. For the length of any arrays inside a parameter group struct (directly or nested), 2. applies;
  4. As a consequence of 1. and 2., all of the parameters required for the configuration of the feature or driver should be contained within this parameter group. If a parameter is required by more than one feature or driver, it shall be moved 'upwards' into a generic parameter group that all the features or drivers requiring the parameter depend upon - if necessary such a parameter group has to be created;
  5. New parameters should always be appended at the end of the parameter group. If this is the only change to the parameter group, there are no further changes required. Previously stored versions of the data in this parameter group can still be read. New elements will be initialised to 0 in this case. If 0 is an invalid value for a new parameter, this has to be treated as described in 6., in order to ensure the parameter is initialised to a valid value. If the parameter group that the new parameter is appended to is a parameter group array declared with PG_DECLARE_ARRAY, then the version of the parameter group has to be incremented as described in 6. as well, in order get the change in the struct properly handled;
  6. Any changes to a parameter group that are not covered in 5. (e.g. removing elements, changing the type of elements), the version of the parameter group (as defined in PG_REGISTER...) has to be incremented in order to make the code handling parameter groups aware that the format of the parameter group has changed and previously stored versions of it are now invalid;
  7. All changes to parameter group arrays (declared with PG_DECLARE_ARRAY()) or arrays contained within the struct of a parameter group require that the version of the parameter group (as defined in PG_REGISTER.. has to be incremented as well, and the same considerations as for 6. apply;
  8. When creating a new parameter group, the PG_DECLARE() / PG_DECLARE_ARRAY() shall be placed right after the definition of the struct used as the type of the parameter group in the code. This serves the purpose of making it easy for developers to determine when a struct they are working on is used in a parameter group and subject to these rules;
  9. Any struct that is used as an element in a struct that is used in a parameter group (directly or indirectly) is subject to constraints 6. and 7. above. In order to make it possible for developers to determine that this is the case, a comment // Used in parameter group <group name> shall be added after the definition of the struct for every parameter group that the struct is used in.

docs.title: Gripora rule: bump the version on every change
docs.text:
Gripora is stricter than rule 5 above. Bump the PG version, the last argument of PG_REGISTER* (for example PG_REGISTER_WITH_RESET_TEMPLATE(pidConfig_t, pidConfig, PG_PID_CONFIG, 3)), in the same change whenever a parameter group changes at all:

  • fields added, removed, reordered or resized;
  • array lengths changed;
  • default values changed;
  • value ranges changed.

When the firmware loads a stored group whose version does not match, pgLoad() (src/main/pg/pg.c) keeps the defaults instead of restoring it. So a bump makes settings saved by an older build reset to the current defaults, rather than being misread or keeping a stale default. That is the intended behaviour for an upgrade, and the change should be noted in Changes.md (for example "the mixer config PG is reset on upgrade (v3)").

The version is stored in the top 4 bits of the PG number (PGR_PGN_VERSION_MASK), so it runs from 0 to 15 and wraps after 15.

docs.title: PG numbers
docs.text: PG numbers are defined in src/main/pg/pg_ids.h. Gripora's own groups take numbers from 1000 up, for example PG_DRIVE_CONFIG (1028) and PG_DRIVE_AIDS_CONFIG (1029). Numbers of removed groups are kept as reserved comments and are never reused, so an old stored record is never read as a new group.

docs.title: RX serial wiring auto-detect — design
docs.text: Scope: for the currently selected serial RX protocol, detect the right serialrx_inverted / serialrx_halfduplex / serialrx_pinswap combination by trying each live and watching for signal. Protocol selection itself stays manual (see prior discussion — 8 combos per protocol is tractable, ~160 across all protocols is not, and most of the value is here anyway: users know "it's an FBUS receiver," they don't know if their board's inverter or their wiring guess was right).

docs.title: Why this needs a firmware change, not just a configurator loop
docs.text:
rxInit() (rx.c:281) only ever runs once, at boot (init.c:770). Every RX_CONFIG field is SET + EEPROM_WRITE + reboot today (Receiver.svelte:110-124). Cycling 8 combos that way means 8 real EEPROM writes and 8 full reboot/MSP- reconnect cycles — slow, disruptive, and needless flash wear for something that's inherently transient (only the final answer should ever be persisted).

The good news: closing and reopening the RX serial port generically, without provider cooperation, is already possible with existing plumbing:

  • findSerialPortConfig(FUNCTION_RX_SERIAL) gives the identifier of whatever UART is assigned to the main RX.
  • findSerialPortUsageByIdentifier(identifier) is already public (serial.h:144) and returns the serialPortUsage_t* holding the live serialPort_t* for that identifier.
  • closeSerialPort() (serial.c:445) releases it and marks the slot FUNCTION_NONE again.
  • Each provider's own init (e.g. sbusInit, sbus.c:225-234) just reopens the port itself, building portOptions_e straight from rxConfig->serialrx_inverted/halfDuplex/pinSwap. Nothing provider-specific needs touching — mutate those three fields in the live (RAM-only) rxConfigMutable() and re-run the existing serialRxInit() dispatch (rx.c:172) for the current serialrx_provider.

So the mechanism is: close current port → flip the trial bits in RAM → re-run the same init switch that already exists → poll rxIsReceivingSignal() (rx.c:391), which is already exposed to MSP as mainLinkUp in MSP2_GRIPORA_RX_INPUT_BACKUP_STATUS and already polled every 200ms by the configurator today.

docs.title: Firmware: new state machine (rx.c)
docs.text:
A small non-blocking state machine, ticked from the scheduler like any other periodic task — not run inside the MSP handler, since a combo can take up to ~1s to settle and MSP processing must stay non-blocking.

typedef enum {
    RX_TRIAL_IDLE,
    RX_TRIAL_RUNNING,
    RX_TRIAL_SUCCESS,
    RX_TRIAL_FAILED,
} rxTrialState_e;

typedef struct {
    rxTrialState_e state;
    uint8_t comboIndex;         // 0..7, current attempt
    uint8_t comboOrder[8];      // walk order, see below
    timeMs_t comboStartedAt;
    timeMs_t lastPollAt;        // watchdog: configurator must keep polling
    bool savedInverted, savedHalfDuplex, savedPinSwap; // restore point
} rxSerialTrial_t;
  • rxSerialTrialStart() — guards: FEATURE_RX_SERIAL active, a serial port is actually assigned, no trial already running. Snapshots the three current bits as the restore point, builds comboOrder (below), sets comboIndex = 0, applies combo 0, closes+reopens the port, calls serialRxInit(), records comboStartedAt.
  • rxSerialTrialTick() (called every scheduler pass, cheap early-out when idle):
  • If state != RUNNING, nothing to do.
  • Watchdog: if now - lastPollAt > 3000ms, treat as an abandoned trial (configurator crashed / USB unplugged mid-scan) → restore + IDLE.
  • If rxIsReceivingSignal() has been continuously true for the debounce window (see below) → SUCCESS, stop touching the port further (leave the winning combo live so the user can literally see channels move before deciding to save).
  • Else if now - comboStartedAt > settleMs[provider] → advance comboIndex; if that was the last of 8, restore original bits, reinit, → FAILED; else apply next combo, close+reopen, reinit.
  • rxSerialTrialStop() — always restores the snapshotted bits and reinits, regardless of current state. Idempotent. This is the only way a SUCCESS combo becomes "real" from the firmware's point of view — it doesn't persist anything itself, ever.

docs.title: Debounce
docs.text: rxSignalReceived already flips true on the very next valid frame and false after an internal invalid-frame timeout (rx.c:545-554), so a single stray checksum-lucky garbage byte is already unlikely to read as sustained signal. Still, require it held for a short continuous window (e.g. 150–250ms) before calling a combo a SUCCESS, rather than trusting one instantaneous poll — cheap insurance, and easy to tune from bench testing.

docs.title: Per-protocol settle timeout
docs.text: Streaming protocols (S.BUS, CRSF, IBUS, FPort/FBUS, GHST) lock on within a frame or two — a few hundred ms of budget is generous. Handshake-based ones (SRXL2, Jeti EXBUS, Spektrum bind-flavored modes) need materially longer before anything valid shows up. Rather than guess exact numbers here, add a settleMs[] lookup keyed by serialrx_provider with a conservative default (~600ms) and larger values (~1200-1500ms) for the handshake protocols, then tune from real receivers on the bench. Worst case (8 combos × slowest timeout) is ~10-12s if every combo fails — acceptable for a manual "click and wait a few seconds" action, and the scan order below makes the common case much faster.

docs.title: Scan order — walk outward from current settings, not 0..7
docs.text: Most real-world misconfigurations are "one thing is wrong" (usually inverted, from a board with/without a hardware inverter), not "everything is wrong." Order the 8 combos by Hamming distance from whatever's currently configured: distance 0 (current — confirms the existing setting still isn't the problem, cheap to rule out first), then the three distance-1 flips, then the three distance-2 flips, then the distance-3 (all flipped) as last resort. Converges in 1 try for the common single-bit-wrong case instead of averaging 4.

docs.title: New MSP2 commands
docs.text:
Next free IDs after 0x5F11 (msp_protocol.h:305-322):

Command ID Request Response MSP2_GRIPORA_RX_SERIAL_TRIAL_START 0x5F12 (none — always trials the currently-configured serialrx_provider) U8 accepted (0 = rejected: no serial RX feature/port, or trial already running) MSP2_GRIPORA_RX_SERIAL_TRIAL_STATUS 0x5F13 (none) U8 state (idle/running/success/failed), U8 comboIndex, U8 inverted, U8 halfDuplex, U8 pinSwap, U16 elapsedMs — also is the watchdog keep-alive (updates lastPollAt) MSP2_GRIPORA_RX_SERIAL_TRIAL_STOP 0x5F14 (none) U8 ack — always restores + reinits, idempotent

Mirrors the existing MSP2_GRIPORA_RX_INPUT_BACKUP_STATUS handler pattern (msp.c:1321) closely enough to reuse its shape.

docs.title: Configurator side (gripora-configurator)
docs.text:
• ReceiverType.svelte: a "Detect wiring" button next to the protocol select, enabled only when RX_PROTOCOLS[rxProtoIndex]?.feature === "RX_SERIAL" (same guard already used for the signaling SubSection at ReceiverType.svelte:65).
  • On click: send TRIAL_START; if accepted, poll TRIAL_STATUS on the same ~150-200ms cadence the tab already uses for MSP2_GRIPORA_RX_INPUT_BACKUP_STATUS (Receiver.svelte:89-91), showing "Trying combo N of 8…".
  • On SUCCESS: send TRIAL_STOP (commits nothing on the FC, just cleans up the trial and restores original live bits), then apply the returned inverted/halfDuplex/pinSwap into local FC.RX_CONFIG — this is the only place the result becomes visible, and it flows through the tab's existing dirty-diff/Save/Revert machinery exactly like any manually-edited field. Nothing is pushed to the FC until the user hits the normal Save/Reboot button. Toast a friendly success message.
  • On FAILED: send TRIAL_STOP, toast "no signal found on this protocol — check wiring/provider," touch nothing.
  • Always send TRIAL_STOP on component unmount / tab navigation, not just on terminal states — covers the user clicking away mid-scan. (Firmware's 3s watchdog is the last-resort backstop if even that doesn't arrive.)

This keeps the trial's blast radius genuinely contained: the FC can wander across up to 8 electrical configs for a few seconds while the button spins, but from the user's (and the rest of the tab's) point of view nothing is "real" until the ordinary Save button is pressed — same contract as every other field on this page today.

docs.title: Open items to settle before/while implementing
docs.text:
1. Exact settleMs[] values per provider — needs bench time with real receivers, not a guess from reading code.
  2. Where the scheduler task hook goes (need to check fc/tasks.c task table conventions) and confirm ticking a lightweight trial state machine there doesn't need its own TASK_* slot vs. piggybacking on the existing RX task.
  3. Whether SUCCESS should leave the winning combo live (so the user sees channel bars move as confirmation before saving) vs. immediately restoring and just reporting the numbers — leaning toward "leave it live until STOP," since seeing channels twitch is a much stronger confidence signal than a text result, but it does mean the FC sits on unsaved wiring for slightly longer.

docs.title: SmartFuel internals
docs.text:
This page describes how the SmartFuel estimator works and how it is wired into telemetry and MSP. For setting it up from the Configurator, see the Power tab.

SmartFuel provides an intelligent remaining-charge percentage for the drive battery. It is intended to give a more useful "fuel remaining" value than the simple linear voltage-to-percent curve, especially for telemetry display on the radio.

SmartFuel always uses pack voltage as its primary input. A configured battery voltage sensor is required; if no voltage sensor is configured, SmartFuel stays off (the saved mode is kept, so it starts working once a voltage source is set). In CURRENT and COMBINED modes, when both bat_capacity and used mAh are non-zero, the mAh counter is folded in against the initial voltage-derived anchor (see Modes below).

Measured consumption is reported separately by the battery monitoring code and is unaffected by which SmartFuel mode is selected.

docs.title: Modes
docs.text:
smartfuel is a four-way lookup parameter (default CURRENT):

  • OFF — SmartFuel does not run; getBatteryChargeLevel() falls through to the legacy sources.
  • VOLTAGE — voltage-only estimator. Pack voltage drives the percentage (with throttle-based sag compensation); current/consumption are ignored.
  • CURRENT — when both bat_capacity and used mAh are non-zero, the level is initial − used / capacity, where initial is the first voltage-derived fraction (0–1) after the pack is seen and used / capacity is the fraction of configured capacity counted by the current meter. Voltage is not blended in on this path. When either capacity or used is zero, this mode behaves the same as VOLTAGE.
  • COMBINED — the level is the minimum of the voltage-derived estimate and initial − used / capacity, i.e. whichever indicator is more pessimistic in the moment. When either capacity or used is zero, this mode behaves the same as VOLTAGE.

In all enabled modes, the displayed percentage is monotonically non-increasing: each update can only hold steady or drop, never rise. It is also clamped to the initial anchor sampled when the pack is first seen. The CURRENT and COMBINED paths typically pull the value down faster than voltage alone when mAh used is significant.

If you plug in a pack that is not “full” (the first sample is well below 100%), initial − used / capacity is a simple subtraction of the mAh counter from that starting anchor, not a full state-of-charge model.

docs.title: How charge level is chosen
docs.text:
getBatteryChargeLevel() picks the most accurate source available, in this order:

  1. SmartFuel, if smartfuel != OFF. SmartFuel always wins when enabled.
  2. Consumption-based, if bat_capacity is non-zero. Reported as 100 × (capacity − used) / capacity. Without a configured current sensor used stays at zero, so this path will report 100% indefinitely — set bat_capacity = 0 to fall through to the linear-voltage estimate instead.
  3. Linear voltage, if cell count is known. A simple linear interpolation between vbat_min_cell_voltage and vbat_max_cell_voltage.

bat_capacity, battery_cell_count and the vbat_*_cell_voltage settings are arrays with one value per battery profile (bat_profile); the active profile's values are used. SmartFuel is re-initialised when the profile changes, as soon as the model is disarmed.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
SmartFuel is enabled by setting smartfuel to VOLTAGE, CURRENT, or COMBINED. Set smartfuel = OFF to disable it; the firmware then falls back to consumption-based or linear-voltage charge level as described above.

SmartFuel anchors its initial percent on the first voltage sample after the battery monitoring code declares the pack present (i.e. once cell-count auto-detection has completed). It does not run its own settling timer.

CLI example:

set smartfuel = VOLTAGE
set smartfuel_voltage_drop_rate = 10
set smartfuel_charge_drop_rate = 50
set smartfuel_sag_gain = 40

docs.title: SmartFuel tuning parameters
docs.text:
CLI parameter names:

  1. smartfuel_voltage_drop_rate
  2. smartfuel_charge_drop_rate
  3. smartfuel_sag_gain

Default values:

smartfuel_voltage_drop_rate = 10
smartfuel_charge_drop_rate = 50
smartfuel_sag_gain = 40

docs.title: smartfuel_voltage_drop_rate
docs.text:
Maximum allowed downward slew of the filtered per-cell voltage used for the fuel estimate. It only slows drops; when the voltage recovers, the estimate is not held down by this parameter.

  • Increase it (more mV/s) if SmartFuel reacts too slowly to real pack depletion.
  • Decrease it if throttle punches or brief sag make the estimate fall too quickly before sag compensation catches up.

Units: millivolts per second (mV/s). Valid range 0–250 in the CLI and MSP. The value applies to per-cell voltage, not the full-pack total, so it does not depend on cell count.

docs.title: smartfuel_charge_drop_rate
docs.text:
Maximum allowed SmartFuel percentage drop rate on the voltage path once the model is armed or has ever been armed in this power cycle (ARMED or WAS_EVER_ARMED). It limits how fast the displayed percentage can fall when the voltage-based estimate would otherwise drop faster.

  • Increase it if the displayed percentage lags too much behind the real pack condition.
  • Decrease it if the percentage drops too aggressively during load spikes.

Units: 0.01% points per second (e.g. 50 → 0.50 %p/s). Valid range 0–250 in the CLI and MSP.

This limiter only applies to the voltage half of the estimate. In CURRENT mode with non-zero used mAh, the level is initial − used / capacity and is not rate-limited — fall speed is determined entirely by how fast used accumulates. In COMBINED mode, the voltage half is rate-limited but the initial − used / capacity half is not, so the combined min(…) can still fall faster than this parameter would suggest. The limiter is fully in effect only on the VOLTAGE path and on the CURRENT/COMBINED fallback when consumption data are unavailable.

docs.title: smartfuel_sag_gain
docs.text:
Amount of sag compensation applied to the voltage reading before it is turned into a percentage. Voltage sag follows motor current, so the compensation is driven by the motor outputs actually being sent (after the output slew), taken as magnitudes because a motor braking or reversing draws current too, and averaged across motors: 0 at neutral, 1 at full power on every motor. The firmware adds smartfuel_sag_gain hundredths of a volt, multiplied by that load, to the per-cell voltage. It runs whenever the motor is working.

  • Increase it if SmartFuel is too pessimistic under load.
  • Decrease it if SmartFuel is too optimistic under load.

Units: hundredths of a volt per cell at full power, so the default 40 adds up to 0.40 V per cell at full throttle. Valid range 0–100 in the CLI and MSP.

A model with no motor output gets no compensation, and a channel that drives something else cannot inject any.

docs.title: Tuning guidance
docs.text:
Start with the defaults and change one parameter at a time.

Suggested workflow:

  1. Drive with the default values.
  2. Check whether SmartFuel settles quickly and sensibly after plugging in.
  3. Watch how it behaves during hard acceleration, long full-throttle straights and coasting.
  4. Compare the displayed remaining fuel at the end of the run with the pack voltage and with how much reserve you wanted to keep.

Use these adjustment patterns:

  • Drops too hard during load: reduce smartfuel_charge_drop_rate or increase smartfuel_sag_gain.
  • Feels too pessimistic overall under load: increase smartfuel_sag_gain.
  • Feels too optimistic overall: reduce smartfuel_sag_gain.
  • Tracks real depletion too slowly throughout the run: increase smartfuel_voltage_drop_rate (mV/s) or increase smartfuel_charge_drop_rate.

docs.title: Practical notes
docs.text:
• Tune with the battery type and driving style you actually use.
  • Large changes are rarely needed; make small adjustments and drive again.
  • Different packs may want slightly different behaviour, but the defaults are intended to be a reasonable starting point.
  • SmartFuel is still an estimate. If you have a well-calibrated current sensor and a correctly configured bat_capacity, smartfuel = CURRENT derives the percentage directly from used mAh (initial − used / capacity), independent of voltage sag, and smartfuel = COMBINED takes the more pessimistic of the voltage track and that consumption-derived value. To bypass SmartFuel entirely, set smartfuel = OFF; getBatteryChargeLevel() then uses the legacy behaviour (consumption-based when bat_capacity is non-zero, otherwise linear voltage when cell count is known).

docs.title: Telemetry
docs.text:
When smartfuel is VOLTAGE, CURRENT, or COMBINED, SmartFuel drives the existing fuel/charge-level telemetry output (CRSF, FrSky hub fuel, Flysky iBUS shared fuel, MSP battery state, LED strip, …) — anything routed through getBatteryChargeLevel().

FrSky D-series hub (ID_FUEL_LEVEL) and Flysky iBUS shared fuel used to send consumed mAh when bat_capacity was zero; they now always send the same 0–100 charge level as the other getBatteryChargeLevel() paths. Set bat_capacity and use consumption telemetry if you need mAh on the radio.

docs.title: MSP (v2)
docs.text:
When the firmware is built with USE_SMARTFUEL:

  • MSP2_GET_SMARTFUEL_CONFIG (0x4000) — response: U8 mode (0 = OFF, 1 = VOLTAGE, 2 = CURRENT, 3 = COMBINED); U8 smartfuel_voltage_drop_rate (mV/s, 0–250); U8 smartfuel_charge_drop_rate; U8 smartfuel_sag_gain.
  • MSP2_SET_SMARTFUEL_CONFIG (0x4001) — payload: same four fields in the same order. Values use the same limits as the CLI parameters.

docs.title: Driving Modes & Features
docs.text:
Gripora stabilises one thing: the steering. A turn-rate (yaw-rate) gyro loop turns the steering servo so the car rotates at the rate the steering wheel asks for, and pushes back when the car starts to slide or is knocked off line. The throttle goes to the ESC as you give it, shaped only by the optional drive aids.

Page Summary Car Mixer and Channels The default car setup: steering on S1, a reversible ESC on M1, optional rear steering and second ESC, the car channel order (CH1 steering, CH2 throttle) and the gyro direction setting Drive State How the controller works out which way the car is travelling and how fast, so the gyro corrects the right way in reverse and fades out near a standstill Drive Aids ABS and traction control: timed shaping of the brake and throttle you give, per PID profile GYRO OFF Turns the steering gyro off from a switch: the steering wheel goes straight to the steering servo DRIFT For drifting: the steering wheel goes straight to the servo and the gyro only counter-steers when the car rotates too fast Ready-to-Arm Wiggle The steering twitches to show the car is ready to arm, armed, or can't arm Backup RX Input A second or third receiver takes over if the main link is lost

docs.title: Modes
docs.text:
Modes are put on transmitter switches on the Modes tab. The ones that change how the car drives:

Mode What it does ARM Arms the ESC output. Arming needs the throttle at neutral. PREARM Optional safety switch that must be on before ARM works. GYRO OFF Steering without the gyro. See GYRO OFF. DRIFT The steering wheel steers the wheels directly; the gyro only counter-steers turn rate beyond an allowance. See DRIFT. DRIVE AIDS OFF ABS, traction control and launch control off; the gyro still steers. See Drive Aids. LAUNCH Stages a launch for launch control. See Launch control. FAILSAFE Tests or triggers failsafe from a switch. See Failsafe.

The other modes (beeper, LED, Blackbox, telemetry, camera control, user outputs) are described on the Modes tab page.

docs.title: Throttle, brake and reverse
docs.text:
The throttle is signed around the centre of the throttle channel (rc_center, 1500 µs by default): forward above it, brake and reverse below it, with a small neutral deadband. "Throttle off" always means the trigger at neutral, not at full brake. That is what arming, auto-disarm and failsafe check for, and what failsafe sends to the ESC (failsafe_throttle, 1500 µs).

What the ESC does below neutral (brake, reverse, or brake then reverse) is set in the ESC itself. Tell the controller which it is on the Motors tab's Drive panel; see Drive State.

Racing rules

Sensor-based driving aids are banned in sanctioned racing. The steering gyro is one; class rules may also ban ABS and traction control even though Gripora's versions use only the stick and time. Check the rules of your class and sanctioning body before running Gripora at a race.

docs.title: Backup RX Input
docs.text:
Backup RX Input lets spare UARTs carry up to two independent backup receivers ("satellites") purely as fallbacks for the main RF link. If the main receiver's signal is lost, the controller takes over all RC channels -- including aux/mode switches, so arm state and mode switching keep working -- from the first backup that is receiving, bypassing the normal failsafe stages entirely. The moment a higher-priority link's signal comes back, control reverts to it automatically. Takeover and revert happen within the main receiver's own signal-loss detection window (up to ~100ms), not on a per-missed-frame basis -- see Behavior.

This is a cheap way to get a backup-receiver setup (e.g. a small FrSky/compatible satellite bound to a second transmitter module or a different protocol entirely) without needing a full second RF system. A second backup gives three-way redundancy for cars where a single lost link is not an acceptable risk.

Each backup port speaks a single, configurable protocol, chosen from the Protocol dropdown on its Backup Receiver box (see below): SBUS, FBUS (also F.Port2 receivers), F.Port, Jeti EXBUS, or TBS CRSF (Crossfire/ELRS). The two backups may use the same protocol or different ones. By default (before a protocol is chosen) a port is reserved but not decoding anything.

Controller telemetry only ever travels over the main receiver. The backup links are receive-only: nothing is sent to a backup receiver, whatever its protocol.

docs.title: Priority
docs.text: Failover is a fixed chain: Primary, then Backup 1, then Backup 2. Whichever is highest in that order and currently receiving valid frames is in control. There is no signal-quality comparison -- a backup's own telemetry or RSSI is never read -- so the order you assign the ports is the order they take over. Put the receiver you trust most as Backup 1.

docs.title: Setting it up
docs.text:
1. Wire an RX-capable satellite receiver to a spare UART, then assign that port the Receiver: Backup 1 function from the port function dropdown on the Configuration tab's serial ports list. It's named to pair with the main receiver's own Receiver: Primary option -- this is a second, independent one. For a third receiver, wire it to another spare UART and assign that port Receiver: Backup 2.
  2. On the Receiver tab, a Backup Receiver 1 box (and a Backup Receiver 2 box, if that port is assigned) appears below the Primary Receiver box. Pick each satellite's protocol from its Protocol dropdown, then Save & Reboot.
  3. Bind each satellite as you would any receiver of that protocol. If it isn't decoding (the box's Link badge stays down), check wiring against the UART's pinout -- the box's Pin Swap and Inverted switches cover boards where the port's natural RX pin isn't the one that's wired, or where the signal needs the opposite electrical inversion from the protocol's default assumption; Half-Duplex covers satellites that only expose a single, shared signal wire for this protocol. All three are independent of the main receiver's own equivalent settings and of the other backup's, since each is a different physical UART, and each protocol has its own natural wiring convention (SBUS is inverted by default; every other supported protocol isn't) -- OFF always means "this protocol's normal wiring," not "no inversion" in an absolute sense. The box's Detect button tries every combination on the live port and reports the one that receives frames. Changing any of these needs Save & Reboot to take effect.
  4. Turn off telemetry on the backup receivers themselves. These links are receive-only -- the controller never reads anything a backup receiver's own telemetry system might send, so this has no effect on how the feature controls the car at all. It matters for a different reason: a second, independent telemetry stream is exactly what can confuse your radio's Lua scripts about which link is the real telemetry path back from the controller.
    • FrSky/compatible satellites: in the receiver's own RX options (on the transmitter, not the Configurator), turn telemetry off for this receiver.
    • ExpressLRS receivers: use the ELRS web configurator to disable telemetry on this receiver.
  5. Once bound and decoding, each Backup Receiver box's Link and Active Source badges update live, and each entry in Channel Assignment grows a smaller meter per backup showing that receiver's own live channel value -- refreshed several times a second, the same readout used for bench-testing below.

All three receivers must use the same channel order: the backups are read through the primary receiver's channel map.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
• Bypasses staged failsafe, but isn't sub-frame instant. This does not go through the normal Failsafe stage machine at all -- no failsafe_delay/failsafe_recovery_delay involved. It reacts to the same signal-presence detection the main receiver already uses for its own signal-loss tracking, which is bounded to roughly 100ms after the last good main-link frame (not "next frame"). That's a deliberate choice: a feature-specific faster threshold could false-trigger a takeover on a legitimately slower RX protocol's normal frame spacing. It's still far quicker than doing nothing here -- an un-caught channel would otherwise hold its last value for 300ms before failsafe even declares it failed. Between the two backups the hand-over is quicker: a backup counts as down after about 50ms without a valid frame, and Backup 2 takes over the moment Backup 1 is down while it is still receiving.
  • Full channel takeover. All channels are taken from the backup in control during fallback, not just steering and throttle -- aux switches (modes, arming, etc.) are driven from the backup stick exactly as they would be from the main receiver. Channels a backup doesn't carry go to stick center (1500 by default): for example CH19-24 when the main receiver sends 24 channels but the backup sends a 16-channel F.Bus frame. A mode or switch on those channels moves to its middle position on takeover, so keep safety-relevant switches on channels every receiver carries. F.Bus and F.Port2 backups carry up to 24 channels, SBUS and F.Port 18, EX Bus and CRSF 16.
  • Auto-revert. As soon as a higher-priority receiver's signal is valid again (the main receiver within that same ~100ms window, Backup 1 within ~50ms), control reverts to it -- a backup does not latch for the rest of the run.
  • Not a second failsafe system. If the main link and every backup link are down, ordinary staged failsafe behavior (neutral, then disarm, per the Failsafe tab) takes over exactly as it would without this feature. Backup RX input is a bridge for lost links, not a replacement for failsafe.
  • A Failsafe switch on an aux channel still invalidates control channels even while a backup link is otherwise healthy -- the switch is honored the same way regardless of which link is currently active.

docs.title: Arming check
docs.text:
Every configured backup receiver has to prove it works before you can drive relying on it. Once the boot arming-grace window has passed, arming is blocked -- the Status tab shows the BACKUP_RX arming-disable flag -- until each backup receiver that has a protocol selected has linked at least once, so a mis-wired or dead backup can't go unnoticed until the moment you need it.

The check only guards the first arm after power-up. Once you have armed successfully, a backup that later drops out during the same powered session will not block re-arming for the rest of that session; a battery change that powers the controller off starts a new session and the check runs again. A backup port left unconfigured (no protocol chosen) takes no part in the check. A backup with a protocol chosen whose port fails to open counts as configured but never linked, so it blocks the first arm until the wiring or port conflict is fixed.

docs.title: Alerts on the radio
docs.text:
With the Gripora Lua suite on an Ethos radio, the backup receivers' state is also shown on the dashboard and announced:

  • BACKUP RX NO SIGNAL (amber banner, "Backup receiver lost" / "Backup receiver OK"): at least one configured backup isn't receiving. Check this before a run. The Rx Backup diagnostics page shows which one.
  • BACKUP RX IN CONTROL (red banner, "Backup receiver active" / "Main receiver restored"): a backup is driving the car.

Telemetry normally travels over the main link, so while the main link is down the radio often can't hear the controller. See Radio Callouts and Alerts for when each callout can reach you.

docs.title: Bench-testing before you drive
docs.text:
As with any failsafe-adjacent behavior, test this on the bench (wheels off the ground) before relying on it on the track:

  1. Power up with the backup satellites bound and powered, and confirm the BACKUP_RX flag on the Status tab clears once every backup's Link badge comes up (arming stays blocked until then).
  2. With every receiver bound and powered, confirm the Receiver tab's Primary Receiver box shows its Active Source badge as Main RX, and moving a backup satellite's sticks has no effect on outputs.
  3. Power off (or walk the main receiver's transmitter out of range), and confirm control switches to Backup 1 within roughly 100ms, arm state is preserved, and aux switches on the backup radio work as expected. The Active Source badges name the backup in control.
  4. With a second backup fitted, power off Backup 1 as well and confirm control moves to Backup 2; power Backup 1 back on and confirm it takes control back.
  5. Restore the main link and confirm control reverts to it within that same window.
  6. Power off every receiver and confirm ordinary staged failsafe triggers as configured.

docs.title: CLI settings
docs.text: Backup 1 uses rx_input_backup_provider, rx_input_backup_inverted, rx_input_backup_halfduplex and rx_input_backup_pinswap. Backup 2 uses rx_input_backup2_provider, rx_input_backup2_inverted, rx_input_backup2_halfduplex and rx_input_backup2_pinswap. The serial command takes the port functions as numbers, 8388608 for Backup 1 and 16777216 for Backup 2; serialdebug shows them as RX_BACKUP and RX_BACKUP2. See Serial Ports for the details.

docs.title: Car Mixer and Channels
docs.text: Gripora's defaults are set up for a car out of the box: the steering servo on S1, a reversible ESC on M1, and the channel order of a car radio. This page describes those defaults and the one setting that fixes a gyro that corrects the wrong way. Day-to-day setup is done on the Mixer tab or with the setup wizard (Set Up Your Car).

docs.title: Model type
docs.text:
model_type is Car (CAR, the default) or Custom (CUSTOM).

  • Car: the Mixer tab builds the rules from a few options and shows a summary.
  • Custom: keep a mix built by hand, rule by rule.

The firmware stores only the mixer rules; the options below are how the Configurator builds them.

docs.title: The car mixer preset
docs.text:
Output From What it drives S1 Stabilized Steering (steering wheel through the gyro) Steering servo, front wheels M1 Stabilized Throttle (signed: forward, brake and reverse) Reversible ESC

These are the firmware's default mixer rules:

mixer rule 0 set SY S1 1000 0 1000 0 0 0 0
mixer rule 1 set ST M1 1000 0 1000 0 0 0 0

Two options can be added on the Mixer tab (Edit Configuration) or in the wizard's Model step:

  • Rear steering (4-wheel steering): a second steering servo on S2, also from Stabilized Steering. Opposite to the front wheels gives tighter turns, Same direction as the front wheels gives crab steering. Amount (0-100 %, default 50 %) is how far the rear wheels turn compared with the front ones.
  • Second ESC (dual motor, or front and rear motors) on M2, with the same throttle as M1: forward, brake and reverse.

Steering and throttle weights stay positive. If a servo turns the wrong way, reverse it on the Servos tab; if the motor runs the wrong way, reverse it in the ESC. The mix itself stays as it is.

Feed the ESC from Stabilized Throttle

The throttle reaches the ESC through Stabilized Throttle. That is where the drive aids act, and where failsafe puts the throttle at neutral. A custom rule that feeds an ESC straight from the RC throttle channel bypasses both.

The throttle input is signed, -1000 to 1000 in the mixer: above zero is forward, below zero brake and reverse. Every motor output is bidirectional by default, so a zero command is neutral: the midpoint of min_throttle and max_throttle (1500 µs with the defaults of 1000 and 2000).

Only steering is stabilised. The roll and pitch mixer inputs exist but are always zero, so a rule fed from them never moves anything.

docs.title: Channel order
docs.text:
The default channel map is RT1234AE, the order of a car radio:

Channel Function CH1 Steering CH2 Throttle (trigger): forward above centre, brake and reverse below CH3-CH6 AUX1-AUX4, for mode switches, the gain knob and trims CH7, CH8 Roll and pitch, unused on a car

On the Receiver tab the Car preset sets this order; the setup wizard can also detect the steering and throttle channels if your radio sends them elsewhere. Reverse a channel on the radio, not in the controller.

The throttle channel's centre (rc_center, default 1500 µs) is neutral. Make sure the trigger at rest reads neutral on the Receiver tab: the car only arms with the throttle at neutral.

docs.title: Gyro direction
docs.text:
With the wheels off the ground, turn the car by hand around its vertical axis: the steering should turn against the movement. If it turns with the movement, the gyro is correcting the wrong way. This usually happens after the steering channel was reversed with a servo reverse.

Turn on Reverse gyro (steering) on the Mixer tab (CLI: yaw_gyro_reverse = ON, default OFF). It reverses only the gyro feedback of the steering loop, not the wheel. Board orientation and the attitude estimate don't change.

Don't use servo reverse to fix the gyro direction: that reverses your steering too.

Check this driving forward only. In reverse the controller turns the gyro correction round by itself; see Drive State. The setup wizard's Gyro direction step does this check and can set it for you.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text: The car defaults reset older settings on the first boot after an upgrade to a firmware that introduced them: the channel map returns to RT1234AE, the model type to Car and the mixer rules to the preset above. Take a backup before upgrading, and check the mixer and channel order afterwards. See Backup & Restore.

docs.title: DRIFT
docs.text:
DRIFT is a mode for drifting. While it is on, the steering wheel steers the wheels directly, as with GYRO OFF, and the gyro only catches the car when it rotates too fast: it adds counter-steer against the turn rate beyond an allowance. There is no heading hold.

The normal gyro loop treats the steering wheel as a turn-rate request and steers the wheels to get that rate. In a drift that is the wrong way round: the car rotates one way while the front wheels point the other way (counter-steer), so you need to set the wheel angle yourself. DRIFT gives you the wheel angle, and keeps the gyro for what it is good at in a drift: holding the slip angle and stopping a spin.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
Normal DRIFT GYRO OFF Steering wheel A turn-rate request, through the rates and expo Straight to the servo: full stick = full servo travel Straight to the servo Gyro Steers the car to the requested turn rate Counter-steers only the turn rate beyond Allowed turn rate None Steering I-term (heading hold) Yes Held at zero Held Steering D-term Damps as set in the profile Damps as set in the profile None Throttle Through the drive aids Unchanged: through the drive aids Unchanged: through the drive aids

The counter-steer grows in a straight line with the turn rate past the allowance:

  • Counter-steer gain 100 % gives full lock 360 °/s past the allowance. 200 % gets there twice as soon (180 °/s past it); 0 % turns the counter-steer off, and DRIFT then steers like GYRO OFF (the D-term still damps, if the profile has any).
  • Counter-steer limit caps it, as a share of full lock.

With the defaults (gain 100 %, allowed rate 30 °/s, limit 100 %) the gyro leaves the car alone up to 30 °/s, and reaches full counter-lock at 390 °/s. With gain 150 % and limit 60 % it starts at 30 °/s and reaches its 60 % cap at 174 °/s. The Configurator's Drift panel shows these two rates for the values you enter.

The counter-steer is added to the wheel angle you give, so if you already hold full counter-lock the gyro can't add more: the total is held to full servo travel.

docs.title: Setting it up
docs.text:
1. Set the steering throw first. In DRIFT, as in GYRO OFF, full steering is full servo travel. Set the end points with GYRO OFF on, as described in Setting the steering throw.
  2. Put DRIFT on a switch, on the Modes tab or in the setup wizard's Mode switches step. A switch you can reach while driving is best; a 3-position switch can carry DRIFT and GYRO OFF together.
  3. Check the settings on the Profiles tab, in the Drift panel, on the Ethos Lua suite's Drift page (Tuning → Steering), on the EdgeTX tool's Drift page, or in the CLI (drift_gain, drift_allow, drift_limit). They belong to the PID profile, so a drift profile and a grip profile can each have their own.
  4. Bench check, disarmed: with DRIFT on, the wheels follow the steering wheel. Turn the car quickly by hand around its vertical axis: past the allowed rate the wheels steer against the turn. (Armed with an RPM source, the counter-steer is faded out at a standstill, see below, so check it disarmed.)

Switch DRIFT on or off on a straight. The steering changes from the stabilised command to the raw wheel angle (or back) at once, so switching in mid-corner moves the wheels.

docs.title: Tuning
docs.text:
Start from the defaults and change one value at a time.

What you see Try The gyro fights the drift and pulls the car straight Raise Allowed turn rate The car spins out before the gyro catches it Lower Allowed turn rate, or raise Counter-steer gain The counter-steer snaps the car straight, or swaps the drift to the other side Lower Counter-steer limit, then the gain The steering shakes in a drift Lower the gain; check the steering D-term on the Profiles tab is not too high

The allowed rate depends on the car and the surface: a car that drifts at a large angle on a polished floor rotates faster than one on carpet. A Blackbox log of a few drifts with DRIFT off shows the turn rates you actually use; set the allowance a little above the steady rate of a good drift.

The setup wizard's Drift driving style is a different thing: a set of rates (300 °/s, 60 % expo) for the normal gyro loop. It does not turn on the DRIFT mode.

docs.title: Interactions
docs.text:
• GYRO OFF wins. With both on, the steering is GYRO OFF: no gyro at all.
  • Failsafe wins. While failsafe is active, DRIFT is ignored and the normal gyro loop steers, so a switch left on when the link dropped doesn't matter. See Failsafe.
  • Drive state. The counter-steer and the D-term are scaled by the drive state's gyro correction, as the normal loop's P and D are: none at a standstill (with an RPM source), reduced in reverse, and faded back in after a direction change without RPM. In reverse the gyro is negated, so the counter-steer still works against the rotation. See Drive State.
  • Gain attenuation. The throttle and speed attenuation on the Profiles tab scale the counter-steer and D-term. The wheel angle you give is never scaled. The profile's P gain and Master Gain don't change the counter-steer: Counter-steer gain alone sets it.
  • Drive aids. DRIFT doesn't touch the throttle: ABS, traction control and launch control work as usual. Use DRIVE AIDS OFF to turn them off.
  • Mixer input limits apply. Unlike GYRO OFF, DRIFT goes through the stabilised steering input, so a min or max set on it with the CLI mixer input command still limits the steering.
  • No heading hold. The steering I-term is held at zero while DRIFT is on, so leaving DRIFT starts the normal loop clean, without a stored correction.
  • PID mode 0 (feedforward only, no gyro) has no gyro to counter-steer with; DRIFT does nothing there.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Configurator Ethos EdgeTX Default Range drift_gain Counter-steer gain Counter Gain Counter gain 100 % 0-200 % drift_allow Allowed turn rate Allowed Rate Allowed rate 30 °/s 0-720 °/s drift_limit Counter-steer limit Counter Limit Counter limit 100 % 10-100 % of full lock

DRIFT is mode id 68. The settings of the profile in use are recorded in the Blackbox log header as drift (gain, allowed rate, limit).

Racing rules

DRIFT uses the gyro. Check the rules of your class before running it at a race.

Source: pidApplyDrift() in src/main/flight/pid.c and src/main/pg/drift.h in the firmware.

docs.title: Drive Aids
docs.text:
The drive aids shape the throttle and brake you give before they reach the ESC. There are three:

  • ABS pulses the brake when you brake hard, so the wheels keep turning and the car keeps steering instead of locking up and sliding.
  • Traction control limits how fast the forward throttle may rise, so the wheels don't spin up when you pull the trigger hard.
  • Launch control caps the throttle for a standing start from a switch, then ramps it up to full, so the car leaves the line without wheelspin.

All are off by default. They work from the throttle, steering and time only: no wheel speed, slip or acceleration sensor is read. Speed-based steering and sensor-based aids are planned as separate modes.

They are set on the Profiles tab, in the Drive aids panel, from the Ethos Lua suite's ABS, Traction and Launch pages, the EdgeTX Drive Aids page, or in the CLI (drive_abs_*, drive_tc_*, drive_lc_*).

Racing rules

Sensor-based driving aids are banned in sanctioned racing, and class rules may ban any electronic driving aid. Check the rules before racing with the drive aids, or the steering gyro, switched on.

docs.title: When the aids work
docs.text:
The aids only ever move the command towards neutral, never past it, and never into the opposite direction. They pass the command through unchanged:

  • while disarmed;
  • in failsafe (the failsafe throttle replaces their output, so it is never shaped);
  • while the DRIVE AIDS OFF mode is on. Put it on a switch on the Modes tab to turn all the aids off from the transmitter. The steering gyro keeps working.

GYRO OFF does not turn the drive aids off: it bypasses only the steering gyro.

The aids act on the Stabilized Throttle mixer input, which is what the car mixer preset sends to the ESC. A mixer rule that feeds an ESC straight from the RC throttle channel bypasses them. See Car Mixer and Channels.

docs.title: Per PID profile
docs.text: The drive aids settings belong to the PID profile, like the speed attenuation settings: each of the six profiles has its own, and switching profile (from the Profiles tab, an adjustment or the radio) switches them with the tune. That makes a profile a track or surface preset. Copying a profile, or resetting one, includes its drive aids settings.

docs.title: ABS
docs.text:
ABS works only while the ESC is braking a car that is still rolling: the controller's drive state must have the ESC in its brake state, and, if there is an RPM source, the car must not show as stopped. It never works in reverse or on forward throttle.

Past the trigger the brake is pulsed. Each pulse lasts one cycle (1 / pulse rate):

  1. Full brake (the brake you give) for half the cycle plus the hold, but never more than 85 % of the cycle.
  2. Release: the brake eases to the release brake for the rest of the cycle, a percentage of the brake you give.

The release brake never drops below 10 % brake. Most car ESCs brake first and reverse after the throttle has been back at neutral: if ABS released the brake to neutral, the ESC would take the next pulse as a request to reverse. Keeping at least 10 % brake keeps the command on the brake side of neutral, so the ESC (and the controller's drive state) stay in brake through the whole stop. If your brake is lighter than 10 %, the release keeps the brake you give.

Below the trigger the brake goes to the ESC unchanged, and the pulse cycle starts again from the beginning the next time the brake passes the trigger or after any forward throttle.

With the defaults (10 pulses per second, 20 ms hold, 40 % release brake) a full brake is 70 ms of full brake, then 30 ms at 40 % brake, ten times a second. The Drive aids panel shows this preview for your settings.

docs.title: Modes
docs.text: Panel CLI drive_abs_mode What it does Off OFF (default) The brake goes to the ESC as you give it Fixed STATIC Past the trigger the brake pulses at a fixed rate, release brake and hold Follows brake depth DYNAMIC Like Fixed, but the harder you brake (from the trigger to full brake), the more the pulse rate moves towards the full-brake rate, the release brake eases towards 60 % of its setting, and the hold moves towards the full-brake hold

docs.title: Steering
docs.text:
Two settings change the pulses with steering lock, measured from the steering wheel (not the servo): none with the wheel centred, full at full lock.

  • Extra pulse rate adds pulses per second at full lock, less with less steering.
  • Hold (with steering) moves the hold towards this value as the steering approaches full lock.

The pulse rate never goes above 40 pulses per second, whatever is added. Where a full-brake hold (Follows brake depth) and a steering hold both apply, the shorter hold wins; neither can lengthen the hold beyond the base Hold.

docs.title: ESC setups ABS can't run on
docs.text:
ABS needs to know the ESC is braking, not reversing:

  • Reverse directly (drive_esc_mode = FWD_REV) without an RPM source: every command below neutral is taken as reverse, so ABS never runs. Automatic picks Reverse directly on DShot, so this includes a DShot ESC without RPM telemetry. The Drive aids panel warns about this. Fit an RPM source (bidirectional DShot, ESC telemetry or an RPM sensor), or set the ESC to brake, then reverse if it supports it, and set the Drive panel to match.
  • With an RPM source, ABS stops once the car is stopped (below 1 km/h for 0.1 s).
  • Forward and brake only and Brake, then reverse ESCs work with or without RPM.

docs.title: ABS settings
docs.text: Panel CLI Range Default Mode drive_abs_mode OFF, STATIC, DYNAMIC OFF Trigger drive_abs_trigger 5-100 % of full brake 30 Pulse rate drive_abs_freq 2-33 pulses per second (Hz) 10 Release brake drive_abs_floor 0-100 % of your brake (never below 10 % brake) 40 Hold drive_abs_hold 0-100 ms 20 At full brake: Pulse rate drive_abs_dyn_freq 2-33 Hz (Follows brake depth only) 15 At full brake: Hold drive_abs_dyn_hold 0-100 ms, 0 = keep the hold above (Follows brake depth only) 0 With steering: Extra pulse rate drive_abs_corner_freq 0-10 Hz added at full lock, 0 = off 0 With steering: Hold drive_abs_corner_hold 0-100 ms at full lock, 0 = off 0

docs.title: Traction control
docs.text:
Panel CLI drive_tc_mode What it does Off OFF (default) The throttle goes to the ESC as you give it Ramp RAMP The forward throttle rises no faster than zero to full in the ramp time

With Ramp, letting off is instant. After a brake or a let-off the throttle rises again from where it is, not from where it was. Traction control never touches the brake or reverse, nor a command above neutral that the ESC uses to brake a car still rolling backwards.

Turning traction control on, or switching DRIVE AIDS OFF back off, while the trigger is held never cuts the throttle: while traction control or the aids are off, its limit follows the throttle.

Panel CLI Range Default Mode drive_tc_mode OFF, RAMP OFF Ramp time drive_tc_ramp_time 50-2000 ms, zero to full throttle 500

A longer ramp time is gentler: try longer on a slippery surface, shorter on high grip.

docs.title: Launch control
docs.text:
Panel CLI drive_lc_mode What it does Off OFF (default) No launch control LAUNCH switch SWITCH The LAUNCH mode stages a launch; the first forward throttle starts it

Put LAUNCH on a switch on the Modes tab. Then, for each launch:

  1. At the line, with the throttle at neutral or on the brake, turn LAUNCH on. The launch is staged. The brake, and ABS, work as usual while you wait.
  2. Pull the trigger. The throttle sent to the ESC is at most the start throttle at once, and the limit rises to full over the ramp time. A throttle below the limit goes through as you give it.
  3. The launch ends at the end of the ramp, when you let off to neutral or brake, or when you turn LAUNCH off.

A launch runs once per LAUNCH activation: lifting in the middle of the run never caps the throttle again. Turn LAUNCH off and on for the next one. Turning LAUNCH on with the throttle already forward stages nothing, so flicking the switch while driving can't cut the throttle. Arming with LAUNCH already on stages a launch.

A command above neutral that the ESC uses to brake a car still rolling backwards never starts a launch. Traction control stands aside while a launch runs and carries on from the throttle the launch reached, so the handover never cuts the throttle.

Panel CLI Range Default Mode drive_lc_mode OFF, SWITCH OFF Start throttle drive_lc_throttle 10-100 % 50 Ramp time drive_lc_ramp_time 100-5000 ms, start throttle to full 1000

Launch control uses the throttle and time only. Start with the defaults, lower the start throttle if the car still spins up off the line, and lengthen the ramp if it spins up partway through.

docs.title: Checking it
docs.text:
The Drive aids panel's Live box shows whether the aids are on, what ABS is doing (Idle, Braking past the trigger, Releasing the brake), what traction control is doing (Idle, On while driving forward, Holding the throttle back), what launch control is doing (Idle, Staged, Launching), and the throttle from the transmitter next to the throttle sent to the ESC.

For logs, set debug_mode = DRIVE_AIDS. The debug fields are:

Field Value 0 Throttle from the transmitter, x1000 1 Throttle to the ESC, x1000 2 Flags: bit 0 aids on, bit 1 ABS braking past the trigger, bit 2 ABS releasing, bit 3 traction control on while driving forward, bit 4 traction control holding the throttle back, bit 5 launch staged, bit 6 launching 3 While braking with ABS: pulse rate x10. While driving forward with traction control or launching: the throttle allowed, x1000 4 ABS release brake share, x1000 5 ABS hold, ms 6 ABS position in the pulse cycle, ms 7 Steering wheel, x1000

Blackbox logs also carry the settings of the profile in use in the drive_abs, drive_tc and drive_lc header lines.

Source: src/main/flight/drive_aids.c in the firmware.

docs.title: Drive State
docs.text:
A car's turn response to a steering angle depends on its speed and its direction of travel. Driving backwards the response changes sign, so a gyro correction tuned going forward would steer the wrong way and become positive feedback. Near a standstill the car doesn't rotate at all, however far the wheels are turned, so a gyro left fully on would wind up and slam the steering to full lock.

The drive state is how the controller handles this. It works out which way the car is travelling and how fast, and the steering loop uses that to:

  • turn the gyro correction round in reverse. The steering wheel keeps meaning "wheel angle" in both directions; only the gyro feedback is reversed;
  • fade the gyro correction out at low speed, so at a standstill the steering follows the wheel alone;
  • reduce, or switch off, the correction in reverse;
  • clear the steering I-term whenever the travel direction changes.

The settings are on the Motors tab, in the Drive panel, which also shows the drive state live. The drive state is also used by ABS to know when the ESC is braking.

docs.title: ESC behaviour
docs.text:
RPM sensors report how fast the motor turns, not which way. The direction comes from what the controller tells the ESC, so it needs to know what your ESC does with a command below neutral:

Drive panel CLI drive_esc_mode Below neutral the ESC... Automatic AUTO (default) Picked from the ESC protocol: Reverse directly with DShot (AM32's default), Brake, then reverse otherwise (PWM and the rest) Brake, then reverse FWD_BRK_REV Brakes after driving forward. Back to neutral, then below neutral again, and it reverses. Most car ESCs, and AM32 with "RC car reverse" on Reverse directly FWD_REV Reverses straight away; while the car still rolls forward it brakes or coasts first. AM32's default bidirectional mode Forward and brake only FWD_BRK Only ever brakes. The car never reverses

An AM32 with "RC car reverse" turned on behaves like most car ESCs and needs Brake, then reverse set by hand; Automatic would pick Reverse directly for it because it runs DShot.

If you aren't sure which your ESC does, the setup wizard's ESC step has a test: with the wheels off the ground, hold forward, let go, then hold reverse straight away. If the wheels only stop, and turn backwards only after you let go and hold reverse again, it is Brake, then reverse.

docs.title: Speed from motor RPM
docs.text:
With a motor RPM source, the controller turns motor RPM into the car's speed:

speed = motor RPM / gear ratio x tyre circumference
  • RPM sources: bidirectional DShot RPM telemetry, ESC telemetry that reports RPM, or an RPM (frequency) sensor input. Set the motor's pole count so electrical RPM becomes motor RPM. See Motors. DShot150 can't carry bidirectional DShot RPM.
  • Gear ratio: motor turns per wheel turn, the final drive ratio. The Drive panel shows it as motor : wheel, so for a 10.4 : 1 final drive enter 104 : 10. In the CLI the two numbers are the other way round, wheel first: motor1_gear_ratio = 10,104. The default is 1 : 1. The RPM filter uses it too, and it applies after a save and restart.
  • Tyre diameter: outside diameter of the driven tyres, drive_wheel_diameter, 20-300 mm, default 100 mm.
  • Two motors: motor 1's speed is used, averaged with motor 2's when motor 2 has an RPM source too. Each has its own gear ratio (motor1_gear_ratio, motor2_gear_ratio).

The car counts as stopped once its speed has been below 1 km/h for 0.1 s. The same speed is used by speed attenuation on the Profiles tab, in place of GPS speed.

Wheel speed is what is measured, not ground speed: wheelspin and locked wheels show as faster or slower than the car is really going.

docs.title: Travel direction
docs.text:
With RPM, the direction only changes at zero speed: when the car is stopped, or as the wheels move off from (near) zero. Braking while rolling forward is never taken for reverse. Wheels speeding up from zero under a command below neutral are taken as reverse (in every mode that can reverse, since a brake can't set them turning), and under a command above neutral as forward. So a reversal the model didn't expect, such as an ESC reversing at its own threshold, is still caught.

Without RPM, the direction follows the command straight away:

  • forward when the ESC is driving forward, reverse when the ESC model says it reverses. Braking and neutral keep the last direction;
  • the ESC may brake or coast for a while before the car really changes direction, so after each change the gyro correction drops to zero and fades back in over 1 second.

Reverse directly without RPM

With Reverse directly (FWD_REV, which is also what Automatic picks on DShot) and no RPM source, the controller can't tell braking from reversing: any command below neutral is taken as reverse, even while the car is still rolling forward on the brake. The gyro correction is then turned round (fading in from zero over 1 s) and ABS doesn't run. Use an RPM source, or an ESC set to brake, then reverse.

With Brake, then reverse and no RPM, the controller expects reverse once the throttle has been at neutral for at least 50 ms after a brake and then goes below neutral again. If your ESC needs a longer pause, or a full stop, before it reverses, the controller will think it is reversing early. An RPM source avoids the guess.

docs.title: Steering gyro correction
docs.text:
The gyro's part of the steering (P, I and D) is scaled by three factors. The feedforward (F and B), the part that comes straight from the stick, is never scaled.

  1. Speed (needs motor RPM). No correction below Gyro starts at (drive_gyro_min_speed, default 2.0 km/h), rising to full at Gyro fully on at (drive_gyro_full_speed, default 6.0 km/h). Without RPM this factor is always full.
  2. Reverse. While reversing the correction is Reverse gyro gain (drive_gyro_reverse_gain, default 50%) of the forward correction, or none with Gyro in reverse off (drive_gyro_reverse = OFF).
  3. Direction change fade (without RPM only): zero right after a change of direction, back to full after 1 s.

The steering I-term is cleared on every change of travel direction, since it was built up for the other direction.

While disarmed the car is on the bench: the direction is held at forward, the speed fade doesn't apply, and the I-term is held at zero. That is why turning the car by hand on the bench shows the gyro correcting, which the setup wizard's gyro direction check relies on. Every arming starts from neutral and forward.

Gyro direction is set once, going forward

The reversal for reverse is automatic. If the gyro corrects the wrong way, that is a forward setting: see Car Mixer and Channels.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Drive panel Range Default drive_esc_mode ESC behaviour AUTO, FWD_BRK_REV, FWD_REV, FWD_BRK AUTO drive_wheel_diameter Tyre diameter 20-300 mm 100 motor1_gear_ratio, motor2_gear_ratio Gear ratio (shown motor : wheel) two numbers, wheel turns, motor turns 1,1 drive_gyro_min_speed Gyro starts at 10-1999, in 0.1 km/h 20 (2.0 km/h) drive_gyro_full_speed Gyro fully on at always above the start speed, up to 2000 (200 km/h) 60 (6.0 km/h) drive_gyro_reverse Gyro in reverse OFF, ON ON drive_gyro_reverse_gain Reverse gyro gain 0-100 % 50

These are global settings, not per profile. The start speed can't go below 1.0 km/h, the speed at which the direction may flip, so the correction is always faded out before the direction changes. The controller refuses a Drive panel save as a whole if a value is out of range or the full speed isn't above the start speed.

docs.title: Checking it
docs.text:
The Drive panel's Live box shows the ESC behaviour in use (never Automatic: it shows what Automatic picked), the ESC state (Neutral, Forward, Braking, Reverse), the direction, the speed and the gyro correction in percent.

For logs, set debug_mode = DRIVE and record a Blackbox log. The debug fields are: throttle command x1000, ESC state (0 neutral, 1 forward, 2 brake, 3 reverse), direction, speed x10 (km/h), speed known, correction scale x1000, motor 1 RPM, stopped.

Source: src/main/flight/drive.c in the firmware.

docs.title: GYRO OFF
docs.text:
GYRO OFF turns the steering gyro off from a switch. While it is on, the steering wheel goes straight to the steering servo: no gyro correction, and no rates or expo either. Full steering is full servo travel.

Put it on a switch you can reach while driving, on the Modes tab or in the setup wizard's Mode switches step. Use it to compare the car with and without the gyro, as a bail-out if the gyro misbehaves, and on the bench.

Normal GYRO OFF Steering Stick through the rates and expo, plus the gyro correction Raw stick, full stick = full servo travel Throttle Through the drive aids to the ESC Unchanged: still through the drive aids Steering I-term Builds up as usual Held: it doesn't build up while GYRO OFF is on
  • Only the steering is bypassed. The throttle path is the same as normal, so ABS and traction control keep working if they are on. To turn those off, use DRIVE AIDS OFF.
  • Failsafe wins. If failsafe starts, it takes over whatever the GYRO OFF switch says, so a switch left on when the link dropped can't keep driving the steering from a stale stick value.
  • Steering direction is the same as with the gyro on: the raw stick is sent with the same sign the stabilised steering uses.
  • Mixer input limits don't apply. GYRO OFF skips the min and max set on the stabilised steering input with the CLI mixer input command, so the bail-out always has the full throw. Servo Min / Max on the Servos tab still apply.
  • Because the I-term doesn't build up while GYRO OFF is on, switching the gyro back on doesn't kick the steering.

GYRO OFF is mode id 12, the id WingFlight used for PASSTHROUGH, so switch assignments carry over.

docs.title: Setting the steering throw
docs.text:
In GYRO OFF full stick is full servo travel, the same limit the stabilised steering is held to. So set the steering end points with GYRO OFF on (or with the setup wizard, which holds the steering itself):

  1. With the wheels off the ground, switch GYRO OFF on.
  2. Turn the steering wheel to full lock each way.
  3. Adjust the servo's Scale Neg / Scale Pos on the Servos tab until full lock is where you want it, and use Min / Max to keep the servo off a mechanical stop.

docs.title: The setup state
docs.text:
SETUP is not a mode you put on a switch. It is the state the controller is in while a setup tool holds the outputs on the bench: the Configurator's setup wizard, or a servo, mixer or motor override. While it lasts, arming is blocked and the Status tab shows the SETUP arming-disable flag. Nothing the tool holds is saved, and if the Configurator is closed or the cable is pulled, the controller drops it within a few seconds.

Source: src/main/flight/mixer.c in the firmware.

docs.title: Ready-to-Arm Wiggle
docs.text:
The wiggle moves the steering to tell you what the controller is doing, so you can see it without a beeper or LEDs in view. On a car only the steering moves.

Wiggle When What the steering does CLI Default Ready Nothing is blocking arming any more One full left-right sweep, a quick twitch each way, then eases back to centre wiggle_enable_ready ON Armed You arm A quick left-centre-right twitch (about 0.15 s); arming waits for it to finish wiggle_enable_armed OFF Error The ARM switch is on but arming is blocked Shakes for 0.75 s, every 3 s wiggle_enable_error OFF Fatal The ARM switch is on and arming is blocked by something that needs fixing on the bench: no gyro, CPU load, RPM filter, a reboot required, accelerometer calibration, motor protocol, DShot bitbang Pulsed shaking for 2.5 s, every 5 s wiggle_enable_fatal OFF

All of them happen only until the first arm after power-up. The error wiggles don't start during the boot grace time or while the Configurator or CLI is connected. The Status tab, or CLI status, names the flags that block arming.

Two settings shape the movement:

Setting Range Default Meaning wiggle_strength 0-100 50 How far the steering moves, % of full travel wiggle_frequency 2-50 10 Shake rate of the error and fatal wiggles, Hz

A wiggle drives the steering while the car is disarmed, so keep hands clear of the steering linkage when you power up.

Source: src/main/flight/wiggle.c and src/main/fc/core.c in the firmware.

docs.title: EdgeTX Lua Scripts
docs.text:
The Gripora Lua scripts for EdgeTX and OpenTX put the controller's settings on your transmitter. At the track you can change settings, hear what an adjustment did, and see telemetry and run statistics in widgets, without a computer. For FrSky Ethos radios, use the Ethos Lua Suite instead.

Roll and pitch

The scripts came from WingFlight's along with the firmware. The tuning pages label the steering rows Steer or Steering, and keep the roll and pitch rows and columns, marked (unused) where there is room: Gripora stabilises only the steering.

docs.title: What they install
docs.text:
• The Gripora tool (gr.lua in /SCRIPTS/TOOLS), opened from the radio's Tools menu. Its pages read settings from the controller over telemetry, let you change them, and save them back.
  • The GR Tool and GR Stats widgets, on colour radios. GR Tool shows the name of the connected car and one telemetry value of your choice, and runs the background script for you. GR Stats shows run statistics.
  • A background script (grbg.lua), optional: it sets the controller's clock from the radio (so Blackbox logs get the right time), turns on the Gripora telemetry sensors over CRSF/ELRS custom telemetry, and runs the Adjustment Teller, which says what adjustment you just made.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• EdgeTX 2.5.0 or OpenTX 2.3.12 or later. The GR Tool widget needs a colour radio running EdgeTX 2.11 or later.
  • A receiver that supports remote configuration:
    • a FrSky Smartport or F.Port receiver, or
    • a Crossfire v2.11 or newer receiver, or
    • an ELRS 2.0.1 or newer receiver. With ELRS, set the baud rate to 1.87M or higher in the radio's Hardware menu.
  • Gripora firmware. The scripts check the firmware's MSP API version when they connect and refuse one they don't support.

docs.title: Installing
docs.text:
• With the updater: the Gripora EdgeTX/OpenTX Lua Updater downloads the scripts and copies them to the radio's SD card.
  • By hand: download the latest release from GitHub and copy the contents of its SCRIPTS folder to the SCRIPTS folder on the radio's SD card, either with the radio connected by USB as a drive or with the SD card in a computer.

When it is right, gr.lua is in /SCRIPTS/TOOLS and Gripora is listed in the radio's Tools menu. The first start shows Compiling... for a while; that is normal.

To run the background script, either add the GR Tool widget to a screen (colour radios with EdgeTX 2.11 or later), or set grbg as a special or global function that runs when the model is selected (on EdgeTX, with Repeat on).

docs.title: Using the tool
docs.text: Open Gripora from the Tools menu, or put the GR Tool widget in full screen mode. Nothing is written to the controller until you choose Save: on colour radios it is the button in the top right corner, on black and white radios it is in the menu you get by long-pressing the wheel.

docs.title: Pages
docs.text:
Pages shown by default:

Page What it is for Status The current PID and rate profiles, load, the arming disabled flags and the dataflash free space (with an erase button). Rates The rates. On a car only the Steer row is used. Rate Dynamics Response time, acceleration limit and setpoint boost, and the Steering Dynamics ceiling and deadband. Only the steering values are used. PID Gains P, I, D, F and B per PID profile. On a car only the Steer row is used. PID Controller I-term relax level, I-term decay limit, error limits and the steering bandwidth and D- and B-term cutoffs. Profile - Various Throttle and Speed gain attenuation (wheel speed from motor RPM, or GPS speed), Driving Feel (master gain, I-term decay and I-term relax), gain curves and the speed range. Battery, Smart Fuel Battery profiles and the fuel estimate. Servos Servo centre, limits and direction. Mixer The Model type: Car (the car mixer preset) or Custom (a mix edited on the Mixer Inputs and Mixer Rules pages). Gyro Filters The gyro filters. Accelerometer Trim Accelerometer trim. ESC Sensor ESC telemetry settings. Drive Aids ABS, traction control and launch control for the current PID profile (see below). Drift The DRIFT mode settings for the current PID profile (see below). Model The model ID, the statistics the controller keeps (total runs, time and distance) and radio settings. Settings Which pages to show, and the background script options.

Mixer Inputs, Mixer Rules, Experimental and the ESC programming pages (AM32, BLHeli_S, Bluejay, FLYROTOR, Hobbywing Platinum V5, Scorpion Tribunus, XDFly/OMP/ZTW, YGE) are hidden until you turn them on under Settings.

docs.title: Drive Aids
docs.text:
The page has the PID profile switcher of the other profile pages, because the firmware keeps the drive aids per PID profile.

  • ABS: Mode (Off, Static, Dynamic), Trigger, Rate, Floor, Hold, Dyn rate and Dyn hold (Dynamic only), Corner rate and Corner hold.
  • Traction: Mode (Off, Ramp) and Ramp time.
  • Launch: Mode (Off, Switch), Start throttle and Ramp time.

See Drive Aids for what each setting does.

docs.title: Drift
docs.text: The settings of the DRIFT mode, with the PID profile switcher, because the firmware keeps them per PID profile: Counter gain (0-200 %), Allowed rate (0-720 °/s) and Counter limit (10-100 % of full lock). The mode itself is turned on by the DRIFT switch, set up on the Configurator's Modes tab. The page is shown by default and can be turned off under Settings. On firmware without drift mode its fields are read-only and it can't be saved.

docs.title: Adjustment Teller
docs.text:
Turn it on under Settings → Grbg Options → Adjustment Teller. It reads the adjustment function and value from telemetry:

  • S.Port/F.Port: the sensors 5110 and 5111 must be discovered.
  • CRSF/ELRS custom telemetry: include the Adjustment Function sensor.

The scripts' README also describes a CRSF setup through the FM sensor and a crsf_flight_mode_reuse CLI setting. Gripora firmware has no such setting, so use CRSF custom telemetry instead.

Some black and white radios don't have enough memory for both the Adjustment Teller and CRSF/ELRS custom telemetry; the screen then freezes at random.

More detail, including building the scripts from source, is in the scripts' README.

docs.title: Ethos Lua Suite
docs.text:
The Gripora Lua suite puts the controller's settings on your FrSky Ethos radio. At the track you can retune the steering gyro, the rates and the drive aids, change setup, read logs and check the car's status without a computer.

Screenshots predate the car names

The screenshots in this section were taken before the suite was renamed for cars, so they still show WingFlight, Flight Tuning, Flight Feel and roll, pitch and yaw rows. The text describes the suite as it is now.

The suite installs three things on the radio:

  • The Gripora app, opened from the radio's System menu. Its pages read settings from the controller over telemetry, let you change them, and save them back. See Using the app.
  • A dashboard widget for the model's home screen, showing the arming state, battery, fuel, RPM and profile at a glance. See Dashboard.
  • A background task that keeps the link to the controller and plays the callouts and alerts.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A FrSky radio running Ethos 1.6.2 or later: X10, X12, X14, X18, X20 or Twin X Lite.
