  • A receiver that carries telemetry to the radio:
    • FrSky, over S.Port or F.Port (ACCESS, ACCST, TD or TW receivers), or
    • ExpressLRS, on a module Ethos supports.
  • Gripora firmware with MSP API 33.0 or later. The suite refuses older firmware (including WingFlight firmware) when it connects.
  • A suite version that matches your firmware. Each release says which firmware it is for.

On an EdgeTX or OpenTX radio, use the EdgeTX Lua scripts instead.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
1. Installing: put the suite on the radio and turn it on for your model.
  2. Using the app: getting around, and how saving works.
  3. A tour of each part of the app:
    • Tuning: PIDs, rates, the drive aids
    • Setup: board, radio, mixer, servos, power and ESC
    • Tools and Logs: the setup wizard, profiles, diagnostics and logs
    • Settings: the suite's own options
  4. Dashboard: the home-screen widget, and its themes.

The settings themselves are the same ones the Configurator shows, so each page in the tour links to the matching Configurator page for what they do.

docs.title: Dashboard Themes
docs.text:
The dashboard widget comes with several themes. A theme decides what the dashboard shows and how it looks. Each theme has three layouts: before you arm (Before Run), while you drive (During Run) and after you disarm (After Run). The dashboard switches between them by itself.

Choose the theme under Settings → Dashboard: one theme for all three phases or a different one for each, and optionally a different theme for a particular model. Themes with their own settings have a tile under Settings → Dashboard → Settings.

Theme Own settings Screen Default Yes Any AERC Yes Any AERC Nitro Yes Any Basic Timer Any Claude Yes Any DanielRC Any Gismo Yes Any Kevd Yes 784 × 294 or larger KSE4 Any KSE5 Yes Any RF Status Yes Any RT-RC Yes Any RT-RC Nitro Yes Any SRB-RC Yes Any

docs.title: Default
docs.text:
A large voltage arc beside the run time and link quality. Before the run it also shows the model image, profiles, run count and Blackbox use.

Before runDuring runAfter run

docs.title: AERC
docs.text:
Arcs for throttle, RPM and ESC temperature, each with its maximum, under the run time and a fuel bar with pack voltage and mAh used.

Before runDuring runAfter run

docs.title: AERC Nitro
docs.text:
For nitro cars: RPM and throttle arcs either side of a segmented BEC voltage bar, with the run time on top.

Before runDuring runAfter run

docs.title: Basic Timer
docs.text:
A large run timer, with the profiles, run count and link quality below it.

Before runDuring runAfter run

docs.title: Claude
docs.text:
A voltage arc, a large fuel ring and an RPM dial, with the timer and arming state.

Before runDuring runAfter run

docs.title: DanielRC
docs.text:
A text panel in three groups (power, RPM and status, or the second motor on twin-motor cars) with the PID profile and run time.

Before runDuring runAfter run

docs.title: Gismo
docs.text:
A large battery graphic between RPM and timer on one side, and cell and pack voltage on the other.

Before runDuring runAfter run

docs.title: Kevd
docs.text:
Arcs for ESC temperature, RPM and throttle with their maximums, beside a column with the run time, fuel and arming state.

Needs a dashboard area of at least 784 × 294 pixels, so it is hidden on smaller radios such as the X18.

Before runDuring runAfter run

docs.title: KSE4
docs.text:
A tile dashboard after Kyle Stacy's KSE4: a large RPM tile beside the timer, a strip of current, voltage, ESC temperature and throttle, and a full-width fuel bar. It takes its colours from the radio's Ethos theme.

Before runDuring runAfter run

docs.title: KSE5
docs.text:
A ring dashboard after Kyle Stacy's KSE5: rings for fuel, RPM, current and ESC temperature, with the arming state, voltages and mAh used in tiles below. Its settings set the full scale of each ring. It takes its colours from the radio's Ethos theme.

Before runDuring runAfter run

docs.title: RF Status
docs.text:
Voltage and fuel arcs above the arming state, link quality, RPM and timer.

Before runDuring runAfter run

docs.title: RT-RC
docs.text:
Pack voltage and fuel arcs above the arming state, link quality, RPM and timer. Before the run it adds the model image, profiles, run count and Blackbox use.

Before runDuring runAfter run

docs.title: RT-RC Nitro
docs.text:
RT-RC for nitro cars: BEC voltage and throttle arcs in place of pack voltage and fuel.

Before runDuring runAfter run

docs.title: SRB-RC
docs.text:
A grid of tiles: arming state, BEC voltage, link, RPM, profiles, ESC temperature, current and timer above a full-width drive battery bar.

Before runDuring runAfter run

The screenshots come from the Ethos simulator, so the values are examples. The after-run screens use sample figures.

Screenshots from before the car conversion

These screenshots were taken with the WingFlight suite. Since then the themes have been changed for cars: the governor state is replaced by the arming state (or the PID profile on DanielRC), and some flight labels now read run (FLIGHT TIME is RUN TIME, for example). The layouts are otherwise as shown.

docs.title: Dashboard
docs.text: The suite includes a dashboard widget for the model's home screen. It shows the state of the car at a glance, and changes its layout for before, during and after a run.

docs.title: Adding it to a screen
docs.text: The widget is called Gripora Dashboard. On the radio, press DISP to configure the model's screens, pick a full-screen layout for the screen you want, and choose Gripora Dashboard as its widget.

docs.title: Themes
docs.text:
A theme decides what the dashboard shows and how. Each theme has three layouts: one before you arm, one while you drive, and one after you disarm, and the dashboard switches between them by itself.

Choose the theme under Settings → Dashboard: a default for all models, and optionally a different one for a particular model. Some themes have options of their own, under Settings on the same menu.

Dashboard Themes shows each theme's three layouts.

docs.title: Toolbar
docs.text:
Swipe up on the dashboard, or long-press PAGE, to open the toolbar. It closes by itself after 10 seconds, or swipe down.

Button What it does Reset Resets the run's timers and minimum and maximum values, after asking. Erase Erases the controller's blackbox log memory, after asking. Greyed out until the car is connected. Battery Picks the battery profile. Greyed out until the car is connected, or if fewer than two battery profiles are set up. Info Opens the info panel (below). Setup Opens the Gripora app. Needs Ethos 26.1 or later.

docs.title: Info panel
docs.text:
Swipe down on the dashboard, or pick Info on the toolbar, for a summary of the car's state. It stays open until you swipe up, tap the dashboard, press RTN or ENTER, or arm the car.

Shows Controller The telemetry link and its quality, the active mode, whether the car is ready to arm (and if not, why), the active profiles, BEC voltage and how full the blackbox is. Battery The active battery profile's cells and capacity, the pack voltage and the mAh used. GPS Only when the car has a GPS: the fix (No fix, Fix or Home set) and the satellite count.

A row appears once its value is known. With no car connected, both columns say Not connected.

The dashboard's alert banner and the spoken callouts are covered in Radio Callouts and Alerts.

docs.title: Tuning
docs.text:
Tuning holds the settings you change most at the track: the steering gyro's PIDs, the rates, how the car feels, drift mode and the drive aids. The pages are the same settings as the Configurator's, so each section below links to the Configurator page that explains them.

The menu has three groups: Steering (PIDs, Rates, Driving Feel, Drift), Drive Aids (ABS, Traction, Launch) and Advanced (Filters, PID Controller, PID Bandwidth, Gain Curves, Rate Response).

Gripora stabilises only the steering, so the tuning pages show only the steering values. The roll and pitch values the controller still stores are written back unchanged.

Most of these pages belong to a PID profile, shown in the title as PIDs #1 and so on. To work on another profile, switch to it (from the radio, or with Select Profile) and the page follows.

docs.title: PIDs
docs.text:
P, I, D, F and B for the steering gyro.

See Profiles.

docs.title: Rates
docs.text:
RC Rate, Rate and RC Expo for the steering, for the active rate profile (the title shows its number). They set how fast the car is asked to turn at full steering.

See Rates.

docs.title: Driving Feel
docs.text:
Steering Gain, Decay and Relax, plus the overall Throttle Gain and Speed Gain, one per line. The Speed gain follows the car's speed from the motor RPM, or from GPS without an RPM source.

See Profiles.

docs.title: Drift
docs.text:
Under the Steering group, after Driving Feel. The settings of the DRIFT mode for the current PID profile (the title shows it, such as Drift #1): Counter Gain (0-200 %, default 100), Allowed Rate (0-720 °/s, default 30) and Counter Limit (10-100 % of full lock, default 100). A note on the page reminds you that the DRIFT switch, set up on the Modes page, turns the mode on. On firmware without drift mode the fields are greyed out and nothing is saved.

See Profiles.

docs.title: ABS
docs.text:
Under the Drive Aids group. The timed ABS for the current PID profile (the title shows it, such as ABS #1): Mode (Off, Static or Dynamic), Trigger and Release Floor, then a Rate and Hold for each of Pulse, Full Brake (the values Dynamic moves towards; greyed out unless Mode is Dynamic) and At Full Lock (how the pulses change with steering lock). Each PID profile has its own settings, so a profile switch changes them with the tune.

A switch for the DRIVE AIDS OFF mode (on the Modes page) turns the drive aids off from the transmitter. ABS is also off while disarmed and in failsafe.

See Drive Aids for what each setting does and which ESC setups ABS can run on.

docs.title: Traction
docs.text:
Traction control for the current PID profile (the title reads Traction Control): Mode (Off or Ramp) and Ramp Time (50-2000 ms, default 500 ms), which is greyed out unless Mode is Ramp.

See Drive Aids.

docs.title: Launch
docs.text:
Launch control for the current PID profile (the title reads Launch Control): Mode (Off or Switch), Start Throttle (10-100 %, default 50) and Ramp Time (100-5000 ms, default 1000), greyed out unless Mode is Switch. Put the LAUNCH mode on a switch on the Modes page to stage a launch.

See Launch control.

docs.title: Filters
docs.text:
The gyro lowpass filters (type, cutoff, and dynamic range) and the notch filters. The page scrolls.

See Gyro.

docs.title: PID Controller
docs.text:
I-Term Decay Max Rate, I-Term Relax Level and the steering Error Limit. The I-term decay time itself is on Driving Feel.

See Profiles.

docs.title: PID Bandwidth
docs.text: The steering's gyro, D-term and B-term cutoff frequencies.

docs.title: Gain Curves
docs.text:
A gain curve for Steering, Throttle and Speed, and the Speed Range the speed curve covers (10-300 km/h, default 60).

See Profiles and Curves.

docs.title: Rate Response
docs.text:
How quickly the car follows the steering: Response Time, Accel Limit, Setpoint Boost Gain and Cutoff, and the Dynamic Ceiling Gain, Dynamic Deadband Gain and Dynamic Deadband Filter.

See Rates.

docs.title: 1. Download and copy to the radio
docs.text:
Use either way:

  • With the updater: the Gripora Radio Updater for Windows, macOS and Linux downloads the suite and copies it to the radio.
  • By hand: download the suite from the releases page. Each release has one zip per language, for example gripora-lua-ethos-suite-<version>-en.zip for English. Pick the release that matches your firmware version: the release notes say which firmware it is for. Then either:
    • Ethos Suite: connect the radio by USB, open Lua Development Tools, choose Install Lua Scripts, and select the zip, or
    • as a drive: connect the radio by USB as a drive, unzip the download, and copy the grsuite folder into the scripts folder on the radio. Replace the old grsuite folder if there is one.

Then unplug the radio and restart it.

docs.title: 2. Turn on the background task for your model
docs.text:
The suite does its work in a background task that each model has to turn on. On the radio, open the Model menu, go to page 3, and open Lua. Turn Gripora [Background] on.

Until it is on, every tile in the app shows Background task not running when you press it.

docs.title: 3. Check telemetry
docs.text:
The app talks to the controller over telemetry, so the radio needs a working link to the receiver:

  1. In the Model menu, RF system, make sure the RF module you drive with is turned on.
  2. Power up the car, then open Model → Telemetry and discover sensors if the list is empty.

If sensors are missing, see Telemetry for the controller side.

docs.title: 4. Open the app
docs.text:
Press SYS on the radio and go to the second page. The Gripora tile opens the app.

With the car powered and connected, every tile in the app can be opened. Without a connection, only Tools (for the radio-side diagnostics), Logs and Settings work: everything else needs the controller. Continue with Using the app.

docs.title: Updating
docs.text: Install a new release the same way. Your app settings (under Settings) are kept in a separate folder, scripts/grsuite.user, so replacing the grsuite folder does not lose them.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: Settings are the suite's own options. They are stored on the radio, not on the controller, so this menu works with the car switched off. Saving here asks before it writes, like every other page, but the settings go to the radio.

docs.title: General
docs.text:
Grouped into panels; tap a panel to open it.

Panel Settings Display How the radio's own battery is shown (Tx Battery Options), and the temperature unit. Developer Developer mode, which adds a Developer menu under Tools. You won't need it for driving. Safety Prompts Save confirm and Reload confirm: turn off to save or reload without being asked. Integration Sync model name: while the car is connected, the radio shows the name set on the controller as the model name, and puts the old name back afterwards. Battery profile on connect: asks which battery is fitted each time the car connects.

docs.title: Dashboard
docs.text:
Choose and set up the dashboard theme.

  • Themes: the default theme for all models, and optionally a different theme for this model.
  • Settings: one tile per theme, for the options that theme has.

docs.title: ActiveLook
docs.text: For ActiveLook glasses: what the glasses show before, during and after a run (Before Run, During Run and After Run). Settings turns the glasses display on and sets its position; the other three pages each pick a layout and what goes in each slot.

docs.title: Audio
docs.text: What the radio says, and when.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
Callouts and alerts, one page per kind:

Page What it covers Voltage Low battery voltage, and BEC and receiver voltage alerts, with their thresholds. ESC temp An alert when the ESC gets hotter than a threshold. Fuel Fuel (charge left) callouts, and the low-fuel warning. State callouts Arming flags, the mode, GPS fix, PID, rate and battery profile changes, and adjustments. FC status Alerts from the controller, such as the backup receiver taking over or the GPS not responding. Link An alert, and optionally a vibration, when telemetry is lost. Model callout Plays the car's name when it connects, if you have recorded it.

See Radio Callouts and Alerts for what each alert means and what to do about it.

docs.title: Switches
docs.text: Pick a switch for a value, and the radio reads that value aloud when you flip it: voltages, consumption, current, ESC temperature, RPM and more.

docs.title: Timer
docs.text: Callouts for the run timer: when it runs out, and alerts before and after.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Setup covers how the car is built and wired: the board and radio, the sensors, the mixer and servos, and power and the ESC. Each section links to the Configurator page that explains the settings.

For a first setup from the radio, use the step-by-step Setup Wizard under Tools instead. The pages here are for changing one thing later.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Car name, PID loop speed, and the features the board runs: LED strip and the ready-to-arm wiggle. There is no GPS switch: GPS runs when the GPS source matches a port (see GPS).

See Configuration and Ready-to-Arm Wiggle.

docs.title: Ports
docs.text:
What each UART is used for, and its speed.

See Serial Ports.

docs.title: Radio Config
docs.text:
Channel centre and travel, the throttle range, and the steering deadband. The throttle is signed around the centre: forward above it, brake and reverse below.

See Receiver.

docs.title: Telemetry
docs.text:
The telemetry sensors the controller sends, grouped by kind. Open a group to turn sensors on or off. Tool selects the default sensors.

See Receiver and Telemetry.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
A menu of its own:

Page What it is for More Modes Switch ranges for each mode, such as ARM, GYRO OFF, DRIVE AIDS OFF, LAUNCH and DRIFT. Pick a mode, then add or change its ranges. Modes Adjustments Adjustments from a switch or knob while driving, such as a gain knob. Adjustments Failsafe Ch. Fallback: what each channel does when the signal is lost. Stage 2: the failsafe procedure and its delays. Failsafe Beepers Which events sound the beeper, and the ESC beacon. Beepers Blackbox The logging device, rate and fields, and the log memory's status. Tool on Status erases it. Blackbox Stats Run Count, Last Run Time and Total Run Time.

docs.title: Accelerometer
docs.text: Accelerometer trim for roll and pitch. Tool calibrates the accelerometer: keep the car level and still while it does.

docs.title: Alignment
docs.text:
How the board is mounted, with a live 3D view of the car that follows the board as you move it. Tool turns the view so the rear of the car faces you.

See Configuration.

docs.title: Mixer
docs.text:
The steering Throw, Invert and Gyro Direction (Normal or Inverted). The car mix itself (steering on S1, the ESC on M1, optional rear steering and a second ESC) is set by the Setup Wizard's Model step, or in Mixer Rules.

See Mixer and Car Mixer and Channels.

docs.title: Mixer Rules
docs.text: The mixer's rules, one row each. Select a rule to edit it. The rule's Role picker offers only None: the two roles inherited from WingFlight are aircraft mixes. A rule loaded with one still shows it by name, so you can set it back to None.

docs.title: Curves
docs.text:
Mixer, gain and servo curves.

See Curves.

docs.title: Servos
docs.text:
Lists the servos in use, whether they are on a PWM output or a bus; select one to set its centre, limits and direction. Tool turns servo override on, so a servo moves to its centre as you change it. The PWM update rate isn't set here: use the Configurator's Servos tab or the wizard's Servo type step.

See Servos.

docs.title: Power
docs.text:
Page What it is for Battery Battery profiles: capacity and cell voltages. Alerts Run Time Alarm and the BEC and receiver voltage alerts. Sources Where voltage and current are measured. SmartFuel How fuel (charge left) is worked out. Preferences The ESC current limit.

See Power.

docs.title: ESC & Motors
docs.text:
Page What it is for More Motor Override Run the motor from the radio, for testing. Put the car on a stand with the wheels off the ground first. Throttle Throttle protocol, update rate and PWM endpoints. Motors Drive ESC behaviour below neutral, Tyre diameter, Gyro starts at and Gyro fully on at, Gyro in reverse and Reverse gyro gain. Motors, Drive State Telemetry ESC telemetry protocol and corrections. Motors SRXL2 ESC Shown only while the ESC telemetry protocol is SRXL2. Motors RPM Where RPM comes from, Motor 1 Gear Ratio and Motor 2 Gear Ratio (motor turns per wheel turn), and the motor pole count. Motors ESC Prog. Change your ESC's own settings from the radio, through the controller. Pick the ESC's make. ESC Programming

The controller works out the car's speed from the RPM, the gear ratios and the tyre diameter.

Each ESC page shows the ESC it found, then its settings in groups:

docs.title: Setup Wizard
docs.text:
The radio's copy of the Configurator's car Setup Wizard: the same steps in the same order, as a guided sequence for a radio screen, so a car can be set up at the track without a computer.

Wheels off the ground

Put the car on a stand with its wheels off the ground. The wizard turns the steering itself, and the ESC step runs the motor forward and in reverse. While the wizard is open the controller is in its setup state, which blocks arming.

The steps are: Sensors and level, Receiver, Servo bus, Model, Servo type, ESC, ESC telemetry, Center, Steering direction, Binding limits, Gyro direction, Trim and gain, Mode switches (ARM, GYRO OFF, DRIVE AIDS OFF, LAUNCH, DRIFT), Driving style and Finish. A checklist button in the header lists them all and jumps to any one.

What differs from the Configurator:

  • Receiver only checks steering and throttle and can set the car channel order (CH1 steering, CH2 throttle). The receiver's port and protocol can only be set in the Configurator, because the radio talks to the controller through the receiver.
  • Like the Configurator's, it works only on steering servos (the servos the mixer drives from the stabilised steering) and names them STEER, F STEER / R STEER for a pair, or STEER n for more. The Steering direction step reverses any servo that moves the wrong way.
  • Changes reach the car as you make them and are kept only once saved. Leaving the wizard with unsaved changes asks whether to Save or Discard them; closing the tool can't ask, so it leaves them on the controller, unsaved.
  • Steps whose settings need a restart (servo bus, servo type, ESC protocol, ESC telemetry, board orientation) end with Save and restart, and the wizard reopens on the same step.
  • Everything the wizard holds (overrides, the setup state, the motor run) lapses by itself if the radio is switched off or the link drops.

docs.title: Copy Profiles
docs.text: Copies one PID or rate profile over another. Pick the profile type, the source and the destination, then press Save. Copying a PID profile also copies its drive aids settings.

docs.title: Select Profile
docs.text: Switches the controller to another PID or rate profile. The tuning pages, including ABS and Traction, follow the profile you pick.

docs.title: Diagnostics
docs.text:
Read-only pages for checking the link and the controller:

Page What it shows Status Whether the radio side is working: free memory, the RF module, the MSP sensor, the connection to the controller and the API version. ELRS Telemetry Probes the ExpressLRS module and its link. It needs CRSF telemetry. FC Status The controller's arming flags, blackbox space, load, and active profiles. Rx Backup The backup receiver inputs: each backup's protocol and link, which source is active, and their channels side by side. Info Version numbers: the suite, Ethos, the firmware, and the MSP protocol.

When something doesn't work, Status and Info are the first places to look, and worth a screenshot when you ask for help.

docs.title: Logs
docs.text:
The radio logs telemetry while you drive: voltage, current, motor RPM, ESC temperature and throttle. Logs works without the car connected.

Logs are kept per model, under the name the controller reports:

Inside, runs are grouped by date, one tile per run:

Open a run to see it as a graph. The legend on the right shows each value's minimum and maximum over the run, and its value at the cursor. Drag the slider to move through the run. - and + zoom out and in; they are greyed out when the whole run already fits.

docs.title: Menus
docs.text:
The app opens on its main menu. Every menu is a grid of tiles, sorted under headings. A tile either opens another menu or a settings page.

You can use the touchscreen, or the rotary encoder: turn it to move between tiles and press it to open one. When you go back to a menu, the tile you last opened is still selected.

Tiles stay greyed out until the radio is talking to the controller. Tools, Logs and Settings are the exception: they are stored on the radio or check the radio side, so they open with the car switched off (pages under Tools that need the controller still wait for it).

docs.title: The header
docs.text:
Every screen has a header row: the page's title on the left and its buttons on the right.

Button What it does Back Goes back to the previous menu. RTN on the radio does the same. Save Writes the page to the controller. Reload Reads the page from the controller again, discarding changes you have not saved. Tool The page's own extra action, where it has one (see below).

Menus show only the Back button. On a settings page all four are there, but a button is greyed out when it can't be used. For example, Tool is grey on pages that have no extra action.

Pages that belong to a profile show its number in the title, such as PIDs #1 or ABS #1. The number follows the profile the controller is using, so if you switch profiles from the radio, the page follows.

A long title loses its leading parts to fit, for example ... / ESC temp instead of Settings / Audio / ESC temp on a small screen.

docs.title: Changing and saving settings
docs.text:
1. Open a page. The suite reads it from the controller; a Loading dialog shows while it does.
  2. Change a value: tap it, or select it with the encoder and press, then turn.
  3. Press Save. It only lights up once you have changed something.
  4. Confirm the save prompt.

The controller keeps the change for good once it is saved. If you would rather not be asked each time, turn the save and reload prompts off under Settings → General → Safety Prompts.

Saving while armed

Save is greyed out while the car is armed. If the controller refuses a save because the car armed while it was being sent, a red banner says Save not committed: your changes are kept and written as soon as you disarm.

Use Reload to throw away changes you haven't saved. It asks before it reads the page again.

docs.title: The Tool button
docs.text:
These pages have an extra action behind Tool:

Page Tool does Accelerometer Calibrates the accelerometer. Keep the car level and still. Alignment Turns the 3D view so the rear of the car faces you. Telemetry Selects the default telemetry sensors. Servos Turns servo override on or off. While it is on, a servo's centre moves as you change it, so you can trim the steering by eye. Blackbox Status Erases the onboard log memory.

Each one asks before it does anything.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
This section walks through going from a blank controller to a configured car that is ready for its first run.

  1. Install the Configurator -- either as a desktop app, or use the web version at cfg.gripora.org with no install required.
  2. Flash the firmware onto your controller.
  3. Make a first connection and confirm the sensors and receiver are working.
  4. Read Safety before you power the car with the wheels on the ground, and set up your receiver's failsafe.
  5. Set up your car: wire the receiver, steering servo and ESC, then run the Setup Wizard for the receiver, model, servos, ESC, gyro direction and mode switches.
  6. Once you have a working setup, take a backup before you start tuning.

To understand what the controller does on the car (the steering gyro in reverse and at low speed, ABS and traction control), see Driving Modes & Features.

If you get stuck at any point, the issue tracker is the place to ask for help.

docs.title: Backup & Restore
docs.text: Back up your configuration before flashing new firmware, before major tuning changes, and periodically once you have a working setup. A diff all or dump all backup includes every PID profile, so it carries your per-profile drive aids settings too.

docs.title: From the Configurator
docs.text:
The Firmware Flasher wizard has backup and restore built in, and this is the easiest route around a firmware update:

  • On the Backup step (before flashing) you can capture your settings from the connected board over the CLI. The backup type defaults to Dump (the complete configuration) rather than Diff. A Diff backup starts by replaying the board's defaults, which on current firmware can produce a spurious parse error in the CLI output, so a full dump is the more dependable choice. Diff is still selectable, and you can turn the backup off entirely.
  • The backup is held in memory and offered for restore on the Restore step once the new firmware boots, so you don't have to do anything by hand. Saving a copy to a file is optional but recommended in case something goes wrong.
  • If the board isn't currently running Gripora, the backup is still captured and saveable, but it isn't offered for automatic restore -- another firmware's settings aren't guaranteed to carry over.
  • Backup and restore need a normal serial connection; a board flashed over DFU alone can't be backed up this way. If the connection drops after the board reboots mid-restore, the wizard retries and offers a Select Port option to reconnect.

You can also save a dump/diff snapshot to a file from the CLI tab at any time.

docs.title: Via the CLI
docs.text:
The most portable backup is a CLI dump:

diff all

This prints only the settings that differ from firmware defaults -- compact, and easy to review by eye. To capture a complete configuration regardless of defaults, use:

dump all

Save the output to a text file. To restore, paste the same commands back into the CLI followed by save.

Backups from WingFlight or older snapshots

Gripora removed the aircraft features it inherited from WingFlight. A backup from WingFlight, or from an early Gripora snapshot, contains settings that no longer exist (governor_*, gps_rescue_*, angle_* and so on); the CLI reports them as unknown and skips them. Some settings groups were also reset to the car defaults (channel order, mixer, model type), so don't restore an aircraft mixer or channel map onto a car. Check the mixer, channel order and servo directions after any restore. See the CLI reference for the removed settings.

Tip

A diff all backup is the most useful format for sharing a tune with someone else or asking for tuning help, since it only shows what you've actually changed.

docs.title: Set Up Your Car
docs.text:
This page takes a controller that has been flashed and connected through to a car that is ready for its first run: wiring, then the Configurator's Setup Wizard.

Wheels off the ground

Several steps move the steering, and the ESC step runs the motor. Put the car on a stand with the wheels off the ground for the whole setup. Read Safety first.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
A basic car needs three things plugged into the controller:

What Where Notes Receiver A serial port (UART), or the board's receiver input Serial receivers (CRSF/ELRS, FBUS, F.Port, SBUS, SRXL2, Jeti EX Bus and others) go on a UART; the wizard's Receiver step sets the port and protocol. See Receivers. Steering servo Servo output S1 With rear steering, the rear servo goes on S2. Servos on an F.Bus or SBUS line plug into a serial port instead. ESC Motor output M1 A reversible car ESC: forward, brake and reverse. A second ESC goes on M2. An SRXL2 ESC goes on a serial port, not M1.

Power the servo as your board's manual describes; many car ESCs supply servo power through their BEC. If the ESC sends telemetry or has an RPM wire, connect that too: motor RPM is what lets the controller know the car's speed and direction (see Drive State).

Mount the controller firmly, flat and away from the motor where you can. The wizard finds the board orientation, so any of the usual orientations works.

docs.title: The Setup Wizard
docs.text:
Open the Wizard tab once you are connected. It asks one thing at a time, in the order the settings depend on each other, and checks each answer on the car as you go.

  • The steps are in order. Each relies on the ones before it: the Model step says which servo steers and which output is the ESC, the steering direction comes before the gyro check. You can jump to any step from the list on the left.
  • Changes reach the car straight away, so the steering moves as you adjust it. Save and continue writes them to the controller's memory and moves on. A step you did not change shows Next.
  • Some settings only take effect after a restart: a port, a protocol, the servo update rate. A step that changes one shows Save and Reboot, and the wizard reopens on the same step when the controller is back.
  • The car can't be armed while the wizard is open. The Status tab shows the SETUP flag while a setup tool holds the outputs.
  • Only steering servos. The servo steps (center, direction, binding limits) work on the servos that the mixer drives from the stabilised steering. The wizard names them STEER, or F STEER and R STEER with rear steering. A servo driven by anything else is left alone.

The same wizard is in the Ethos Lua Suite under Tools → Setup Wizard, so setup can also be done from a FrSky radio. Receiver port and protocol setup is only in the Configurator, because the radio talks to the controller through the receiver.

Step What you do 1. Sensors and level Calibrate the accelerometer, find the board orientation (place the car flat, press the button, then lift the rear by at least 20°) and set level on a level surface. Power on with the car still: the gyro calibrates itself at power-up. 2. Receiver Choose the port and protocol, then the channel order: Car (CH1 steering, CH2 throttle, as on most car radios), or Detect for any other order. Check the direction: steering full left and the trigger at full brake should move both bars to the left. Reverse a channel on the radio, not here. 3. Servo bus Optional. For servos on an F.Bus or SBUS line. See Servo bus. 4. Model Car for steering on S1 and the ESC on M1, with optional rear steering on S2 and a second ESC on M2. Custom keeps a mix built by hand on the Mixer tab. See Car Mixer and Channels. 5. Servo type Analog (50 Hz, any servo) or Digital (333 Hz, check your servo supports it). One rate for every PWM servo output. 6. ESC The ESC protocol, how your ESC reverses, a neutral check and a direction check. See ESC. 7. ESC telemetry Optional. If the ESC sends telemetry: its protocol and port, a signal check, battery voltage and current from the ESC, and the motor RPM source and pole count. 8. Center The steering is held at center. Set the servo horn and linkage so the wheels point close to straight ahead, then fine-tune the center here. 9. Steering direction The wizard turns the steering right; confirm the front wheels steer right (and the rear wheels the way you chose). Invert steering fixes it if every servo is wrong. 10. Binding limits Find how far each servo can move before the steering or linkage binds. 11. Gyro direction Overrides are off now and the gyro drives the steering. Turn the car by hand around its vertical axis: the steering should push against the movement. If it doesn't, the step can reverse the gyro for you. 12. Trim and gain Choose how you trim the steering, and put the stabilizer gain on a knob. See Radio mixes. 13. Mode switches Put ARM, and any other modes you want, on switches. Only ARM is required. GYRO OFF turns the gyro off; DRIVE AIDS OFF turns the drive aids off; LAUNCH stages a launch for launch control; DRIFT turns on drift mode. 14. Driving style Beginner (steering 90 °/s, 20 % expo), Sport (150 °/s, 30 %) or Drift (300 °/s, 60 %): how fast the car turns at full steering and how the I-term behaves while you steer. Starting points to tune from. The Drift style sets rates only; it doesn't turn on the DRIFT mode. 15. Finish A summary of what the wizard set, and the checks before the first run.

docs.title: Servo bus
docs.text:
A controller has a fixed number of servo pins. Servos on an F.Bus or SBUS line plug into a serial port instead. Servo 1 is channel 1 on the bus, servo 2 is channel 2, and so on, and a servo can be on a pin and on the bus at once. If every servo plugs into a servo pin, press Next.

  1. Port. Choose None to use the servo pins only, or a free port. On boards with a connector labelled S.BUS, that port is marked as suggested.
  2. Protocol. F.Bus or SBUS.
  3. Channels. The highest servo number the bus carries.
  4. Save and Reboot. The port is opened when the controller starts.
  5. Signal. With the bus powered, the step shows how many F.Bus servos and sensors are answering. If nothing answers, Detect wiring tries each pin of the port and both signal polarities until a device answers.

SBUS is one-way: nothing answers on it, so check it in the later steps, where each servo is moved. A bus servo listens to one channel number, set in the servo itself; for FrSky servos see FrSky Servos.

docs.title: ESC
docs.text:
Protocol. Standard PWM works with any car ESC; the ESC learns neutral and the throttle range in its own calibration. DShot150 and DShot300 are digital and need no calibration (DShot300 for BLHeli_32, BLHeli_S, Bluejay and AM32; DShot150 can't report motor RPM over bidirectional DShot). Other protocols, including SRXL2 and Castle Link, are under Other. A change ends with Save and Reboot.

How does your ESC reverse? Tell the controller what the ESC does below neutral: Automatic, Brake, then reverse (most car ESCs), Reverse directly (AM32's default bidirectional mode) or Forward and brake only. The controller follows the same rules to tell when the car is reversing; see Drive State. Not sure? With the wheels off the ground, hold forward, let go, then hold reverse straight away. If the wheels only stop, and turn backwards only after you let go and hold reverse again, choose Brake, then reverse.

Check neutral. The controller sends neutral to the ESC as the middle of the throttle range: 1500 µs with the default range of 1000-2000 µs. With PWM, calibrate the ESC with its neutral at that value, following the throttle calibration in the ESC's manual with the throttle trigger centred, or the car creeps or brakes with the trigger at centre. With the throttle trigger at centre the wheels must not turn. The car only arms with the throttle at neutral.

Check the direction. Tick The car's wheels are off the ground, then hold Forward or Reverse. The motor runs only while you hold a button, and stops within a second if the connection drops. Forward must turn the wheels forward and reverse backward (many ESCs brake first: let go and hold reverse again). If they turn the wrong way, reverse the motor direction in the ESC. With a second ESC there is a button for each.

  • SRXL2 (Spektrum Smart ESCs): throttle and telemetry share one signal wire, which goes to a serial port, not to M1. Choosing SRXL2 asks which port. See Motors.
  • Castle Link: wired like Standard PWM, on M1. Its telemetry comes back on the same wire, so no serial port is needed. See Castle ESC Telemetry.

docs.title: Radio mixes for a gain knob and mode switches
docs.text:
A knob or a switch does nothing until a mix on the radio puts it on a channel. The wizard's Detect and Assign buttons watch the channels, so without that mix they find nothing. This is the most common reason a gain knob or a mode switch "doesn't work".

Both steps show how, with Ethos as the example. On the radio:

  1. Model → Mixes: add a Free mix.
  2. Name it (GAIN, ARM and so on). Set Source to the knob or switch, and Output to a spare channel. Leave the weight at 100 %.
  3. Do the same for each control, each on its own spare channel. One 3-position switch can carry two modes.

Then in the wizard, click Detect and turn the knob from end to end, or press Assign and flick the switch to its on position. On other radios (EdgeTX, OpenTX, Jeti and so on) do the same: one mix per control, with the control as its source and a spare channel as its output.

For the steering trim the step offers A channel per trim (the steering trim on its own spare channel; the radio keeps the trim) or Trim buttons on one channel (the controller keeps the trim and saves it when you disarm), each with its own radio guide. Only the steering trim matters on a car.

Auto trim only

The Trim and gain step also offers Auto trim only, which relies on an AUTO TRIM mode. That mode has been removed from the Gripora firmware, so don't choose this option.

docs.title: Before the first run
docs.text:
The Finish step lists these checks:

  1. With the wheels off the ground, check that forward throttle drives the wheels forward and the wheels are tight.
  2. With GYRO OFF off, steer and turn the car by hand once more: the wheels follow the steering and steer against the movement. With the gyro on, steering held off centre on the bench makes the wheels creep to full lock, because the car can't turn at the rate the stick asks for. This is normal on the bench.
  3. Do a range check with your radio.

Also:

  • Set up your receiver's own failsafe to put the throttle at neutral, and check the controller's failsafe: see Safety and Failsafe.
  • Take a backup before you start tuning.
  • Everything the wizard sets can be changed later on its own tab: Receiver, Mixer, Servos, Motors, Modes and Adjustments.

docs.title: First Connection
docs.text: Once firmware is flashed, connect to the controller from the main Configurator window (not the Firmware Flasher tab).

docs.title: Connecting
docs.text:
1. Plug in the controller via USB (or connect over its configured serial link, e.g. Bluetooth).
  2. Select the correct port in the port picker at the top of the window.
  3. Click Connect.

docs.title: If the firmware version isn't recognized
docs.text: If the Configurator can't validate the firmware version or type it just connected to -- for example, very old/incompatible firmware, or a board that isn't running Gripora firmware at all -- it shows a warning dialog and falls back to CLI mode, which works independent of the normal MSP configuration protocol. This lets you back up settings or investigate over the CLI even when the full Configurator UI can't be used yet.

docs.title: What to check first
docs.text: Once connected, the Status and Sensors tabs are the first useful stops -- confirm the gyro/accelerometer are live and the receiver channels move before moving on to the Setup Wizard, which finds the board orientation and sets up the mixer, servos and ESC.

docs.title: Flashing the Firmware
docs.text: Firmware is flashed from the Configurator's Firmware Flasher tab, which walks you through the whole process as a step-by-step wizard.

docs.title: Picking a build
docs.text:
Gripora firmware is currently published as numbered development snapshots (e.g. 0.0.2) rather than stable releases, while the project is in its early stages. The Firmware Flasher lists available builds per target board, pulled from the project's build history.

Gripora builds one firmware per MCU family (a unified target, such as STM32F405 or STM32F7X2). What makes it fit your board, the pin mapping and board defaults, is a board config from gripora-targets that the flasher combines with the firmware when you pick your board.

docs.title: The flashing wizard
docs.text:
The wizard has seven steps, shown along the top. Back and Next move between them.

  1. Connect -- choose the port your board is on. If it isn't listed, add a Serial, DFU or Bluetooth device from this step. The desktop app picks up newly plugged-in devices automatically; the browser build asks for permission through its device chooser.
  2. Board -- pick your target board. Detect My Board reads it from a connected controller, or Select board manually instead if you would rather choose it yourself (or the board is in DFU mode, which can't be auto-detected). The selected board's default config is combined with the firmware at flash time.
  3. Firmware -- Load Online and Load Local sit side by side on one row: choose an online release or development build for your board, or load a .hex (and optional .config) you already have. What is loaded shows in a status panel beneath the buttons. Skipping the Board step and flashing a local file flashes it exactly as loaded, with no default config combined in.
  4. Backup -- capture your current configuration with Back Up Now before it's erased; see Before you flash.
  5. Flash -- a one-line summary of the target and version; Show details reveals the full release info and lets you save the firmware (.hex) and config (.config) files. Start the flash from here.
  6. Restore -- once the new firmware boots, the wizard offers to restore the backup taken in step 4.
  7. Finished -- shown once the restore succeeds or is skipped, or when you flashed without a backup. It says plainly that the update is complete, so you know it is safe to close the window or disconnect the board.

Flash Another Board starts the wizard over when you're done. Anyone who prefers the previous, single-page flasher can switch to it from a link on the Connect step and return with Back to wizard.

docs.title: DFU mode
docs.text:
Most Gripora boards flash over USB using STM32's built-in DFU (Device Firmware Upgrade) bootloader:

  1. Put the board into DFU mode (usually a boot button held while powering on, or a dedicated bootloader pin/jumper -- check your board's documentation).
  2. On the Connect step, select the DFU device (use Add DFU Device or Select DFU Device if it isn't listed).
  3. Choose your board and firmware version.
  4. Flash.

A DFU connection is enough to flash, but not to auto-detect the board or run the backup and restore steps -- those need a normal serial connection.

docs.title: Before you flash
docs.text:
If you're updating an existing setup rather than flashing a fresh board, back up your configuration first. The wizard's Backup step does this for you (see Backup & Restore); you can also take a CLI diff all / dump all snapshot yourself. A firmware update can change parameter layouts between versions, and having a backup makes it much easier to recover your tune afterward.

Updates can reset your configuration

Some firmware updates change how settings are stored. When the firmware finds saved settings it can't read, it discards them and starts from defaults, so some or all of your settings may be reset on first boot. Always take a backup first -- the wizard's Backup step does this -- and restore it afterward.

docs.title: If you lose communication with a board
docs.text: Power off, enable Full chip erase, jumper the BOOT pins (or hold the BOOT button), and power on -- the activity LED will not flash if that worked. Install the correct USB driver if your OS asks for one, then flash again.

docs.title: Installing the Configurator
docs.text: The Gripora Configurator is the desktop/web application used to flash firmware, set up the car, and tune how it drives.

docs.title: Web version (recommended for most users)
docs.text:
The Configurator runs directly in a Chromium-based browser (Chrome, Edge, Brave, Opera) at cfg.gripora.org -- no installation required. It uses the browser's WebSerial and WebUSB APIs to talk to your controller, so it needs:

  • A Chromium-based browser (Firefox and Safari do not support WebSerial/WebUSB)
  • A secure (HTTPS) connection, which cfg.gripora.org provides automatically

Multiple versions are available under the same domain -- master tracks the latest development build, and specific version numbers are available for anyone who needs to stay on a known-working release.

docs.title: Desktop app
docs.text: A desktop build (NW.js-based) is also available for Windows, macOS, and Linux, for anyone who prefers a native app or needs functionality not yet available in the web build. See the project's release page for download links.

docs.title: Which should I use?
docs.text: For most users, the web version is the easiest way to get started -- there's nothing to install, and it's always up to date. The desktop app exists for platform-specific needs and offline use.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
An RC car with a powerful motor can hurt you or damage itself on the bench as easily as on the track. Some simple rules:

  • Always put the car on a stand with the wheels off the ground when you set it up for the first time, flash firmware, change the mixer, servo or motor settings, or if in any doubt.
  • Never arm the car on the bench with the wheels on the ground.
  • Keep fingers, cables and clothing clear of the wheels, the drivetrain and the steering linkage while the car is powered. The steering can move on its own while disarmed (the wiggle) and while a setup tool holds it.

docs.title: Arming
docs.text:
Gripora arms from an ARM switch, set up on the Modes tab or in the setup wizard. The car only arms with the throttle at neutral (trigger at rest), not at full brake. Use the Receiver tab to check that the throttle channel reads neutral (1500 µs by default) with the trigger at rest, and that every channel reaches about 1000 and 2000 µs at the ends of travel. Adjust the end points and sub-trims on your transmitter if they don't.

If the car won't arm, the Status tab and CLI status list the flags that block it (for example THROTTLE when the trigger isn't at neutral). See also Arming and Stick Commands.

If the car is disarmed by accident while running, after it has been armed for at least 5 s (rearm_min_armed_seconds), it can be re-armed within 10 s (rearm_grace_seconds) without the throttle and attitude checks, so it can be re-armed while it is still moving.

docs.title: Failsafe
docs.text:
Configure failsafe in two places, and bench-test both before you drive:

  1. The receiver's own failsafe. Set it to put the throttle at neutral (or to send no pulses, as your receiver offers). It is the fastest and does not depend on the controller at all.
  2. The controller's failsafe, on the Failsafe tab. When the link is lost, the controller first holds the channels with the throttle at neutral for the guard time (failsafe_delay, 1.5 s by default), then runs its failsafe procedure: by default it disarms (DROP); AUTO-LAND holds failsafe_throttle (1500 µs, neutral) for failsafe_off_delay and then disarms. If the throttle had been at neutral for failsafe_throttle_low_delay (10 s by default) before the link was lost, it disarms straight away.

Once the failsafe procedure runs, the throttle to the ESC is failsafe_throttle, and the drive aids, GYRO OFF and DRIFT are ignored.

docs.title: Check the directions
docs.text:
After any change to the mixer, servo reversal, ESC direction, channel order or board orientation, check on the bench, wheels off the ground, that:

  • the steering turns the right way for the steering wheel, including GYRO OFF if you use it;
  • turning the car by hand around its vertical axis makes the steering push against the movement (the gyro direction; see Car Mixer and Channels);
  • forward throttle drives the wheels forward and the brake and reverse work as your ESC should.

docs.title: Racing
docs.text: Sensor-based driving aids, such as a steering gyro, are banned in sanctioned racing, and class rules may ban ABS and traction control too. Check the rules of your class before racing with Gripora.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
Technical reference material for Gripora:

  • CLI Command Reference -- the controller's command-line interface, used both interactively (via the CLI tab) and for backup/restore, with every setting, its range and default.
  • MSP Overview -- the MultiWii Serial Protocol used between the Configurator, the radio scripts and the firmware (API 33.0).

Pages on operating the car:

  • Arming and Stick Commands -- arming, the stick combinations for profiles and calibration, and what each arming-disable flag means.

Receivers, serial ports and telemetry:

  • Receivers -- receiver protocols and wiring, signal-loss detection and the fallback settings.
  • RSSI -- getting signal strength to the controller.
  • Spektrum Binding and FrSky SPI RX -- binding, and the built-in FrSky receiver.
  • Serial Ports -- assigning functions to ports, and passthrough.
  • Telemetry and Castle ESC Telemetry -- telemetry protocols and sensors.
  • Radio Callouts and Alerts -- what the Lua suite's spoken callouts and dashboard banners mean, and what to do about them.

Peripherals:

  • GPS Hardware and Module Setup -- wiring and configuring an optional u-blox or NMEA GPS.
  • LED Strip -- addressable LED strips, functions and colors.
  • Buzzer -- buzzer hardware and beeper sequences.
  • OLED Display -- the optional on-board status display.

docs.title: Buzzer
docs.text:
Gripora supports a buzzer, used for:

  • Low and critical battery alarms (when battery monitoring is on)
  • Arm and disarm tones, and warning beeps while armed with the throttle at neutral
  • Calibration complete
  • Beeping from a switch (the BEEPER mode) - useful for finding the car in long grass
  • Signal loss and failsafe
  • GPS fix and satellite count, when a GPS is fitted

Which events beep is set on the Beepers tab.

Three beeps shortly after power-up mean the gyro calibration has finished. Gripora calibrates the gyro at every power-up, so keep the car still until the beeps sound. If the car is moved during calibration, Gripora detects it and restarts the calibration once the car is still again, which delays the beeps. A small movement can still spoil the calibration; power-cycle the board to calibrate again.

The CLI command play_sound plays the tones: repeat it to step through them, or give it the tone's number.

docs.title: Tones
docs.text: Number Name When 0 GYRO_CALIBRATED Gyro calibration finished 1 RX_LOST Transmitter off or signal lost (repeats until the signal is back) 2 RX_LOST_LANDING Failsafe AUTO-LAND is holding the throttle (SOS) 3 DISARMING Disarming 4 ARMING Arming 5 ARMING_GPS_FIX Arming with a GPS fix 6 ARMING_GPS_NO_FIX Arming with a GPS fitted but no fix 7 BAT_CRIT_LOW Battery critically low (repeats) 8 BAT_LOW Battery getting low (repeats) 9 GPS_STATUS GPS satellite count 10 RX_SET The BEEPER switch is on 11 ACC_CALIBRATION Accelerometer calibration finished 12 ACC_CALIBRATION_FAIL Accelerometer calibration failed 13 READY_BEEP GPS fix found after power-up (once) 14 MULTI_BEEPS A count of beeps (confirmations) 15 DISARM_REPEAT Stick held in the disarm position (stick arming only) 16 ARMED Armed with the throttle at neutral (repeats until the throttle moves or the car is disarmed) 17 SYSTEM_INIT Power-up 18 ON_USB Whether the buzzer sounds while powered from USB 19 BLACKBOX_ERASE Blackbox flash erased 21-22 CAM_CONNECTION_OPEN, CAM_CONNECTION_CLOSE Camera control connection opened or closed

docs.title: Types of buzzer supported
docs.text: The buzzer is switched by a GPIO output pin on the board, so it must make its own tone when power is applied. Buzzers that need an analog or PWM signal make clicking noises or no sound at all, unless the board drives the buzzer pin with PWM (beeper_frequency).

docs.title: Connections
docs.text: Connect a supported buzzer to the buzzer pins of your board, observing polarity. See your board's documentation. On the bench, outside the car, you may need to supply 5 V and ground to the board (for example through the ESC or BEC connection) or the buzzer will not sound.

docs.title: Castle ESC Telemetry (Live Link)
docs.text:
Instead of providing telemetry on a separate serial port, Castle Creations ESCs provide telemetry on the same wire as the throttle. To use this, you must use the Castle Link software to enable Live Link on the ESC.

In addition, you must add a pull-up resistor between the throttle line and the ESC power line (or some other source of power if not using the ESC BEC). The size of this resistor must be such as to provide a logic 1 on the input port (V_Ih) but not to exceed the voltage tolerance on the port. The Castle ESC includes a 6.65Kohm pull-down, so an 8.2Kohm pull-up resistor will work for 5V-11V on a 5V tolerant pin, and up to 7.4V on a 3.3V pin.

Once this is done, enable CASTLE PWM mode with

set motor_pwm_protocol = CASTLE

The motor_pwm_rate is limited to a maximum of 100Hz when using CASTLE PWM mode.

Leave the serial ESC sensor protocol off:

set esc_sensor_protocol = OFF

ESC Telemetry will be automatically collected from the Castle ESC when the CASTLE PWM protocol is selected.

Note that some Castle ESCs do not provide current values.

docs.title: CLI Command Reference
docs.text: The CLI provides direct, text-based access to the controller, available from the CLI tab in the Configurator, or over any serial terminal at the configured baud rate.

docs.title: Common commands
docs.text: Command Description help List available commands status Show system status version Show firmware version info dump Print the full configuration (including defaults) dump all Print the full configuration for all profiles diff Print only settings that differ from defaults diff all Print changed settings across all profiles save Save changes and reboot exit Exit the CLI (without saving) defaults Reset to firmware defaults

docs.title: Backup and restore
docs.text: diff all is the preferred backup format for day-to-day use -- compact, and easy to review. Paste the saved output back into the CLI and run save to restore it. See Backup & Restore for the full workflow.

docs.title: Serial port diagnostics
docs.text:
serialdebug helps when a device on a serial port (GPS, receiver, telemetry, ESC sensor) isn't working. It shows how each port is set up, what the function on a port reports, and the raw data a port receives.

Command Description serialdebug Show every port serialdebug <port> One port in detail, with what its function reports serialdebug monitor <port> [<baud>] [<seconds>] [inverted] Print what a port receives serialdebug scan <port> [inverted] Try common baud rates and look for known protocols

<port> is the port number used by the serial command (UART1 is 0, UART7 is 6, UART10 is 9) or its name, such as UART7. serialdebug with no arguments lists the numbers, and serialdebug help prints the usage.

docs.title: All ports
docs.text:
# serialdebug
port     id  rx   tx   functions         open  baud
VCP      20  -    -    MSP               yes
UART1     0  -    -    -                 no pins
...
UART3     2  D09  D08  RX_SERIAL         yes   460800 (irq rx)
UART7     6  E07  E08  GPS               yes   57600
UART10    9  E02  E03  -                 no
...
  • rx / tx: the pins assigned with resource SERIAL_RX / SERIAL_TX.
  • open: whether the port is running. NO (in capitals) means it has a function but did not open. no pins means no pins are assigned, so the port can't be used. PIN CONFLICT means one of its pins is also used by something else, such as a servo or LED; see resource show.
  • (irq rx): the port's owner reads incoming bytes as they arrive (for example a serial receiver); monitor still works on it.

Lines starting with # point out setup problems: a port whose function did not open, a pin conflict, or a gps_provider with no matching port (for example UBLOX with no port set to GPS, so GPS is off).

docs.title: One port
docs.text:
serialdebug 6 shows UART7 in detail: its pins and functions, the baud rates configured for each function type, and if it is open, the live baud rate, direction, inversion, half duplex and how many bytes are waiting to be read. Then each function on the port that can report its state adds a block. GPS reports:

GPS: provider UBLOX, active yes
GPS: state RECEIVING_DATA, last valid message 85ms ago, at 57600 baud
GPS: bytes 91230, packets 1520, errors 0, timeouts 0, sats 11, fix yes
  • active: whether GPS was started at the last boot. GPS starts only when gps_provider matches a port (see the GPS tab). setup changed: save and reboot means the port or provider changed since the last boot.
  • state: INITIALIZING or LOST_COMMUNICATION means no valid messages are arriving. RECEIVING_DATA means the module is talking.
  • bytes / packets / errors / timeouts: everything received, valid messages, bad messages (wrong checksum, usually noise or a wrong baud rate) and times the module went silent.

The hints tell the cases apart: no bytes at all points at wiring or power, bytes without packets at the baud rate or protocol, and GPS set on more than one port means only the first one is used.

docs.title: Watching a port
docs.text:
serialdebug monitor 6 prints what UART7 receives for 5 seconds. Readable text is shown as is, other bytes as <hex>. A working NMEA GPS shows lines like $GNGGA,..., a u-blox in binary mode shows <B5>b..., a CRSF receiver shows <C8><18><16>.... If nothing arrives, check that the device's TX goes to the controller's RX pin, and check power and ground.

The baud rate defaults to the port's current rate (or its GPS baud rate if the port is closed). Give one to try another, for example serialdebug monitor 6 9600 10 listens at 9600 baud for 10 seconds (up to 60). Add inverted for a signal that is inverted, such as S.Bus; a port that is already open keeps its own setting.

docs.title: Finding the baud rate and protocol
docs.text:
serialdebug scan 6 listens for 1.5 seconds at each of 9600, 19200, 38400, 57600, 100000, 115200, 230400, 400000, 416666, 420000 and 460800 baud, and counts the NMEA, UBX, CRSF and FBUS frames it recognises at each:

   9600:   960 bytes, 100% text, 16 NMEA
  19200:   480 bytes,  41% text
...
# looks like NMEA at 9600 baud

Set the port's baud rate (or for GPS, turn on gps_auto_baud) to match. S.Bus is not recognised; use monitor with inverted for it.

Note

While monitor or scan runs the controller does nothing else, so only use them on the bench. Press any key to stop early. A port already in use (such as the GPS port) is borrowed and set back afterwards.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
set <name> = <value> changes a setting, get <name> shows its value and allowed range (get with part of a name lists every setting that matches), and save stores the changes and reboots.

The tables below list every setting in the firmware, grouped by topic.

  • Scope: global settings apply whatever profile is active. PID profile settings belong to the PID profile selected with profile <n> (0-5), rate profile settings to the one selected with rateprofile <n> (0-5): select the profile first, then set. diff all and dump all list every profile. global (hw) settings describe the board (buses, sensor orientation, pins); they normally come from the board configuration and are listed by dump hardware.
  • Default: the value on a unified target before a board configuration (gripora-targets) is applied. A board configuration can change it, and board means the value depends on the board. defaults in the CLI resets to the board's own defaults.
  • Some settings only exist when the firmware includes the feature (LED strip, SD card, a built-in SPI receiver, the F.Bus mux FPGA, a particular MCU), so get on a given board may not list all of them.

Gripora stabilises only the steering (the yaw axis). Roll and pitch keep their settings in the PID and rate profiles so backups and MSP keep their layout, but they hold zero and have no effect on a car.

docs.title: Drive state
docs.text:
How the controller tells the travel direction and speed, and how the steering gyro is faded at low speed and in reverse. See Drive State.

docs.title: Drive aids (per PID profile)
docs.text:
ABS, traction control and launch control, one set per PID profile (select it with profile <n> first; a profile switch changes them with the tune). Everything is off by default. They act only while armed, outside failsafe and with the DRIVE AIDS OFF mode off. See Drive Aids.

Setting Scope Values Default Description drive_abs_mode PID profile OFF, STATIC, DYNAMIC OFF ABS: OFF, STATIC (fixed pulses) or DYNAMIC (pulses follow brake depth) drive_abs_freq PID profile 2..33 10 ABS pulse rate, Hz drive_abs_floor PID profile 0..100 40 Brake kept while a pulse releases, % of the brake command (never below 10 % brake) drive_abs_hold PID profile 0..100 20 Full brake per pulse beyond half the pulse, ms (at most 85 % of the pulse) drive_abs_trigger PID profile 5..100 30 ABS runs past this brake command, % drive_abs_dyn_freq PID profile 2..33 15 DYNAMIC: pulse rate at full brake, Hz drive_abs_dyn_hold PID profile 0..100 0 DYNAMIC: hold at full brake, ms; 0 = off drive_abs_corner_freq PID profile 0..10 0 Pulse rate added at full steering lock, Hz; 0 = off drive_abs_corner_hold PID profile 0..100 0 Hold at full steering lock, ms; 0 = off drive_tc_mode PID profile OFF, RAMP OFF Traction control: OFF or RAMP drive_tc_ramp_time PID profile 50..2000 500 RAMP: quickest zero-to-full forward throttle, ms drive_lc_mode PID profile OFF, SWITCH OFF Launch control: OFF, or SWITCH (the LAUNCH mode stages a launch) drive_lc_throttle PID profile 10..100 50 Forward throttle allowed as a launch starts, % drive_lc_ramp_time PID profile 100..5000 1000 From the start throttle to full, ms

docs.title: Drift (per PID profile)
docs.text:
The DRIFT mode's settings, one set per PID profile (select it with profile <n> first). They act only while the DRIFT mode is on, outside failsafe and with GYRO OFF off. See DRIFT.

Setting Scope Values Default Description drift_gain PID profile 0..200 100 Counter-steer gain, %: 100 gives full lock 360 °/s past drift_allow; 0 = no counter-steer drift_allow PID profile 0..720 30 Turn rate the gyro leaves alone, °/s drift_limit PID profile 10..100 100 Most counter-steer the gyro adds, % of full lock

docs.title: Motors and ESC
docs.text:
Throttle is signed around neutral. With the defaults, 1000 µs is full brake/reverse, 1500 µs neutral and 2000 µs full forward, and every motor is bidirectional.

Neutral is the midpoint of min_throttle and max_throttle max_throttle global 50..2250 2000 ESC pulse at full forward throttle, µs min_command global 50..2250 1000 Pulse sent to a motor that is not bidirectional when stopped, µs dshot_burst global (hw) OFF, ON, AUTO OFF DShot DMA burst mode dshot_bidir global OFF, ON OFF Bidirectional DShot (RPM telemetry) dshot_bitbang global (hw) OFF, ON, AUTO AUTO DShot bit-banging dshot_bitbang_timer global (hw) AUTO, TIM1, TIM8 AUTO Timer used for DShot bit-banging use_unsynced_pwm global OFF, ON OFF Run motor PWM at its own rate instead of the loop rate. Forced on for PWM and Castle motor_pwm_protocol global PWM, ONESHOT125, ONESHOT42, MULTISHOT, RESERVED, DSHOT150, DSHOT300, DSHOT600, PROSHOT1000, CASTLE, SRXL2, DISABLED PWM ESC protocol motor_pwm_rate global 50..8000 50 Motor PWM rate, Hz motor_control_mode global array of 4 1,1,1,1 Per motor: 0 = one direction, 1 = bidirectional (forward and brake/reverse around neutral) motor_poles global array of 4 0,0,0,0 Motor pole count, for RPM from eRPM motor_rpm_lpf global array of 4 100,100,100,100 Motor RPM low-pass cutoff, Hz motor_rpm_factor global array of 4 0,0,0,0 Motor RPM correction factor motor1_gear_ratio global array of 2 1,1 Motor 1 final drive as two numbers: output (wheel) turns, then motor turns. A 10.4 : 1 final drive is 10,104 (the Configurator shows it as motor : wheel). docs.title: Arming and failsafe
docs.text:
Arming needs the throttle at neutral. See Arming and Stick Commands and the Failsafe tab.

Setting Scope Values Default Description failsafe_delay global 2..200 15 Stage 1 length before stage 2 starts, 0.1 s failsafe_off_delay global 0..200 10 AUTO-LAND: how long failsafe_throttle is held before disarming, 0.1 s failsafe_throttle global 750..2250 1500 Throttle held during AUTO-LAND, µs; 1500 is neutral failsafe_switch_mode global STAGE1, KILL, STAGE2 STAGE1 What the FAILSAFE mode switch does: stage 1, kill (disarm at once) or stage 2 failsafe_throttle_low_delay global 0..300 100 Disarm at once on signal loss if the throttle was at neutral this long, 0.1 s; 0 = off failsafe_procedure global AUTO-LAND, DROP DROP Stage 2: DROP disarms, AUTO-LAND holds failsafe_throttle for failsafe_off_delay, then disarms failsafe_recovery_delay global 0..200 10 Valid signal needed to leave failsafe, 0.1 s auto_disarm_delay global 0..60 5 Stick arming only: disarm after this long at neutral throttle, s; 0 = off gyro_cal_on_first_arm global OFF, ON OFF Recalibrate the gyro on the first arm pwr_on_arm_grace global 0..30 3 No arming for this long after power-up, s rearm_grace_seconds global 0..30 10 After a disarm while the car was running, re-arm within this time without the throttle and attitude checks, s; 0 = off rearm_min_armed_seconds global 0..30 5 The car must have been armed this long for rearm_grace_seconds to apply, s enable_stick_arming global OFF, ON OFF Arm and disarm with stick positions (no ARM switch set) enable_stick_commands global OFF, ON OFF Stick commands while disarmed (profiles, calibration, save) wiggle_strength global 0..100 50 Servo wiggle size, % wiggle_frequency global 2..50 10 Servo wiggle rate, Hz wiggle_enable_ready global OFF, ON ON Wiggle the steering when ready to arm wiggle_enable_armed global OFF, ON OFF Wiggle the steering on arming wiggle_enable_error global OFF, ON OFF Wiggle an error code when arming is refused wiggle_enable_fatal global OFF, ON OFF Wiggle on a fatal error
